News.title: When is the Budget 2026? Exact date, start time and predictions for this week’s announcement
News.content:
Next

CHANCELLOR John Healey will deliver the Budget tomorrow under pressure to ease the cost of living and shore up Britain’s stretched public services.

This will be the first Budget Healey has delivered since his appointment in July.



The statement will outline the government’s plans for taxes, public spending and economic growth.

And it could have a big impact on your wallet.



With the Iran conflict pushing up borrowing costs and energy bills, people across the country will be watching Westminster to see whether help is on the way as the Prime Minister has vowed to give households ‘breathing space’.

Here is everything you need to know about the Budget.

When is the Budget 2026?

The 2026 Autumn Budget will take place on Wednesday, October 28.

It will happen straight after Prime Minister’s Questions, with the Chancellor expected to deliver his speech in the House of Commons around 12.30pm.

While there is no time limit for the speech, previous Budget statements have usually lasted about an hour.

Alongside the statement, the independent Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) will publish its latest economic and fiscal forecasts.



It will lay out how much it expects the Budget measures to cost taxpayers and raise for the Treasury.

These forecasts will extend to the 2031/32 financial year for the first time.

The OBR’s previous forecast in March was finalised before the conflict in the Middle East escalated, which has since led to rising global energy prices and higher inflation.

What happens after the Budget announcement?

Once Healey finishes his speech, the Leader of the Opposition will give a response.

A four-day debate on the Budget proposals will then take place in the House of Commons.



But some measures, such as any announced changes to taxes on alcohol or tobacco, can take effect at 6pm on the day of the announcement if MPs agree to a provisional motion.

What are the key predictions for the announcement?

The government faces a difficult economic situation, worsened by international market turmoil and rising energy prices.

The UK’s national debt also exceeded £3trillion for the first time in September.

Because of these pressures, Healey is expected to have limited room for major spending giveaways, though easing the strain on hard-pressed households is still expected to be a major theme.

He has promised that the Budget will meet the government’s fiscal rules, which require day-to-day spending to be funded by taxes rather than borrowing by 2029/30.



The government has said it will shield ordinary workers from tax increases, but with income tax, National Insurance and VAT staying put, ministers will look to protect working families by finding cash elsewhere.

But instead of targeting working people’s wages, the Chancellor is reportedly considering increasing the tax rate banks pay on their profits to help fund cost-of-living support.

Healey has, however, ruled out increasing capital gains tax, resisting calls from within his own party to bring the levy on wealth and asset sales in line with taxes on earnings.

What might be done about household bills and fuel prices?

In a bid to bring down household bills, the Prime Minister has ordered Healey and Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh to examine scrapping standing charges on gas bills.

There are also reports that targeted help with energy bills is coming for low income households.



The government is also looking at breaking the link that lets wholesale gas set the price of electricity, a rule that currently drives up power bills across the country despite cleaner and cheaper energy generation.

And motorists facing high fuel prices will be watching to see if Healey cancels a planned fuel duty increase in January, keeping the rate frozen as it has been since 2011.

What else could be announced?

Closer to home, the focus will be on shifting resources out of Whitehall.

In a video message, Healey said: “This will be a Budget that moves money and power out of Westminster, and into every postcode around Britain.”

This devolution package is expected to include a roadmap handing mayors and local leaders direct control over a share of local taxes.



This comes alongside a major £900million drive to tackle the homelessness crisis and get vulnerable people off the streets.

High streets are also set for support, with a confirmed 20% cut to business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues starting in April 2027.

The Chancellor is expected to set out the qualifying details this week.

Elsewhere, the Chancellor has promised to fill a £4.7billion black hole in the UK’s defence investment plan, lifting defence spending to 2.7% of the economy by 2027.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Healey has also pledged to harness AI to bolster national cybersecurity and defence systems.



Finally, the Treasury’s plans to slash red tape and paperwork are expected to save British firms around £800million.

News.title: M6 closed both ways after major crash as drivers warned of ‘severe delays’ with queues of four miles
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

ROAD CARNAGE M6 closed both ways after major crash as drivers warned of ‘severe delays’ with queues of four miles







Next

A MAJOR motorway has closed in both directions, causing rush hour traffic to grind to a halt.

Both carriageways on the M6 have been closed at J20 near Warrington due to the crash.

Motorists have reported 30 minute delays and 4 miles of congestion on the approach.

Emergency services are currently at the scene, transport bosses said.





In a statement released at 5.40am, National Highways said: “The M6 northbound is closed at J20 warrington due to a collision.

“Traffic is being diverted via the exit and entry slip roads.

“There are 20 minute delays and 3 miles of congestion on the approach.”

In an update at 6.50am, they said: “The M6 northbound remains closed at J20 Warrington due to a collision.

“Southbound is now also closed within J20.”

They added that delays had increased to 30 minutes, with 4 miles of congestion on the approach.

CCTV images show long tailbacks building up in the area.

The critical junction links the motorway to the M56, which runs to Trafford, Manchester Airport and south Manchester.

News.title: Man ‘holding a gun’ spotted on city bus as cops release CCTV
News.content:
Next

COPS have released CCTV after a man with a gun was reportedly spotted on a bus.

The man was holding the gun while he was talking to two other people, police said.



Cops have released CCTV of a man in a white t-shirt and a chain necklace who they want to speak to in connection.

Nobody was hurt or threatened, police reassured.



The man was seen on the 89 bus, which travels from Nottingham city centre to Arnold, at around 4.30pm on October 9.

Detective Constable Natalie Gooderham from Nottinghamshire Police said: “As the public rightly expects, we will always treat any reported sighting of a firearm seriously.



“While nobody was hurt or threatened in this incident, we’d clearly like to establish what actually happened.

“On that note, we can now release these three images of a man we’d like to speak to urgently as part of our inquiries.

“If you’re the man in these pictures, we’d ask that you make yourself known to us, so that we can ask you a few questions.

“Likewise, if anyone recognises this person, we’d ask that you share that information with us too.”



Information can be reported to the police directly on 101, quoting incident 559 of 9 October 2026, while Crimestoppers can be contacted anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Woman ‘sexually assaulted by man who came up to her outside McDonald’s 15 minutes before second victim targeted’
News.content:
'ASSAULT' PROBE Woman ‘sexually assaulted by man who came up to her outside McDonald’s 15 minutes before second victim targeted’







Next

COPS have launched an investigation after two women were allegedly sexually assaulted just 15 minutes apart.

A woman was approached by a man outside a McDonald’s in Reading who touched her over her clothing at 8.11am on June 24, police said.

Around 15 minutes later, the same man allegedly approached another woman down the road.

She was also touched over her clothing outside Lightbox on Castle Hill.





Thames Valley Police have released a picture of a man they want to speak to in connection.

Investigating officer PC Jacques Mitchell said: “I am releasing this image of a man who may have vital information to assist our investigation into this sexual assault.

“If you recognise this man or if this is you, please get in touch.

“You can make a report online, or by calling 101, quoting reference 43260318028 for the incident on Oxford Road and reference 43260319967 for the incident on Castle Hill.

“Alternatively, for 100% anonymity, you can also call the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.”

News.title: You could be Sydney Sweeney’s neighbour… if you have £13m to splash out on private island complete with own beach
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SLICE OF PARADISE You could be Sydney Sweeney’s neighbour… if you have £13m to splash out on private island complete with own beach







Next

SYDNEY Sweeney fans have the chance to be neighbours with the stunning actress, if you have a spare £13million to splash out on a private island.

A slice of paradise in the Florida Keys has hit the market, promising the ultimate luxury escape.



Howell Key, a 10-acre island near Summerland Key, offers the perfect opportunity for off-grid living fit with a five-bedroom home.

The property comes complete with a sandy beach, helipad, pool and even a pickleball court.



And its neighbouring island is home to one of Hollywood’s hottest stars.

Sydney, 29, purchased her £9.7million Summerland Key mansion back in 2024.



The Housemaid and Euphoria actress completed her six-bedroom property with a wine room, elevator, gym and aquarium.

Howell Key has been listed by agent Lisa Ferringo of Coldwell Banker Schmitt Real Estate as ready to go – with no refurbishments needed.



The sellers bought the island in 2012 and finished construction on the 3,352 sq ft main house in 2015.

Accessible only by boat or helicopter, the island feels far removed from the mainland despite being just a five-minute ride from Summerland Key.

Off-grid features include solar power, batteries, a desalination system for drinking water, a septic system and a backup generator.



Natural light streams into the property through glass walls offering panoramic views of a beautiful sea front.

Cathedral ceilings are adorned with fans above tile floors and an open kitchen with island seating, according to the listing.

The island is being sold fully furnished, so the new owner won’t have to splash out on a single item.



“It’s 100 percent turnkey – the art, the dishes, the linens”, listing agent Lisa Ferringo told Mansion Global.

“What you see is what you get.”

And a separate guest wing accessed by a covered walkway can accommodate for friends and family flocking to marvel at the tropical views.

The wing comes with its own living room, breakfast bar and two private bedrooms.

Outside offers even more luxury with a saltwater pool, sandy beach, private dock, fire pit, outdoor kitchen and balconies for dining.



Ferringo said: “The pool is beautiful. It ranks up there with the nicest hotel pools.”

The property also sits within a rolling pasture area which the sellers previously used to keep goats and chickens.

The purchase also includes a 21ft Sea Hunter fishing boat, barge, tractor and golf cart.



But a private tropical island does come with its own challenges.

In September 2017, Hurricane Irma struck the Florida Keys as a powerful Category 4 storm.

Irma triggered severe storm surges which wiped out power in the area and destroyed more than 1,000 homes.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

To withstand powerful tropical storms the house is built about 10ft above base flood level.

The building has also been kitted out with a standing-seam metal roof and impact-rated windows and doors.

News.title: Pedestrian in his 80s dies after being hit by van in supermarket carpark
News.content:
SHOPPING HORROR Pedestrian in his 80s dies after being hit by van in supermarket carpark







Next

A MAN in his 80s has tragically died after being hit by a van in a supermarket car park.

Police were called to a Sainsbury’s car park in Knotty Ash, Liverpool, on October 10 over reports of a serious collision.

According to cops, the OAP was a pedestrian involved in a “serious” accident with an orange coloured van.

The man was taken to hospital shortly after the incident, but sadly passed away yesterday due to his injuries.





The driver of the van stopped at the scene and is helping police with ongoing enquiries.

Detective Sergeant Kurt Timpson said: “My thoughts are with the man’s family at this desperately sad time.

“We have launched an investigation and our priority is to ensure we get answers for his family and establish the facts about what happened.

“The car park was busy at the time of the collision and, while we already have some witness accounts and CCTV footage, I would ask people to cast their minds back to 10 October.

“If you saw the collision or feel you have information that may help our enquiries, please get in touch.

“Equally, if you have any additional footage, it could help us to establish exactly how this collision took place.”

Anyone with information has been asked to contact police on (0151) 777 5747, or email SCIU@merseyside.police.uk, quoting reference 26000833315.

News.title: Burnham’s Brexit bluster and toe-curling TikToks won’t fix Britain – it’s time the PM got serious about running nation
News.content:
Be serious, PM







Next

ANDY Burnham yesterday took time away from posting toe-curling TikTok videos to give his first live TV interview since entering No10.

If Britain wanted more evidence the Prime Minister is not an honest dealer, his antics over Brexit prove it.



In another masterclass in duplicity, he blamed leaving the EU for the small boats crisis. “We can’t return people,” he moaned.

This is flannel of the highest order. Even when in the bloc, the mechanism for repatriating asylum seekers to the EU was useless.



Of the tens of thousands who sneaked into the UK in the five years to 2020, the Home Office returned a pathetic 1,972. Yet we accepted 5,176 from EU states — three times more. How is that a good deal?

Meanwhile, Burnham has tied himself in knots over his desire to re-adopt the EU’s freedom of movement.



If he truly believes the public will accept unfettered migration from Europe, he totally misunderstands what people voted for in 2016.

It would be a catastrophe for getting jobless Brits into work, for wages, housing, public services and social cohesion.

Within hours of his appearance on the GMB sofa, Downing Street was frantically insisting the PM only ever wanted an “evidence-based debate” on signing up to freedom of movement, and didn’t have a firm view either way. Really?

If Burnham wants to be taken seriously, he should knuckle down to solving the ginormous deep-rooted challenges facing the nation.



Not give us more of the ill-thought-out witterings and banal socia media videos that have marked his first 100 days.

Doing his duty?

IT sounds like there may be some welcome relief for our hard-pressed readers in tomorrow’s Budget.

All the signs are that John Healey WILL freeze fuel duty and keep the 5p cut, saving workers, firms and families further pain at the pumps.

We’re pleased the Chancellor has listened to our Keep It Down campaign.

Many will argue he should have gone further — given misery for drivers at the forecourt has led to billions of pounds of extra revenue pouring into the Treasury.



Let’s see if there is anything else worth cheering in the Budget.

Sickening

HOW do the hardliners at the British Medical Association sleep at night?

NHS salaries of consultant doctors average £150,000, but in the fantasy parallel universe occupied by their hard-left union, it’s still not enough.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They want an immediate £16,000 pay rise and a 35-hour working week — and are going on strike for two days next month to try to get it from a Government they perceive to be weak.

Consultant doctors are meant to save lives, not put more in danger.

News.title: Good Samaritan dad-of-four left ‘brain dead’ after being shot in face trying to break up road rage row
News.content:
ROAD HORROR Good Samaritan dad-of-four left ‘brain dead’ after being shot in face trying to break up road rage row







Next

A GOOD Samaritan shot in the head trying to break-up a road rage row was clinging to life last night.

The dad of four pulled over in his van and tried to intervene when two motorists argued.

One then riddled the lift engineer’s vehicle with bullets as he got back into it to drive to his nearby home.

The victim, 32, who police have asked us not to name for family reasons, is said to have been shot in the face.





He is said to have a one per cent chance of surviving the shooting in Woolwich, South London.

A relative wrote on Facebook: “An innocent man at the wrong place at the wrong time.

“Family man who was on his way home from work.”

Police are still hunting the gunman who opened fire in Florence Street, near the home of the Royal Artillery, on last Thursday evening.



Officers kept details under wraps but finally issued an appeal yesterday for information about the suspect, who sped off in a dark saloon.

The victim was airlifted to hospital.

A friend said: “He is critically ill and doctors have assessed his chances of survival at just one per cent.

“His family are understandably in pieces and his children, all very young, have yet to even be told about what has happened.”

News.title: ANDY BURNHAM: 'This is just the beginning - we need to go further to earn people’s hope'
News.content:
ANDY BURNHAM: 'This is just the beginning - we need to go further to earn people’s hope'

EXCLUSIVE: Prime Minister Andy Burnham reflects on his first 100 days in office - and pledges more change that people 'can see in their lives and feel in their communities'

View 2 Images Andy Burnham said he knew his Government needs to 'go further to earn people's hope' (Image: Temilade Adelaja/Pool Reuters vi)

A hundred days ago I stood in Downing Street and promised to do things differently.

‌



‌



I promised to put decisions back into the hands of the people they affect, to tackle the problems Westminster had got too comfortable ignoring, and to make this the moment when Britain starts believing in itself again.

‌



There were plenty of people who told me all of this would be impossible. But we’re just a few months in, and together we’re proving them wrong.

‌



Already, we’ve started handing power back to our towns, cities and communities on a scale not seen in decades.

Mayors will be given more control over transport, skills and housing, a share of the income tax raised in their area, and I want areas without mayors to get new powers and funding so that no postcode is left behind. And with the creation of No10 North, we’re putting the full force of government behind those people and places too.

Andy Burnham blames Brexit for small boats crisis and 'absolutely' rules out early election READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham and his wife Marie-France on his first day as Prime Minister (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

‌



We’ve started confronting the problems that government after government has ducked. This includes building a National Care Service that treats people with the respect they deserve and bringing the country together to get people sleeping rough off the streets once and for all.

And while we’ve had one eye on those big issues, we’ve kept the other on those everyday things that make life harder than it needs to be.

‌



We’ve banned subscription traps, ended rip-off discounts and unfair parking charges, cut costs for school uniforms, capped bus fares and scrapped VAT on electricity bills.

I’m not pretending the job’s done. Not even close. I know how much pressure families across the country are still under.

Article continues below

And I know that we’ll need to go further to earn people’s hope, including in the Budget. Not with words – people have had plenty of them – but with more of that change people can see in their lives and feel in their communities.

This is just the beginning. So stick with us. Because we’ve got big plans to transform our country – and I won’t stop until people can look to the future with hope again.

News.title: Pharmacist explains 6pm problem for people using amlodipine - and symptom never to ignore
News.content:
Pharmacist explains 6pm problem for people using amlodipine - and symptom never to ignore

More than 35million prescriptions were issued for the medication which works to reduce the risk of heart attacks or strokes

View 2 Images Millions of people in the UK take amlodipine (Image: Getty)

Millions of people regularly take medication to tackle issues that affect the heart, including high blood pressure, reducing the risk of heart attacks and stroke, and also to prevent angina attacks. Figures show more than 35million prescriptions for amlodipine are issued through the NHS in the UK every year, making it one of the most frequently dispensed cardiovascular medications.

‌



‌



Pharmacist Raj R Patel has now turned to social media to explain the reason why some people taking amlodipine find themselves with swollen ankles - and what you should do if you think you might be affected. Posting as Pharmacist Health Raj, he said in a TikTok: "You put your shoes on in the morning. Come 6 o'clock, you wonder whose ankles you've come home with.

‌



"Now, if you're taking amlodipine to help with your blood pressure, that little tablet could be part of the reason." He goes on to explain the reason for the issue.

‌



View 2 Images One of the symptoms can be swollen ankles (Image: Antonio Hugo Photo via Getty Images)

Mr Patel says: "Amlodipine relaxes the blood vessels. That's what keeps the blood pressure down. Does exactly what we want, but there's a catch.

"It can also allow some fluid to leak out of tiny blood vessels into the surrounding tissues. As you're on your feet all day, that fluid can collect around your ankles, and so by the evening, your shoes feel tighter and your ankles are all puffy."

‌



He says while that might sound familiar it doesn't happen to everyone. He explains: "Swollen ankles aren't always caused by your tablets. There can be other reasons.

"If you've noticed this since starting amlodipine, don't just stop taking it. Get it checked. Sometimes just changing the dose or the medication can make a huge difference."

‌



Ensure our latest health news always appears at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings

The pharmacist answers some common questions on the subject including confirming those taking a higher dose can be more likely to suffer from the problem. He also warns of a key time when the swelling needs urgent care.

‌



He says: "Amlodipine can cause swelling, often around both ankles, but a new swollen, painful, or tender single leg needs prompt assessment because a blood clot is one possible cause." He says you should call NHS 111 for urgent advice but adds: "If leg swelling comes with sudden breathlessness or chest pain, call 999."

‌



According to the NHS swollen ankles are one of several common side effects of amlodipine. It says: "Like all medicines, amlodipine can cause side effects, although not everyone gets them. Some side effects should ease after a week or so as your body gets used to the medicine, but others can last longer."

Common side effects

The NHS lists seven common side effects that can affect people who are taking amlodipine. These include:

Article continues below

swelling in your ankles, feet and legs (oedema)

headaches, dizziness and feeling sleepy

a fast heartbeat, or feeling like your heartbeat is more noticeable (palpitations)

a red and warm face or neck (flushing)

tummy pain and feeling sick (nausea)

constipation or diarrhoea

feeling weak and tired (fatigue)

It advises: "If you feel dizzy or sleepy after taking amlodipine, do not drive, ride a bike or use machinery until you no longer have these symptoms."

News.title: Cars and police motorcycle set alight as riots break out over Bilbao right-wing event
News.content:
Cars and police motorcycle set alight as riots break out over Bilbao right-wing event

Several hooded individuals crossed containers, launched flares and set fire to parked cars and a motorcycle of the Bilbao Municipal Police, according to local media.

View 3 Images Riots broke out in response to a scheduled event hosted by right-wing activist and influencer Vito Quiles (Image: Getty Images)

At least six cars and a police motorcycle were set alight after riots broke out in the Spanish town of Bilbao. At least nine people have been arrested.

‌



‌



The "anti-fascist" riots on Monday came as a response to right-wing activist and influencer Vito Quiles. The scenes followed the peaceful protest against his event outside the University of Deusto scheduled for 7pm. The university campus was closed at 3pm after suspending all its activity at 2pm.

‌



In the morning, thousands of students marched through the centre of Bilbao in a demonstration called by the group Ikasle Antolakunde Sozialista. By the afternoon, clashes had broke out between hooded individuals and police.

‌



View 3 Images Several people set fire to cars and rubbish bins following a rally organised by various social groups against what they dubbed "fascism" (Image: Getty Images)

Several hooded individuals crossed containers, launched flares and set fire to parked cars and a motorcycle of the Bilbao Municipal Police, according to local media.

Firefighters extinguished the blazes while the Ertzaintza, a police force of the Basque Country in northern Spain, moved through the streets to disperse the participants.

‌



In a post on X shortly before the event, Mr Quiles wrote in Spanish: " I have just spoken with the head of the Ertzaintza security operation, who has warned me of a "very high" risk of incidents in Bilbao in connection with my event scheduled for 7:00 PM.

"Given that former ETA members, street-level terrorists, and other criminals are spearheading the protests, the talk is being called off," he said.

‌



View 3 Images Vito Quiles was due to have an event on Monday in Bilbao (Image: Getty Images)

Mr Quiles continued: "Freedom of expression is sacred, but it is no more important than protecting the safety of all the decent young people who attend these events—people who do not deserve to be exposed to violent situations caused by such riffraff.

Article continues below

"We will return to Bilbao—but only after we have given them the response they deserve on November 29th."

Spain will hold its general election on November 29.

News.title: Ukraine and Russia ceasefire begins after Melania Trump brokers deal for humanitarian aid
News.content:
Ukraine and Russia ceasefire begins after Melania Trump brokers deal for humanitarian aid

The ceasefire follows renewed pressure from US President Donald Trump on Ukraine to reach an agreement with Russian after Vladimir Putin invaded the country more than four years ago

View 3 Images Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since 2022 (Image: Ukrinform/Shutterstock)

A localised ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia came into effect early on Tuesday to allow a humanitarian mission led by US First Lady Melania Trump to get underway. The ceasefire began at 3am local time in the southern Ukrainian town of Oleshky.

‌



‌



It will enable aid tocould reach people in the Russian-occupied town, where around 2,000 people are stranded with dwindling supplies of food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, the UN has said.

‌



Ukrainian, Russian and US negotiators reached a deal Friday to provide humanitarian relief to Oleshky. The US president's wife, who worked with officials from both countries on a separate matter, initiated talks about the town after learning about the situation at one of her events during the UN General Assembly session in September.

‌



View 3 Images Donald and Melania Trump (Image: AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

The ceasefire follows renewed pressure from US President Donald Trump on his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy to reach an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war, which has gone on for more than four years.

A White House statement quoted Mrs Trump as saying that Oleshky was "on the brink of disaster". She also said its remaining population, mainly elderly residents, was in urgent need of medical attention, medicine, food and clean water.

‌



"The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks," she said.

"It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."

‌



Ukrainian media has featured interviews with those escaped the town and spoke to relatives that remain.

View 3 Images Melania Trump became aware of the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky in September 2026 (Image: AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein)

‌



Some said the town was nearing starvation and residents were relying on homegrown produce to survive, with others reportedly resorting to eating grass.

Both Russia and Ukraine have blamed one another for the dire situation.

‌



Ukraine has accused Russian forces of mining nearby roads and using the remaining residents as human shields to prevent the army from conducting offensive operations in the town.

Russia has blamed Ukraine for "laying siege to the town" with drone strikes and preventing humanitarian aid from getting in.

Article continues below

In September, the Kremlin acknowledged issued with food and medical supplies getting into the town. At the time, it said its military was working to resolve them.

News.title: Heckler slams Donald Trump during rally speech over White House ballroom as President yells 'oh, go home'
News.content:
Heckler slams Donald Trump during rally speech over White House ballroom as President yells 'oh, go home'

The United States President immediately branded the heckler a 'paid protester', before crowds booed and chanted 'USA! USA!', and the heckler was thrown out

View 2 Images Two security officers had to escort a heckler shouting about the $400 million White House ballroom during a rally Monday evening

A heckler at President Donald Trump's midterm rally was escorted out by security after shouting about the White House ballroom and interrupting Trump's speech on Monday evening.

‌



‌



The protester began shouting about the White House ballroom before being escorted away by two security guards, the Mirror US reports, shown in live footage from the rally in Mississippi.

‌



The ballroom is among several renovation projects that the real estate mogul and former reality TV star has embarked on during his second term, sparking major backlash across the political spectrum for overhauling the historic landmark of the White House.

‌



View 2 Images President Donald Trump (Image: AFP/Getty Images)

Trump, 80, immediately branded the heckler a "paid protestor" given $250 by billionaire George Soros to disrupt the event, without any evidence.

The president then told the heckler repeatedly, "oh, go home", as he faced the disruption during his speech in the southern state.

‌



"They think it's Soros. And they ruin their lives. They get booked. We don't usually press it that hard. It's terrible," Trump continued.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Live footage from the rally shows two security officers walking the man, dressed in a red hoodie, out of the venue as the animated crowd "boo'd" and chanted "USA! USA! USA!" while throwing thumbs down in his face as he left the rally.

"I was just at the punchline, too!" Trump added, after an attendee could be heard shouting, "We love you!"

‌



The Trump-led $400 million ballroom project required the demolition of the century-old East Wing of the White House in October 2025, a move that enraged some Americans.

"President Trump is a builder at heart and has an extraordinary eye for detail.

‌



"The President and the Trump White House are fully committed to working with the appropriate organisations to preserving the special history of the White House while building a beautiful ballroom that can be enjoyed by future Administrations and generations of Americans to come," said White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

The incident occurred at one of the many rallies Trump has attended to boost Republican candidates in the final crunch before the midterm election on Tuesday, November 3.

‌



Some of the rallies have been in historically red states that are in danger of flipping in what is expected to be a bloodbath for Republicans.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Article continues below

Trump was stumping for incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) ahead of his race with Democratic nominee Scott Colom, an African-American district attorney, for the historically Republican Senate seat.

Mississippi has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.

News.title: Met Office issues new yellow weather warning - full list of 50 areas impacted today
News.content:
Met Office issues new yellow weather warning - full list of 50 areas impacted today

Fresh weather warnings have been issued by the Met Office after the UK was battered by Storm Austen and Storm Boelo

View 3 Images Further weather warnings have been issued across the UK (Image: Getty Images)

Fresh weather warnings have been issued as the UK is braced for more strong winds and heavy rain after storms caused major disruption over the weekend.

‌



‌



Original weather warnings for Tuesday have been extended. The Met Office has put two yellow wind warnings in place for western areas of England and parts of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland on Monday evening into Tuesday, with the potential for ongoing disruption.

‌



As conditions appeared to slightly calm on Monday, recovery efforts were underway after Storm Boelo battered parts of the north and brought 84mph gusts and a third of a month’s rain to some areas in Scotland. The fresh weather warnings are likely to halt this recovery.

‌



View 3 Images The warnings come as recovery work was underway on Monday (Image: Alasdair MacLeod/Ayrshire Post)

The warning in place from 6pm Monday until 3am Tuesday covers parts of north-west England, Northern Ireland, south-west England, Strathclyde, south-west Scotland and Wales.

It forecasts gusts of 45-50mph inland and 60-65mph along exposed coasts and over high ground. These strong winds could be accompanied by heavy rain, with disruption expected in the early hours of Tuesday.

‌



Another yellow Met Office warning for strong winds and potentially damaging gusts is in place from 3am on Tuesday until midnight for most of Scotland and the far north-east of Northern Ireland.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



On Tuesday, early rain is to clear eastern and south-eastern England, while heavier rain in the north west of Scotland will gradually turn to showers, the forecaster said.

The strongest winds will continue to affect Scotland, particularly in the far north and north west where gusts in excess of 70mph are possible.

‌



The Hebrides are most likely to experience the strongest winds which could potentially last several hours. Elsewhere, there will be sunny spells and showers will continue, with some heavy rain in western areas.

View 3 Images The fresh weather warnings have been updated with heavy winds expected to continue to batter the nation

From Wednesday the forecaster says that conditions will begin to settle, as high pressure increasingly begins to influence the UK.

This will bring lighter winds and drier weather across much of the UK on Wednesday evening and Thursday, though western areas may remain breezy and experience a few light showers.

‌



Mist and fog could be dense and slow to clear, leaving some areas chilly and grey, while brighter spells elsewhere will allow temperatures to rise into the teens.

Although conditions are expected to be much calmer over the weekend, there still remains a chance of rain affecting northern Britain on Saturday and into the night.

‌



Greg Dewhurst, senior operational meteorologist at the Met Office, told the Press Association: “Most will have a day of sunny spells and blustery showers on Tuesday, showers heaviest and most frequent in the north.

“Thereafter for the week ahead we see a change in the weather. High pressure will build from the south over the coming days so generally settling down but potentially bringing some overnight fog at times. This high pressure looks set to remain over the UK for the weekend too. So most places dry, though perhaps some patchy rain in the north at times.

“Temperatures by day will be near or a little above average reaching around 12-16C, though perhaps some chillier nights are possible by the end of the week as high pressure builds in.”

News.title: Ex-FBI director James Comey 'facing criminal charges' over 'sensitive' data leaks
News.content:
Ex-FBI director James Comey 'facing criminal charges' over 'sensitive' data leaks

These latest counts mark the third time the United States Department of Justice has pursued legal action against President Barack Obama's FBI director since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term in office

View 3 Images Former FBI director James Comey (Image: AP)

Former FBI Director James Comey has been charged for allegedly leaking sensitive national defence information, according to reports.

‌



‌



The former FBI director was charged on Monday with two counts for the alleged leak of sensitive information to the New York Times, the New York Post reports.

‌



These latest counts mark the third time the Department of Justice has pursued legal action against Mr Comey since the beginning of President Donald Trump's second term in office.

‌



View 3 Images James Comey was fired by Donald Trump (Image: AP Photo/Andrew Harnik)

Prosecutors accuse Mr Comey of “knowingly and wittingly” transmitting national defence information as well as conspiring to do so in a “criminal information” filing made in the US District Court for the District of Columbia.

The allegations cover a period from October 4 to 5, 2016.

‌



Mr Comey “through one and more co-conspirators directed Individual #1 to disclose national defence information to a reporter for a national news publication” in violation of federal law, according to prosecutors.

‌



The new charges stem from an article in the New York Times on October 5, 2016, headlined “Yahoo Said to Have Aided U.S. Email Surveillance by Adapting Spam Filter,” written by reporter Charlie Savage.

“The United States’ investigation has uncovered evidence that former FBI Director, James B. Comey, sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before,” Special Assistant US Attorney Dustin Farahnak wrote in a filing, according to NBC News.

‌



“The investigation has uncovered evidence that Mr Comey directed staff to speak to Mr Savage about specific accuracy concerns related to the Reuters article, and thereby illegally transferred classified information.”

The alleged sharing of information happened while Mr Comey was head of the FBI under President Barack Obama.

‌



View 3 Images Former FBI James Comey (Image: Screenshot / Truth Social / MSNBC)

Mr Comey was dismissed by President Trump in May 2017.

‌



“Well, they’re back, again,” Comey said in a video posted on his Substack, reported by the New York Post. “It would almost be funny if it wasn’t such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice, one that we cannot become numb to.”

“Nothing’s changed with me,” the former FBI chief added. “I’m still innocent, and I’m still not afraid of these people and I still believe in the independent judiciary.”

‌



The case was filed under seal by the United States Department of Justice on October 5, 2026, and made public after Mr Comey’s lawyers filed a motion to unseal it.

The former FBI director's attorneys have also asked the court to dismiss the case.

‌



A Justice Department spokesperson told The New York Post that the Department of Justice “filed a waiverless criminal information to toll the statute of limitations as it relates to allegations concerning former FBI Director Comey.”

“Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals,” the spokesperson continued.

‌



“This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further.”

The new charges against Mr Comey surfaced on the same day a US district judge ruled that the former FBI director’s daughter, Maurene Comey, was illegally fired from the US Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York last year, reports add.

‌



The judge ordered the Trump administration to reinstate Maurene Comey and provide her with back pay.

James Comey was indicted by a federal grand jury last September on charges of making false statements and obstruction of justice. The case was dismissed after a judge ruled Lindsey Halligan, then US attorney for the Eastern District of Virginia, was unlawfully appointed.

Article continues below

The former FBI director was indicted again in April on charges of threatening to kill Trump in May 2025 when he posted a photograph on Instagram of seashells arranged to read “8647.”

Mr Comey is still awaiting trial in the seashell case.

News.title: Murderer slips through fence and escapes Tennessee prison as public warned 'do not approach'
News.content:
Murderer slips through fence and escapes Tennessee prison as public warned 'do not approach'

Officials have not explained how Jacob Morley escaped from prison - but warned the public not to approach him and call the police immediately if they spot the murderer

View 2 Images Jacob Morley is a wanted man after escaping from prison in Tennessee (Image: Tennessee Department of Corrections via AP)

A murderer serving a life sentence for killing a colleague four years ago has escaped from prison by slipping through a fence, authorities have confirmed.

‌



‌



Prison bosses realised Jacob Morley, 28, was unaccounted for at around 11:30pm on Sunday, October 25. He was being held at the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee. A statement from the Department of Corrections (TDOC) said: " Morley has been added to the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation’s Most Wanted list, and a reward of up to $2,500 is available for information leading to his arrest.

‌



"Residents in the area are asked to check home security and doorbell cameras, trail and hunting cameras, and other surveillance systems for possible sightings or activity. Anyone who sees Morley or has information about his whereabouts should not approach him. Call 911 immediately or contact TBI at 1-800-TBI-FIND."

‌



View 2 Images The Northwest Correctional Complex (NWCX), located in Tiptonville, Tennessee

Christa Pike's attorney issues new health update weeks after botched execution READ MORE :

Investigators looked at security cameras and saw Morley escaped while wearing his prison uniform, officials said. They did not release any other details, including how Morley got through the fence.

‌



Prison officials said law enforcement throughout the area has searched buildings and other structures near the prison about 90 miles (145 kilometers) north of Memphis in an isolated, rural area of flat land tucked near a bend in the Mississippi River near Missouri. They added 'aviation assets' have been deployed to assist with the search.

Morley is 5-foot-11 (1.8 meters) and 240 pounds (109 kilograms). He has brown hair and green eyes. Morley was sentenced to life for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield’s body was found in a box under Morley’s Carter County home after he had been missing for a few weeks.

‌



Along with first-degree murder, Morley was also convicted of aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. When Morley saw deputies at his home in 2022, he led police on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said.

Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate murders, assaults against staff and inmates and other violence.

Article continues below

News of Morley's escape is the latest scandal to hit the Tennessee prisons system. The state government is reeling after the failed execution of Christa Pike, who was held in another TDOC facility, last month.

Pike, also a convicted murderer, survived two lethal injections and was rushed to hospital. She is now said to be talking in full sentences. Following the incident, TDOC Commissioner Frank Strada resigned, a decision he said is "in the best interests" of the state.

News.title: Israel heads to polls for pivotal election defined by security and democracy
News.content:
Israelis are heading to the polls for what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.

An unprecedented 70,000 people have reportedly flown home from abroad to vote, while half a million are set to cast ballots for the first time.

Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.

But neither of their political blocs are projected to win the 61 seats needed to form a majority government - meaning weeks or months of political wrangling may lie ahead.

Israel's proportional representation system means governments have always been coalitions - and the race to power can, and has, produced unexpected alliances. But this election looks especially tight - and lines in the sand have already been drawn.

Eisenkot, who leads the newly formed Yashar Party, is the main figure in the so-called "change bloc", a collection of parties who have ideological differences but share the goal of ousting Netanyahu.

Other leaders in the bloc include former prime minister Naftali Bennett and Avigdor Lieberman - both right-wingers who take hardline positions on security - and Yair Golan, a left-leaning former general.

For Netanyahu, a titan of Israeli politics who first served as prime minister in 1996, a return to power will hinge on another alliance with the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties that make up his current governing coalition - the most right-wing in Israel's history.

News.title: Chancellor to cut tariffs on some staple goods to offer cost of living help
News.content:
John Healey is removing import taxes on marmalade, gherkins and more than 100 products ahead of the Budget in a move aimed at giving families "breathing space" with the cost of living.

The move is the latest by the government to try to ease cost of living pressures on households.

The measures also include an end to the so-called cliff-edge for those receiving carer's allowance payments and higher tax-free mileage rates being made permanent.

But the Conservatives said the offer of "cheaper gherkins" was "an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises".

Ahead of the Budget, the government said it would remove tariffs on more than 100 "family favourite" products, while supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser costs and households reliant on heating oil.

These include:

Garlic

Gherkins

Chocolate-coated wafers and waffles

Boiled sweets

Toffees, caramels and similar sweets

Citrus jams, marmalades and pastes

Throat pastilles and cough drops

Plant-based drinks including soya, nut, cereal or seed

Kerosene

Fertilisers

The government said getting rid of the tariffs could save households up to Â£21 per year when combined with existing tariff suspensions that were introduced in June and applied to products including pasta, fruit juice and tuna.

Marmalade, for example, will see a 20% tariff, plus an additional Â£19 charge per 100kg imported, suspended.

Healey said that the ongoing wars in Iran and Ukraine had "hit families here at home through higher everyday costs".

"We can't control global events, but we can act where we can make a difference," he added.

Other measures the government announced include:

Making permanent a 55p per mile tax-free mileage rate for those driving up to 10,000 miles for work, with the rate rising from 25p per mile to 35p above that

Allowing carers to earn more than an existing earnings limit without losing their entire allowance, replacing it with a taper mechanism instead

Giving two weeks of paternity pay to self-employed fathers, who have previously missed out on payments of up to Â£194 a week for the period

And rolling out hundreds of additional Post Office drop boxes to make sending parcels easier

The government will also freeze fuel duty again in the Budget, the BBC understands.

As first reported in The Sun, the 5p duty discount is also set to continue. That discount was first introduced in 2022, and was due to last 12 months, but has been extended ever since.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn't mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren't fair.

But the Conservatives said Burnham's "everyday fixes" have already been wiped out by higher borrowing costs, taxes and inflation.

Shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "Shoppers face rising costs at the till and families are struggling to make ends meet, but Burnham's plan is cheaper gherkins. This is an insult to families hammered by Labour's tax rises."

News.title: Kane ends England’s 25-year wait to win men’s Ballon d’Or award
News.content:
Harry Kane has become the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001 after being crowned the world's best player at a ceremony in London.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker is the fifth Englishman to win in total, with Stanley Matthews (1956), Bobby Charlton (1966) and Kevin Keegan (1978 and 1979) the others.

Denis Law of Scotland (1964) and Northern Ireland's George Best (1968) are the other winners from the United Kingdom.

Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second, while Barcelona and Spain attacker Lamine Yamal completed the top three.

"Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane told Dazn.

"I had to go through many ups and downs, especially early in my career. I was never the person that people thought was going to be the superstar like some of the guys now.

"I had to bide my time and work hard, a lot of times it was me against my own mind and I had to come through it, I had to show self-belief, determination.

"I think that grounded me even when I did make it at the highest level to keep improving and keep getting better."

England manager Thomas Tuchel said he was "delighted" to see Kane win the award as he hailed the forward's success as a "huge honour".

Prince William, meanwhile, said the former Tottenham Hotspur player was a "brilliant captain" and "remarkable player".

Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches last season, the most a Bayern player has ever struck in one campaign. Including England matches, it was 73 goals - plus eight assists - in 65 matches.

Only one player at a club in Europe's top five leagues has ever scored more goals in a season.

But he wins it despite not lifting either of football's biggest prizes last season, having lost in both the World Cup and Champions League semi-finals.

Remarkably the Three Lions captain becomes the first Bayern player to win the Ballon d'Or since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981.

To celebrate Kane's success, the Wembley arches were lit up in gold on Monday night.

BBC Sport looks at why Kane won it and how unusual it is to do so without securing one of those major trophies.

News.title: Storm Boelo leaves thousands without power as Met Office issues new wind warning
News.content:
A clean-up operation is under way in parts of the UK after Storm Boelo caused flooding and property damage, leaving thousands without power.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said around 22,600 properties were still without power.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.

A yellow warning for strong winds came in effect on Monday evening across the west coast of England, Wales and Scotland and eastern parts of Northern Ireland and expired on Tuesday morning.

The Met Office has warned about the possibility of further power cuts and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," he told the BBC.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

News.title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
News.content:
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.

The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.

The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.

Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.

The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.

"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.

"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."

News.title: Truce begins in wartorn Ukraine city after it was announced by Melania Trump
News.content:
Ukraine's parliament commissioner for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, confirmed in a social media post that the ceasefire had begun.

"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honouring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.

Oleshky was seized by Russia during the first days of its full-scale invasion in February 2022.

Residents were trapped with scarce food between Ukrainian positions across the Dnipro River and Russian forces to the east.

The city was home to 24,000 people before the war. Now Ukraine estimates that some 6,000 people remain in the city and its surrounding areas, including 200 children.

The White House said last week that Melania Trump had secured the ceasefire in Oleshky.

"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," she said in a press release.

While the US first lady is relatively lower profile than some of her predecessors - and only occasionally seen at White House events - she has become involved in addressing humanitarian issues stemming from the Russia-Ukraine war.

In August 2025, she penned a letter to Putin, telling him it was "time to protect children and future generations worldwide".

News.title: Apple says it will replace iPhone Duo handsets with screen problems
News.content:
Apple says it will replace iPhone Duo handsets that have developed problems with their screens just days after the highly-anticipated smartphone went on sale.

Photos posted on social media show lines that appeared on the screens of the technology giant's first ever foldable device, which has a starting price of Â£1,999 ($2,668) in the UK.

Apple said it is aware of "an issue impacting the inner display on a small number" of the phones and urged affected users to contact the company for a replacement.

The Duo's launch, which attracted crowds at Apple stores around the world last week, comes as the brand tries to reinvigorate its range of devices and challenge the foldable phones made by rivals.

Some Duo owners also posted photos online showing cracks along the screen's centre crease, while others reported a crunching noise when opening the device.

An iPhone Duo user, Justin Lokos, posted an image of a device with lines across the right side of the display and later uploaded a picture of a new handset alongside the broken one, thanking an Apple store in New York for its help.

The extent of the issue remains unclear. Apple did not say how many devices were affected, while some images showing faulty devices may have been created using artificial intelligence.

The Duo's 7.6-inch (19.3cm) inner display is held together by a central hinge - a complex piece of engineering that has resulted in similar flaws in folding devices made by some of Apple's competitors.

Samsung's first foldable phone, the Galaxy Fold, suffered an early setback in 2019 when reviewers reported broken screens on the devices.

News.title: Will the public change its mind about Meghan?
News.content:
Meghan, who recently moved back to the UK with Prince Harry and their children, has frequently been accused of cutting off those once close to her.

Her treatment of her father was seen as a prime example.

"She ditched her family, ditched her dad, ditched most of her old friends, split Harry from William," wrote one commentator in 2020.

"Get on a plane and go see the poor man before it's too late," she was told on social media about her father.

All of that might need to be viewed in a different and more sympathetic light.

By 2019, Meghan had received disturbing allegations about Thomas Markle, in a letter from her father's first wife, Roslyn Loveless.

She says it is why she kept her distance and also why she didn't bring her children to him, including when she moved to the United States with her family.

That letter was shared with Meghan by the police, at a time when she was classified as a working royal. It's not clear who else knew about the letter, including Palace officials, but it must have been a sensitive matter for her.

And according to the Sussexes' spokesman, Meghan believed an investigation into the allegations was going ahead, presumably at a time when she was on official trips and having to put on a brave face.

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham faces crunch decisions and tricky trade-offs in his next 100 days
News.content:
Last week, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh approved drilling in the Jackdaw field in the North Sea, about 150 miles east of Aberdeen.

This is principally a gas field and Fahnbulleh grounded her justification in providing the UK with greater energy security, at a time of war in Ukraine and in the Middle East.

The gas, she said, could be tapped into and serve British homes and businesses pretty much straight away, with the tax revenue put into an "energy wealth fund", with the aim being to invest in renewable and low carbon energy projects.

But what about the Rosebank field, 80 miles north west of the Shetland islands, with its focus on oil?

Labour figures in and outside government acknowledge this is a much, much harder sell to plenty in their own party and beyond. Some, who want to see the project go ahead, fear that the energy secretary is not likely to be convinced that it should.

It is in that context that we should see allies of the chancellor pointedly making it known that he is in favour of it.

His public language was quite telling on the day Jackdaw was approved, when he was talking about the Energy Wealth Fund: "It means the extra tax revenues that come from North Sea oil and gas can be directed into developing more clean energy projects for the future."

Note his reference to oil. Fahnbulleh said that Rosebank was "a different proposition" to Jackdaw.

Can those who worry, in particular, about the emissions from a new oil field, be won over by an argument grounded in this being a geopolitically pragmatic and environmentally credible part of transition to cleaner fuels?

Some Labour MPs hope so, but they know it's a tall order to persuade some, including some in government â which could, if it was approved, raise the question of ministerial resignations. Let's see.

News.title: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
News.content:
Busted star James Bourne has said his brother "saved my life" by donating a kidney, after doctors had given him "a few years left to live".

The guitarist, 43, dropped out of an arena tour featuring his band and fellow punk-pop favourites McFly in September 2025, just a day before it began.

He blamed health problems and was replaced by his younger brother Chris.

James later said he needed major surgery to "extend my life", and has now thanked his "hero" Chris and said they are both recovering from their transplant operations.

News.title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.

The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.

Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.

The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.

"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.

Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.

In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.

Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.

It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder.

Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.

It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.

The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.

The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.

The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."

"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.

"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.

"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.

The review is due to report in five months.

News.title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
News.content:
Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.

Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".

But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.

He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."

"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.

"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."

She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

News.title: Army officer killed by reversing Warrior with faulty alarm - inquest
News.content:
The armoured vehicle was stationary for between 38 and 43 seconds after the collision, the inquest heard, as soldiers shouted "wait" and horns sounded.

A stop call was sent at 10:25, which halted the exercise.

A built-in alarm system, which would have sounded a noise and shown a light to indicate the rear doors were open, did not work as a wire was broken, the inquest was told.

Col Watson said: "The built-in alarm would have alarmed because the rear doors were open, and had that gone off the driver would have almost certainly stopped."

Alarms had been installed on Warriors after two fatal incidents in the 1990s.

Col Watson said several faults with the armoured vehicles were known about, but he told the inquest that these had not meant the vehicle should have been taken out of service.

The inquest also heard the FV-511model involved in the incident was not ordinarily used for disembarking troops and close combat.

"The student commander had done the majority of his training on the FV-510, which is the platoon variant of the vehicle," Col Watson said.

"In general, the crew and service personnel within 5 Rifles were not that familiar with the FV-511 and its differences with the FV-510."

News.title: Drivers who killed mum and girl while racing jailed
News.content:
Two men who killed a mother and her four-year-old daughter as they raced their high-performance cars along a Leeds city centre road have been jailed.

Justyna Hulboj, 27, and her daughter Lena Czepczor were killed when they were hit by an Audi TT RS as they walked to the girl's nursery on the A61 Scott Hall Road on 16 January 2023.

At Leeds Crown Court on Monday, Hardeep Bhachu, 29, was jailed for 12 years and Jasskamal Riyat, 37, for 16 years.

Sentencing the men, Judge Singh said the road was "not a race track" and told them the deaths had consequences that were "immeasurable", with an "immense" impact on those left behind.

Bhachu, of Grant Row in Adel, had earlier admitted two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, while Riyat, of Buckstone Avenue in Moortown, was convicted by a jury after denying he had been racing him.

The court heard the pair, who did not previously know each other, accelerated away from traffic lights on Scott Hall Road shortly before the crash.

Prosecutors said Riyat's BMW reached speeds of up to 89mph in the 40mph zone before Bhachu lost control of his Audi, mounted the pavement and struck Hulboj and her daughter.

News.title: DUP MLA joins Lockhart's call for O'Neill's removal as first minister
News.content:
A Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) assembly member has joined MP colleague Carla Lockhart's calls for Stormont's First Minister Michelle O'Neill to be "removed from office".

Diane Forsythe said "profound consequences" pledged over the Sinn FÃ©in vice-president's handling of the Drumcree parading dispute "must be honoured".

Lockhart last week stepped down from the DUP's officer board in response to party leader Gavin Robinson not removing their deputy first minister to force O'Neill from the joint office.

It follows unionist anger over the first minister's involvement in protests on the Garvaghy Road, which blocked a contentious Orange Order parade from passing along the mainly nationalist street in Portadown, County Armagh.

O'Neill and several other senior Sinn FÃ©in figures have been interviewed by police investigating the demonstrations, with unionists accusing the party of acting unlawfully.

The Sinn FÃ©in deputy leader has defended her attendance at the demonstrations last month, saying she would "continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents".

The political row has sparked differences of opinion over how to respond within the DUP, which shares power with Sinn FÃ©in in Stormont's devolved government.

Forsythe is an assembly member for the South Down constituency and part of the DUP's party officer team.

In a post on Facebook on Monday night, Forsythe said she was "pleased" to show her support for Upper Bann MP Lockhart at a recent rally in Portadown.

She accused Sinn FÃ©in of "arrogance" and described the feelings of anger in the unionist community over O'Neill's actions as "immense".

"There have been commitments made to deliver profound consequences and that it cannot be business as usual. These must be honoured," she added.

"It is my view that Michelle O'Neill should be removed from office. The assembly and other ministerial offices would continue until the next election."

Forsythe added that in the absence of such "meaningful action", official engagements as first minister through the joint Executive Office should be stopped immediately as a "bare minimum".

Last week Robinson said he was "sorry" to see Lockhart quit the DUP's officer board but added that she remained "a key part of our team".

Speaking on the BBC's The View programme, the DUP leader said the party had reached a democratic decision on how to deal with the Drumcree fallout.

He questioned whether it was necessary to "punish everyone in Northern Ireland when actually we should be punishing those who broke the law".

"We have considered all options and we keep all options on the table," he added.

News.title: Daughter wins £127k claim for caring for mum at home
News.content:
A woman has described her "phenomenal" relief after she won a legal case that means she is entitled to be paid Â£127k from her mother's estate for caring for her in her final years.

Bern Rogers, from Bristol, told the BBC of the "harrowing and deeply sad" family dispute since her elderly mother Sheila died in 2020, which led to her facing criminal charges.

Legal experts said the "hugely significant" High Court ruling would lead to other claims.

The executor of Sheila's estate, Bern's brother Andrew, said it had "always been willing to pay" her "genuine expenses" and an extra amount for her efforts. But the estate intends to appeal against the judgment that awarded Bern Â£127,500 for care provided.

News.title: Australian MP Helen Haines’ first concern after waking up revealed as parliament pays tribute
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Australian lawmaker Helen Haines’ first concern after waking up in hospital following a car-ramming attack was for the safety of her staff, a fellow MP has told parliament.

Independent MP Allegra Spender said on Monday that Ms Haines, who had both legs amputated after the attack, had expressed gratitude to the first responders, nurses, and bystanders who helped her.

Ms Haines remains in a Melbourne hospital in a serious but stable condition on Monday.

Parliament resumed for the first time since the alleged attack, with security screening measures tightened at parliament house in Canberra.

Ms Haines was standing at the rear of her car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta on 19 October when a white Toyota LandCruiser struck her, pinning her against her vehicle.

open image in gallery Independent member of parliament Zali Steggall sits next to a cutout cockatoo during a tribute to colleague Helen Haines, who was critically injured on Oct. 19 by a driver who struck her with a vehicle, at Parliament House in Canberra, Australia, Monday ( AP )

A 43-year-old man has been charged with offences including intentionally causing serious injury. Police have not revealed a motive.

“Phil told us about your first words when you woke up after the attack,” Ms Spender said, according to ABC News. “Your first concerns when you awoke were for your staff and gratitude to the first responders, nurses and bystanders.”

Ms Spender said the account reflected Haines’s character, saying: “People have spoken about your empathy and grace, and they deserve recognition. But I think it paints a sort of picture of you as a sort of benign force wandering through the parliament. What I will say is that you are also a force for change.”

Agriculture minister Julie Collins said Haines’s concern for others was characteristic of the independent MP. “After everything that she has been through, she was thinking of others,” Ms Collins said.

Prime minister Anthony Albanese was among several lawmakers to pay tribute to Ms Haines, a respected independent.

He proposed a motion expressing parliament’s wish for her recovery and support for her family. Her husband Phil Haines looked on from parliament’s public gallery.

“While the investigations go on, we must not rush to conclusions. But nor can we shrug off the very real rise in anger that distorts and corrodes our public discourse,” Mr Albanese told parliament.

open image in gallery Independent Australian lawmaker Helen Haines speaks during a debate on amendments for the National Anti-Corruption Commission Bill in the House of Representatives at Parliament House in Canberra, Australia, November 24, 2022 ( Reuters )

“Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but toward workers in hospitality, in retail, in schools and in hospitals, toward police, paramedics and other officials,” Mr Albanese added.

Mr Albanese described a “normalisation of the language of grievance and violence”.

“We must not conflate the robustness of Australian democracy with this rising tide of rage,” Mr Albanese said. Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett told Australian Broadcasting Corp on Sunday threats against lawmakers were evenly spread between male and female politicians. But threats against women were more “personalised.”

Ms Barrett said there was a “direct correlation” between the language political rivals use against each other and threats and abuse directed at lawmakers from the public.

Critics of Australian politics often complain that language that lawmakers sometimes use against each other would not be tolerated in any other workplace in the country.

open image in gallery Floral tributes are placed outside the offices of Australian lawmaker Helen Haines who was critically wounded in a 'targetted' attack, in Wangaratta ( AFP/Getty )

Opposition leader Angus Taylor told parliament he disagreed with those who saw a “casual connection between robust parliamentary debate and political violence.”

“We never allow that vigorous parliamentary debate to spill over into violence,” Mr Taylor said.

Speaker Milton Dick noted that some lawmakers had suggested colleagues sign a so-called civility pledge in response to the alleged attack on Haines.

“This is a personal decision and I encourage all Members (of Parliament) to continue these discussions to decide the best way for themselves” to respond, Mr Dick told parliament.

Two months ago, Ms Haines became the first Australian lawmaker to make such a pledge, advocated by the think tank Compassion in Politics Australia. Around six federal and state lawmakers have since committed to sign.

Independent lawmaker Kate Chaney said she intended to follow Ms Haines’ example by making such a pledge.

“I think there’s something really symbolic about the fact that Helen was the only federal M.P. (Member of Parliament) to have signed this,” Chaney told the ABC.

open image in gallery Floral tributes are placed outside the offices of Australian lawmaker Helen Haines who was critically wounded in a "targeted" attack, in Wangaratta on October 21, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

“It is a very simple thing. It just says ‘in my political life, I pledge to act with honesty, respect and compassion.’ And that feels to me like a simple and poignant way to honour the contribution Helen’s made to the parliament,” Ms Chaney added.

Compassion in Politics Australia did not immediately respond to a request for comment Monday.
