When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement."

Dollar General said it was made aware of the FTC's investigation in early February.

"Inaccurate pricing"

According to the suit, thousands of Dollar General stores unlawfully overcharged shoppers.

Dollar General "has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve," the FTC and states allege in the suit. "Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and s. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country."

The company also faced thousands of consumer complaints claiming it failed to honor advertised prices at checkout, a sign Dollar General knowingly harmed customers, according to the FTC.

The suit seeks a permanent injunction, along with monetary and other relief.

Dollar General in its statement said, "FTC staff also demanded a monetary amount that was untethered to — and orders of magnitude larger than — any realistic assessment of amounts attributable to pricing discrepancies."

The company said it "worked tirelessly and in good faith to resolve this matter without litigation," including an "alternative, and in our view, more reasonable, manner of calculating potential settlement ranges."

"Although we respect the FTC's role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives' role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously," it said.

World.title: Video of police being called to youth soccer game draws outrage
World.content:
Viral video of police being called to a youth soccer game near Orlando, Florida, is drawing outrage, with some claiming the cops showed up because a 3-year-old child was too good, while the league's director says the call was made because the parents were being disruptive.

No one disputes that 3-year-old Nevada, who can be seen in several videos dominating on the pitch against kids one and two years older than him, is a soccer phenom. Even Thomas Hayes, one of the directors of the youth league Nevada was playing in, told the cops when they arrived, "The kid is very good ... He's great. Really good."

"He's really advanced compared to the other ones. He's scoring a lot of goals, but he's pushing the kids and scoring," Hayes was seen saying on police body camera video. Hayes said he's told the kids not to push while they're playing, and that there was another incident with Nevada's parents a few weeks earlier when he swapped some of the players out, including Nevada.

"They don't like that," he said.

He told police Nevada's parents took issue with him telling the refs not to let their son push the other kids, claiming they created "a big scene, arguing with other parents."

Nevada's mom told a different story.

She is seen in the body camera video saying they always stand on the opposite side of the field as the other parents to avoid causing any disruption.

"They're literally kicking him out of this place because he's good at soccer," she told the police.

In one video of the incident taken by the family, Nevada's father is heard saying, "They called the police on a 3-year-old because he's too good."

Nevada's mother told CBS News the coach told Nevada he could stay in his most recent game if he passed the ball, but about halfway through, the cops got involved. She said in the bodycam video that she saw the other parents huddle in a circle talking about him during the game.

In an interview with media personality Lauren Lorosa, Nevada's mom said, "My son is already dressed. I cannot explain to my 3-year-old son that he cannot play today because he is so good."

Hayes said he wanted the family to leave, and he was willing to offer them a refund.

Online, there's been an avalanche of support for Nevada and his family, including from YouTube star Rachel Accurso, better known as Ms. Rachel, who commented on a post about the incident, saying she'd love to have Nevada on her show.

Not everybody has been supportive, with one coach writing, "These parents should be ashamed of themselves."

The league, i9 Sports, wrote on Facebook that it was "aware of concerns being shared regarding an incident at a local i9 Sports program, and we take them very seriously."

"The respectful treatment and well-being of every child and family matter deeply to us," it wrote. "We are working to understand the circumstances and will not speculate or share unverified information."

World.title: 7-year-old yoga instructor sets record
World.content: 7-year-old yoga instructor sets record Phoenix Giselle Hicks was certified as a yoga instructor before her 6th birthday. Now, the 7-year-old is in the Guinness Book of World Records as the youngest female yoga instructor. Tony Dokoupil reports. More

World.title: Harry Kane becomes first Englishman in 25 years to win Ballon d'Or
World.content:
Harry Kane becomes first Englishman in 25 years to win Ballon d'Or

toggle caption i Kin Cheung/AP

LONDON — Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d'Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season.

Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign — he was Europe's top scorer — and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.

The 33-year-old Kane says winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.

"Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief," an emotional Kane said in a message to young players, after reflecting on his early career struggles.

Sponsor Message

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs," he added. "I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well."

Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal — voted best young talent for a third straight year — 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.

Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children — "It's past your bedtime" — and wife Kate, " my best friend. We've been through ups and downs for sure. You're my biggest supporter. You always want the best for me."

Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and German Cup double, scoring a hat trick against Stuttgart in the cup final. Bayern also reached the Champions League semifinals.

At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England's all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semifinals but beat Mbappé's France for third place, England's best World Cup placing in 60 years.

An Englishman hadn't won the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

"It's massive for England, for our country. (The ceremony) being here in London was a good omen for me," Kane said. "It's been too long. Certainly (there have been) incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I'm extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honor, the thing I love to do the most."

Sponsor Message

England coach Thomas Tuchel told Kane the Three Lions are "lucky to have you as our leader."

"I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I'm delighted to see that you have now been formally recognized by the football world," Tuchel said.

Fans packed the streets and climbed light poles near the London Palladium, where the event was held, for a glimpse of the arriving athletes. Kane stopped to sign autographs on his way in.

They stayed through the ceremony and chanted Kane's name as he left the theater near Oxford Circus after midnight.

Kane planned to celebrate with family and friends, but just a little.

"We have a cup game on Wednesday so it can't get too messy," Kane said, noting he has an early Tuesday flight back to Munich in time for team training.

Monday's ceremony was held in London for the first time in recognition of the inaugural winner 70 years ago, England's Stanley Matthews in 1956.

toggle caption i Kin Cheung/AP

Putellas hat trick of awards

Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women's Ballon d'Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season including the Women's Champions League.

Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the offseason, also helped Spain win the Women's Nations League last December.

The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign.

Putellas won the prestigious award in 2021 and 2022, tore her ACL and saw Bonmati rise to stardom. Bonmati, who completed her women's Ballon d'Or three-peat in 2025, was not on this year's shortlist after breaking her leg in December.

There wasn't a women's Ballon d'Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.

Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with "love and passion."

"Believe in yourself, that's the most important thing," she said. "If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero."

Sponsor Message

Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club "something special."

"I'm really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player (at Barcelona)," she said. "What I experienced last year was like a perfect story."

World.title: Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show in Southern California
World.content:
Jay-Z picks himself to headline the Super Bowl halftime show in Southern California

toggle caption i Frank Franklin II/AP

LOS ANGELES — The man who has helped produce the Super Bowl halftime show is stepping into the spotlight: Jay-Z will headline the show himself.

The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Monday night that Jay-Z will be the featured performer for the halftime festivities on Feb. 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself "whenever the moment felt right to him."

"From 'Reasonable Doubt' to standing on the Super Bowl halftime stage, this has been a journey," Jay-Z said in a statement. "Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage. This run continues to be a dream come true."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of "Reasonable Doubt," the mogul's 1996 debut album. The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.

Sponsor Message

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl halftime show. At the time, Jay-Z said he had told Goodell, "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."

Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls. His catalog also includes the albums "The Blueprint" and "The Black Album," and hit songs such as "Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem)," "99 Problems" and "Empire State of Mind," his collaboration with Alicia Keys.

Last year, "Reasonable Doubt" was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests. At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on "The Story of O.J." and "Dead Presidents," while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday's finale.

Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.

Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.

Jay-Z became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021. He is also a four-time Emmy winner.

Roc Nation will executive produce the halftime show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.

Sponsor Message

The halftime show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny's performance in February won a record seven, including best variety special (live), while Kendrick Lamar's show last year won for music direction.

World.title: Brewers rout the Rays 10-1 to move within a win of their first World Series title
World.content:
Brewers rout the Rays 10-1 to move within a win of their first World Series title

toggle caption i Ashley Landis/AP

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Jackson Chourio set the tone at the plate, Brice Turang sparked an historic offensive outburst and Robert Gasser shut the door on the mound.

The Milwaukee Brewers are one victory from their first World Series title after routing the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 on Monday night thanks to a trio of young players who have shined in October.

Chourio bookended Milwaukee's eight-run fifth inning with two of his four hits, and Turang's two-run single opened a barrage of scoring with two outs.

"He was tremendous. Locked in. Gives us a big lift," Brewers manager Pat Murphy said about Chourio, who has eight hits in three Series games.

Sponsor Message

Gasser, a rookie left-hander, pitched one-hit ball and faced the minimum through six innings as Milwaukee rolled to a 3-0 lead in this Fall Classic. Game 4 is Tuesday night at Tropicana Field, where many Brewers fans showed up Monday and cheered from behind the visitors' dugout.

"It is really cool when you go on the road in such an intense atmosphere to have that support," Gasser said. "Normally it's 35,000 against nine, but tonight we had 20,000 people behind us."

Gasser allowed a line-drive single to Yandy Díaz leading off the bottom of the first and then retired 14 straight before Victor Mesa Jr. walked to begin the Tampa Bay sixth.

toggle caption i Ashley Landis/AP

With the help of a caught stealing and a double play, Gasser became the first starter to face the minimum 18 batters through six innings of a World Series game since Arizona's Curt Schilling in 2001 — and the first lefty to do it since Sandy Koufax for the Los Angeles Dodgers in 1965.

Chourio finished 4 for 5 with a double. Turang and William Contreras each went 3 for 5 as Milwaukee racked up 16 hits off "Fastball Freddy" Peralta and five relievers to win its eighth straight game — tying the record for a single postseason.

"I think that you could say this is one of my better games," Chourio said through a translator. "Really I was just taking every at-bat like it could be my last and trying to find any way I could to get on base."

Sponsor Message

Of the 43 previous major league teams to fall behind 3-0 in a best-of-seven postseason series, only the 2004 Boston Red Sox rallied to win four straight when they beat the New York Yankees in the American League Championship Series.

"It's kind of that chip and a chair mentality," Rays manager Kevin Cash said. "We've got a seat at the table. We've got to do something with the chip. Obviously the only thing we can do is win tomorrow."

Gasser became the first starter for Milwaukee to get an out in the sixth inning this postseason. He's allowed one run in 15 innings over three starts, all on the road.

Peralta, the MVP of the ALCS against Cleveland, ran out of gas against the Brewers. He was charged with five runs and seven hits in 4 2/3 innings against his former team.

"Just a little out of sync. I think he felt really good. Tried to power through it a little bit," Cash said. "Just inconsistencies in and out of the strike zone led to a bunch of really good at-bats by the Brewer lineup."

After a pair of tense, down-to-the-final-pitch, one-run games in Milwaukee, the Brewers put this one out of reach in the fifth with a postseason-record seven straight hits — all with two outs.

It was the first time in World Series history a team scored eight two-out runs in one inning.

"I was sitting in the dugout getting ready to go. There was two outs, and next thing you know, 40 minutes later, I have to go out on the field," Gasser said. "It was special. I had a smile on my face the whole time. It's just surreal when something like that happens."

Chourio began the rally with a one-out single and then stole second with two outs. Christian Yelich walked, and Peralta exited after Contreras' infield single loaded the bases.

Sponsor Message

The inning appeared to end when third baseman Junior Caminero fielded Contreras' bouncer and threw to second base for a forceout. But the call at second was overturned after a replay review, and Cam Booser entered.

Turang ripped a liner that shortstop Taylor Walls couldn't short hop. It bounced off his glove and rolled into shallow center field for a two-run single.

"Knife to the chest," Walls said.

Garrett Mitchell followed with an RBI single, Cooper Pratt grounded a two-run double down the left-field line and Sal Frelick lined a run-scoring double to make it 8-0.

"It's definitely deflating," Cash said. "How could it not be?"

toggle caption i Ashley Landis/AP

Cole Sulser replaced Booser and allowed an RBI single to David Hamilton and an RBI double to the 22-year-old Chourio, who became the second-youngest player with four hits and a stolen base in a World Series game behind Ty Cobb in 1908.

Murphy has compared Chourio to Pro Basketball Hall of Famer Kobe Bryant.

"Kobe was one of the best basketball players of all-time," Chourio said. "I had the opportunity to read his book, some of it at least, but the discipline he had, I think that's what you try to (take) from the great ones. You just take little things you can take from them and implement it into your own game. Hopefully I'm doing a little bit of that."

Brandon Woodruff pitched the ninth for the Brewers, allowing one run and two hits in his first appearance in 3 1/2 months. The two-time All-Star had been sidelined by a shoulder injury that originally was thought to require surgery.

Of the 25 previous teams that took a 3-0 lead in the World Series, 21 swept and four won in five games.

Originally the Seattle Pilots for one season in 1969, the franchise moved to Milwaukee and was renamed the Brewers in 1970. Their only other World Series trip came as an AL team and ended with a Game 7 loss to St. Louis in 1982.

Sponsor Message

Led by the 67-year-old Murphy, the Brewers need just one more win to end their championship drought.

The Rays led the AL with 98 wins in the regular season, swept the Yankees in three games in the Division Series and beat the Guardians in six games in the ALCS.

But they made uncharacteristic mistakes on the bases and defense during the first two games in Milwaukee, and completely unraveled at home.

Tampa Bay also has never won a World Series in 29 seasons. The Rays lost to the Phillies in five games in 2008 and to the Dodgers in six games in 2020.

Wearing their white Devil Rays uniforms, they were eager to play in front of their home fans at the quirky, cavernous Trop, which had its roof shredded by Hurricane Milton in October 2024 and needed major renovations.

But their cowbell-ringing, towel-waving fans among a sellout crowd of 40,388 couldn't lift them past the surging Brewers.

Milwaukee led the majors with 103 wins, beat the Padres in four games in their NLDS and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS. With a win in Game 4, the Brewers would become the first team to sweep an LCS and World Series since the 1976 Cincinnati Reds.

Griffin Jax is scheduled to start Game 4 for Tampa Bay. The Brewers hadn't announced a starter.

"We've been preparing for this day a lot," Chourio said. "We have one more to lock in for tomorrow to complete the mission."

World.title: Local ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump starts in southern Ukraine
World.content:
Local ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump starts in southern Ukraine

toggle caption i Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine B/via AP

MYKOLAIV, Ukraine — A localized ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia took effect early Tuesday ahead of a humanitarian mission brokered by U.S. first lady Melania Trump, as missile attacks resumed in Kyiv.

The local pause in fighting started at 3 a.m. to allow an aid mission into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine later this week.

According to her office, Melania Trump led talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine after meeting with U.N. officials who briefed her on the situation in the town.

The aid mission is planned ahead of a new round of U.S.-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine expected next month aimed at ending the war after more than 4½ years of fighting.

Sponsor Message

Up to 2,000 people are stranded in Oleshky with dwindling food and medicine. They are unable to leave because of explosive mines and drone attacks in the area, according to the U.N.

Russian and Ukrainian negotiators as well as the militaries of the two countries confirmed in separate statements that the ceasefire had begun.

The local ceasefire is due to last through Saturday, or longer, though deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine has thwarted previous attempts at ceasefires.

Minutes after 3 a.m., multiple ballistic missile explosions shook Kyiv and air alerts sounded in multiple parts of the country.

toggle caption i Dan Bashakov/AP

Late Monday, the capital also came under attack, when Russian ballistic missiles damaged the grounds of a university in Kyiv, killing one person and leaving 10 injured, city officials said. In Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, authorities said attacks late Monday killed two people and injured four.

"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote in an online post shortly afterward.

Oleshky is in the partially occupied Kherson region, about 550 kilometers (340 miles) southeast of Kyiv, where the Dnipro River separates Russian and Ukrainian forces.

It was captured by Moscow's forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Further calamity struck in June 2023 when floodwaters inundated the town due to a dam collapse.

Oleshky sits across the Dnipro River from the city of Kherson, the region's administrative capital. Russian forces seized Kherson in the early stages of the 2022 invasion but retreated across the river several months later.

Sponsor Message

Negotiators involved in the aid mission said doctors, medicines, food supplies and water would be taken to Oleshky before evacuation corridors are opened.

World.title: Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges
World.content:
Trump campaigns in Mississippi, highlighting Republicans' challenges

toggle caption i Jacquelyn Martin/AP

CORINTH, Miss. — President Donald Trump campaigned Monday in Mississippi, as he continued a closing midterm rally blitz that has highlighted Republicans' challenges ahead of an election that could drastically shift power in Washington and statehouses across the country.

"I'm here because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance," Trump told the crowd, his voice audibly hoarse, as he worked to boost Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, who is facing a surprisingly stiff challenge from Democrat Scott Colom.

Colom was spotted at the rally site, too, creating the rare spectacle of Trump's staunchest supporters interacting directly with a figure the president would soon go on to denigrate as a "Marxist radical" and "fake" and "shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate" from the stage.

Sponsor Message

Mississippi, among the nation's most reliably Republican states, is not where the Republicans envisioned needing a late-October stop from the president. But Colom is one of many Democratic underdogs who have managed to expand the House and Senate battleground maps because of widespread voter discontent over inflation, the Iran war and other aspects of Trump's second presidency.

He said he had planned to go to the rally site to listen to what was on Trump supporters' minds.

"They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they're going through," Colom said ahead of the president's arrival.

Trump's event kicks off a week of aggressive campaigning that will include more stops in states he won comfortably in 2024, including Texas, South Carolina and Iowa. Trump also plans to hold a rally Saturday in Salina, Kansas, officials announced late Monday, marking his second visit to the state in less than two weeks.

toggle caption i Nam Y. Huh/AP

Democrats, including progressives, are expanding their efforts

Top Democratic candidates and their surrogates were also greeting voters — more than 30 million of whom have already cast ballots, according to data collected by The Associated Press from election administrators across the country — as they try to end Republicans' threadbare majority in the House, reclaim control of the Senate and claw back power in state capitals.

Sponsor Message

Former Vice President Kamala Harris, Democrats' 2024 presidential candidate, campaigned in Wisconsin with Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, who faces Rep. Tom Tiffany, a Trump ally, in the governor's race. If elected, Crowley would be the first Black governor to lead the battleground state.

"This is a tight race because the stakes are so high," Harris said at an event billed as a "Women for Crowley" rally.

Meanwhile, in Michigan, Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed distanced himself from an ad created by a group called Rebellion PAC that blames high grocery prices on U.S. support for Israel.

"This ad is not affiliated in any way with the Abdul for Senate campaign," a spokesperson for El-Sayed, Roxie Richner, said in a statement about the spot, which features a couple discussing U.S. support for Israel as they shop for groceries.

"Apparently it's costing us a lot of money to drop bombs on Gaza," the woman says.

The ad had been condemned by U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens, who narrowly lost to El-Sayed in the Democratic primary.

The way to win Michigan "is not by blaming the high costs of our goods on the only Jewish homeland in the world," Stevens wrote on X.

El-Sayed, who would be the country's first Muslim senator, has denounced antisemitism while fiercely criticizing Israel for its military operations in Gaza — a position that has been a frequent point of attack for both Republicans and supporters of Israel in his party.

toggle caption i Finn Gomez//POOL Getty Images North America

Vance campaigning in other Republican states

Vice President JD Vance returned to Kansas to stump for Sen. Roger Marshall, who finds himself in a tight contest with Democratic nominee and pastor Adam Hamilton. Hundreds of people were gathered inside the warehouse of a steel-fabricating company in north Topeka in a state where Democrats haven't won a Senate race since 1932.

Sponsor Message

Marshall, who has raised far less money than Hamilton, told the crowd that Trump is on the ballot, even if his name doesn't appear, because of how Democrats will thwart his agenda if they win control of Congress.

"Democrats are coming out like it's a presidential year," he said, calling on the GOP to match Democrats' energy.

Jace Sullivan, a 50-year-old electrician from Topeka who describes himself as "85% Republican," said Trump supporters need to "circle the wagons" and get out to vote.

Wearing a red "JD Vance for President 2028" shirt, he said he thinks Trump is rightly working to keep Iran from getting nuclear weapons.

"Gas prices are high and it does suck, but it's a means to an end," Sullivan said.

Trump, at the Mississippi rally, said he had, in fact, expected gas prices to rise even higher than they had.

"It worked out fine and it'll be over soon," he said of the war with Iran.

Earlier, Vance was in Belgrade, Montana, to campaign with Republican Aaron Flint, who is facing Democrat Sam Forstag in the race for the state's 1st Congressional District, and Republican Senate candidate Kurt Alme.

Despite the visits to ruby red states, Sen. Tim Scott, who serves as chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told The Associated Press Monday that GOP candidates are "closing very strongly" in races across the country, including South Carolina, which Trump is set to visit for the second time in as many weeks to stump for GOP Sen. Darline Graham.

"One of the reasons why we will be in the majority is because he has invested the time and the energy on the campaign trail," Scott said on the sidelines of U.S. Rep. Russell Fry's 3rd Annual Freedom Fry event.

Trump to rally in another reliably Republican state

But it's Trump's visit to Mississippi that perhaps brings the midterm landscape into the sharpest relief with just a week of campaigning left.

Sponsor Message

To be sure, Hyde-Smith, who is vying for her second full term, remains the favorite in a state Trump won three times by an average of nearly 20 percentage points.

But Colom, a local prosecutor who would make history as Mississippi's first Black senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction, is looking to parlay inflation, Trump's lagging popularity and Hyde-Smith's mistakes into an upset.

Senate Democrats' super PAC has been a late entry in the contest, with a $1.2 million investment. Mississippians have not chosen a new Democratic senator since 1947, and Democrats last won a Senate race there when that senator, the onetime segregationist John Stennis, won his last reelection in 1982.

In New York, meanwhile, one of the party's most vulnerable House members pulled from Trump's campaign playbook. Rep. Mike Lawler, who is in a tight race with Democrat Cait Conley in New York City's northern suburbs, manned a McDonald's drive-thru — mimicking something Trump did two years ago, even as Lawler has tried to emphasize his independence from the president.

World.title: A quick guide to Israel's high-stakes elections
World.content:
A quick guide to Israel's high-stakes elections

toggle caption i Oded Balilty/AP

TEL AVIV, Israel — Israel is holding pivotal elections on Tuesday in what many Israelis call the most consequential vote in their country's history after the last few years of war.

Polls show Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu trailing in the race behind his main challenger, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. But it may take weeks or months before it's clear who will be designated the winner.

That's because voters will not directly choose between Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Instead, they will vote for one of a dozen main parties running for office in the 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset.

The real contest will begin after election day, when party leaders try to assemble a governing coalition of at least 61 lawmakers.

Here is a guide to the leading candidates, the issues shaping the vote and what could happen next.

Who are the leading candidates?

Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, is seeking another term in office.

Sponsor Message

Netanyahu has led the most right-wing government in Israel's history. His coalition has included Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, leaders of far-right, religious nationalist parties that are also running in this election, as well as two ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties.

Netanyahu has led Israel through more than three years of war and regional conflict, from the Hamas-led attacks on Oct. 7, 2023, and the war in Gaza to fighting involving Lebanon, Iran, Syria and Yemen. He is campaigning on Israel's military achievements and his close relationship with President Trump, who recently endorsed him. Netanyahu has also made confronting Iran, and ultimately seeking the fall of its regime, a central part of his campaign.

His principal challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former chief of staff of the Israeli military who is running for prime minister for the first time as the leader of a new center-right party called Yashar, Hebrew for "Straight" or "Upright."

Eisenkot's son, Gal, an Israeli soldier, was killed in Gaza during the war. Recent polls have shown Eisenkot has the strongest chance of replacing Netanyahu, although no party or political bloc appears assured of winning a parliamentary majority.

Eisenkot's Yashar includes figures from Israel's political center and moderate right. The opposition parties he would partner with range from the right and center to the liberal left. He has pledged not to join a government led by Netanyahu.

Sponsor Message

How could Arab parties play a role in the results?

Two predominantly Arab parties are also running, including the United Arab List, also known as Ra'am, which made history in 2021 as the first Arab Islamist party to join an Israeli governing coalition. The party says it is willing to work with predominantly Jewish parties in exchange for policies fighting crime and promoting housing, infrastructure and other problems facing Israel's Arab minority community, which makes up about 20 percent of the country's population.

But nearly all the main predominantly Jewish political parties, including Eisenkot's, remain reluctant to rely on Arab parties to form a coalition. That reluctance could leave the anti-Netanyahu camp without the 61 seats it needs for a governing majority.

What is the election about?

Accountability for Oct. 7: The Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage, looms over the election. Netanyahu has resisted calls to establish a state commission of inquiry into the political and security failures that preceded the attack. Eisenkot and other opposition leaders say they would establish such a commission soon after taking office.

Who should serve in the military: Nearly three years of fighting across several fronts have placed a heavy burden on Israel's standing army and military reservists. The military says it needs additional personnel, intensifying a decades-old dispute over exemptions for ultra-Orthodox Jewish men. Netanyahu, reliant on ultra-Orthodox parties for political support, has resisted enlisting them, while Eisenkot is campaigning to expand military service to more ultra-Orthodox Jews.

Israel's judiciary: Before the Oct. 7 attack, Netanyahu's government pursued a judicial overhaul that would have weakened the supreme court and given the governing coalition greater influence over the appointment of judges. The plan triggered some of the largest protests in Israel's history. Netanyahu's far-right partners are campaigning on renewed efforts to limit the power of the courts, while Eisenkot advocates for an independent and powerful judiciary. Netanyahu remains on trial for corruption, and says the charges are politically motivated.

Sponsor Message

Israel's international isolation

The wars in Gaza and the region, and Israel's policies in the occupied West Bank, have badly strained its relations with many governments overseas, and public support for Israel in the U.S. has plummeted, worrying many Israeli voters. Netanyahu emphasizes his relationship with Trump and argues that military strength has improved Israel's strategic position. Eisenkot and his allies say continued international isolation threatens Israel's economy, diplomatic relationships and security.

What could happen after the election?

A party does not need to finish first in the race for the party leader to be Israel's next prime minister. What matters is whether he can assemble a coalition with majority support in parliament.

Most recent polls suggest that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has a clear path to a majority. That leaves several possible outcomes:

Eisenkot's allies could break their campaign promises and form a coalition relying on support from one or more Arab parties, either as formal coalition members or from outside the coalition, and the opposition would rule with a minority government

Netanyahu and Eisenkot could form a broad unity government, although Eisenkot has publicly ruled out serving under Netanyahu.

Netanyahu could agree to a plea deal that would dismiss his criminal charges in court, in exchange for stepping down as prime minister and serving under Eisenkot as a senior minister.

A deadlock, where neither side may be able to form a government, leaving Netanyahu as a caretaker prime minister, with a repeat election held next year.

Even if Eisenkot cannot immediately form a coalition, a parliamentary majority opposed to Netanyahu could try to elect a new Knesset speaker, establish a state commission of inquiry into the Oct. 7 attacks, and advance legislation on ultra-Orthodox military service.

Netanyahu would try to do everything he can to prevent such an outcome. His Likud party's billboards are already promoting a scenario in which the party could claim that the election was stolen, a move that could lead to chaos in the days after the vote.

Sponsor Message

What direction would Israel take depending on who wins the election?

Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot currently supports the establishment of a Palestinian state in the foreseeable future. Their most significant differences concern democratic institutions, the occupied West Bank and Israel's relationship with the world.

Netanyahu has governed with ultra-Orthodox and far right parties that support settlement expansion in the West Bank and a weaker supreme court. His far-right partners have pushed for annexation of the West Bank and expulsion of Palestinians, drawing sanctions from the U.K. and Europe.

Eisenkot presents himself as a more institutional and pragmatic alternative. He has also taken a tougher position against violence by Israeli settlers and says he would act against settlement outposts that are illegal even under Israeli law.

Eisenkot has opposed settlement construction in E1, a strategically sensitive area just east of Jerusalem. Critics of the settlement plan say Israeli construction there would further divide the West Bank and make the creation of a territorially contiguous Palestinian state much more difficult.

The choice facing Israeli voters is therefore not a straightforward contest between left and right. It is also a contest over Netanyahu's leadership, accountability for Oct. 7, the role of religion in the state, the independence of Israel's institutions and what kind of alliances the country will pursue at home and abroad.

NPR's Daniel Estrin contributed to this story.

World.title: Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again
World.content:
Trump administration attempting to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey again

toggle caption i Alex Brandon/AP

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration is attempting to prosecute James Comey for what it calls a decade-old leak of classified information, an effort the former FBI director's lawyers immediately dismissed as invalid and outside the legal time limit for when the Justice Department can file a criminal indictment.

The allegations from the Justice Department were revealed Monday in newly unsealed court documents that shed light on a closed-door fight that represents an unmistakable escalation in the administration's targeting of Comey, a longtime critic and foe of President Donald Trump who has faced two other criminal cases since the Republican returned to the White House last year. The effort to prosecute Comey is also part of a series of politically charged investigative actions the department has undertaken in the run-up to next week's midterm elections.

Sponsor Message

"Well, they're back — again," Comey said in a video statement Monday. "It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice – one that we cannot become numb to. Nothing's changed with me; I'm still innocent, I'm still not afraid of these people — and I still believe in an independent federal judiciary."

The Justice Department said it had filed what's known as a "criminal information" to extend the statute of limitations for when they can permissibly bring an indictment.

"Filing a criminal information to toll the statute of limitations is a widely recognized practice in federal court and has been approved by multiple Circuit Courts of Appeals. This is an ongoing criminal investigation, and we will not comment further," a department spokesperson said.

An information can be filed without the approval of a judge or a grand jury's finding of probable cause to a court. Comey's lawyers made clear that they intend to fight the charges as invalid and barred by a 10-year statute of limitations.

"For the third time in little more than one year, the Department of Justice has attempted to charge Mr. Comey with a federal crime. Mr. Comey steadfastly maintains his innocence," his attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, said in a statement.

The allegation was previously investigated

The latest allegation concerns an October 2016 New York Times story related to a secret court order that required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. The story cited two government officials who spoke on the condition of anonymity about the order from a judge on the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court that Yahoo was barred from publicly disclosing.

Sponsor Message

Federal authorities, including prosecutor John Durham, began investigating the disclosure in early 2017. Durham, who later investigated the FBI's conduct as it scrutinized potential ties between Russia and Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, wrote a classified memo in December 2018 recommending no criminal charges against anyone in connection with the disclosure, Comey's attorneys said in a recent court filing.

In January 2019, the U.S. Attorney's office for the District of Columbia opened a second investigation of the same matter under the code name "Tropical Vortex." But that investigation was closed without any charges filed in February 2020.

"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone. Now, ten years after the article was published, the Government filed an "Information" against Mr. Comey that was not approved by a judge nor issued by a grand jury. It purports to charge Mr. Comey with crimes that he did not commit," Fitzgerald said.

Prosecutors in a newly unsealed filing said investigators found evidence that Comey "sought to correct misinformation which had appeared in the press by way of Reuters the day before" that New York Times story was published, directed his staff to speak to a journalist at the newspaper related to accuracy concerns "and thereby illegally transferred classified information."

The criminal information was filed under seal on Oct. 6, 2016, 10 years after the story was published. "But," Comey's lawyers said, "the applicable statute of limitations explicitly demands an indictment within 10 years of the offense; an information does not suffice."

They have asked a judge to dismiss the information, a request that is still pending.

Trump and Comey have a long and uneasy history

The first criminal case against Comey, filed in federal court in Virginia, accused him of having lied to Congress in 2020 but was dismissed by a judge who concluded that the prosecutor who brought the charges was illegally appointed. A separate pending indictment charges the former FBI director with threatening Trump through an Instagram photo of seashells in the numerical arrangement of "86 47," a case he has sought to dismiss and some legal experts have greeted with skepticism.

Sponsor Message

The cases are part of a Trump retribution campaign that has even extended to Comey's daughter, Maurene, who was fired from her job as a Justice Department prosecutor in New York last year in a termination that a federal judge on Monday ruled was illegal.

Comey was the FBI director when Trump took office in 2017, having been appointed by then-President Barack Obama, a Democrat, and serving before that as a senior Justice Department official in President George W. Bush's Republican administration.

But the relationship was strained from the start, including after Comey resisted a request by Trump at a private dinner to pledge his personal loyalty to the president -- an overture that so unnerved the FBI director that he documented it in a contemporaneous memorandum.

Trump fired Comey in May 2017 amid an FBI investigation into potential ties between Russia and Trump's campaign. That inquiry, later taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller, found that while Russia interfered in the 2016 election and the Trump team welcomed the help, there was insufficient evidence to prove a criminal collaboration.

The two men have been bitterly at odds ever since Comey's firing. Comey in 2018 published a memoir, "A Higher Loyalty," that painted Trump in deeply unflattering ways, likening him to a mafia don and characterizing him "untethered to truth." Trump, for his part, has repeatedly claimed that Comey should face charges for "treason" — an accusation Comey dismissed as "dumb lies" — and called him an "untruthful slime ball."

World.title: Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud
World.content:
Trump administration pushes for food assistance card upgrade to fight fraud

toggle caption i Damian Dovarganes/AP

In a major step to combat a form of fraud that has robbed food stamp recipients of millions of dollars, the Trump administration is proposing a requirement for states to bolster the security features on their food assistance cards.

In recent years, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, has been the repeated target of card skimming, when thieves extract personal information from payment terminals and drain money from accounts. Most SNAP cards rely on a magnetic stripe for swipe payment – which tends to be vulnerable to skimming because it does a poor job of securing the data stored on cards.

Sponsor Message

Many banks in the U.S. took action against this issue over a decade ago by upgrading their cards to include microchips and tap-to-pay, which are considered more secure. But states have lagged in making such a transition for Electronic Benefits Transfer (EBT) cards, which are what SNAP recipients use to access food aid. Currently, fewer than a third of states have made the switch or are in process of doing so, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

Now, under the proposed rule released by the USDA last week, all states would have to adopt chip-enabled EBT cards. It also requires retailers that accept SNAP benefits to have payment terminals that support tap-pay. The USDA's Food and Nutrition Administration, which administers SNAP, attributed card skimming as a reason behind the proposal.

"These proposed changes will protect SNAP benefits from thieves and ensure benefits are accessible by approved households," the Food and Nutrition Administration said in its summary of the rule.

Back in January, the USDA Office of Inspector General projected that SNAP theft could climb to $233 million between 2025 and 2026 — largely as a result of skimming. A recent ProPublica investigation found that last year, $470 million was stolen electronically from SNAP recipients. The total was calculated using data from Propel, an app that helps SNAP recipients check their food benefits.

Sponsor Message

In most states, stolen benefits are not replaced — leaving recipients to make difficult choices, such as skipping meals or borrowing money in order to pay for groceries, according to Propel.

Earlier this month, NPR reported that food assistance card modernization had widespread support from state officials and federal watchdogs, as well as Republicans and Democrats in Congress. But money has been a major barrier for states to make the switch. According to the Government Accountability Office, chip-enabled cards are about 10 times more expensive to produce than their magnetic strip counterparts.

The federal push for stronger card security features comes as state SNAP agencies are facing new budget pressures triggered by President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The proposed regulation recognized the financial barrier, adding that the USDA is interested in hearing from state agencies about the cost burden.

"As stewards of taxpayer dollars, the Department considers these administrative costs as a necessary investment to deter the loss of Federally-funded SNAP benefits," the proposed rule said.

The public has 60 days to submit comments on the proposal before the USDA publishes a final rule. The department is considering giving states a two-year deadline from that publication date to implement the rule, but it also welcomed input on whether that's enough time.

When asked if the department would consider providing funding to help states upgrade their card technology, the USDA said that "For years, States had access to administrative funds to stop this egregious abuse of taxpayer resources. Yet few acted."

The USDA added that the proposed rule has been in the works for nearly four years. It estimates that the changes will reduce stolen benefits by at least $1.5 billion over the next decade.

SNAP has been one of the focus areas in the Trump administration's war on fraud. Last week, the Justice Department announced that its fraud division helped uncover nearly $42 million in schemes targeting food benefits. The investigations ranged from identity theft to retailers illegally exchanging cash for food benefits.

World.title: Canada-wide freeze on Crime Stoppers programs, partnerships surges to 35 agencies
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Less than a week after an exclusive CBC investigation revealed over 1.5 million Canadian Crime Stoppers tips were compromised in a massive data breach, the fallout continues to grow.

According to CBC's tally, at least 11 Crime Stoppers programs have now announced they are pausing their intake of anonymous tips, and 24 police units across the country have suspended their partnership with the organization.

The wave of temporary suspensions follows a CBC News investigation published last week that revealed anonymous tips attached to over 60 Canadian Crime Stoppers chapters were compromised in a data hack last March — exposing phone numbers, addresses and even the names of some tipsters.

On Friday, Navigate360 — the third-party U.S.-based company that manages all of Crime Stoppers international tips — confirmed its systems had been breached . It was its first public acknowledgment of the hack, seven months after it happened.

CBC has reached out repeatedly to Navigate360 before and after publishing its story, but has received no response.

Most of the police services in Ontario and Manitoba explained they are pausing their partnerships with Crime Stoppers until an investigation can show that it's safe for tipsters to contact them again.

WATCH | Crime Stoppers chapters pause program in wake of data breach: More Canadian Crime Stoppers chapters pause program after CBC investigation | Hanomansing Live | Duration closed caption 4:46 At least seven Crime Stoppers chapters have announced they are suspending programs a day after CBC revealed the extent of a massive data leak. Former RCMP superintendent Garry Clement talks to Hanomansing Tonight about how valuable the program has been for law enforcement agencies.

Among recent additions to the list is the Brantford Police Service, which wrote in a statement Monday that its decision "reflects the importance of ensuring appropriate safeguards are in place to protect the confidentiality of information and the anonymity of individuals who come forward."

The Winnipeg Police Service, one of two police departments in Manitoba to have suspended its use of Crime Stoppers, said in a press release on Friday that "public trust is essential to the success of any reporting platform, and we recognize the importance of maintaining confidence in the security and confidentiality of information shared by members of the public."

Dozens of local chapters contacted by CBC

Over the past week, our team of CBC reporters has contacted at least 35 local chapters of the organization — including all those with the highest number of compromised tips.

We asked them if they intended on following the lead of Toronto Crime Stoppers which announced last Wednesday that it was pausing its program , effective immediately.

Out of a total of 35 chapters contacted, 10 replied directly to CBC News or subsequently issued public statements, while 25 have yet to respond to our requests for comment.

The majority of the programs that replied confirmed to CBC they would no longer be accepting anonymous tips.

Three chapters referred CBC back to their provincial or national associations.

A single chapter, New Brunswick Crime Stoppers, said it intends to continue its program.

Saskatchewan programs say focus is 'getting answers'

On Friday night, all five Crime Stoppers programs in Saskatchewan announced they were pausing all tips intake across the province , effective immediately.

CBC asked representatives of the group for an interview and was told on Monday that "there are too many programs and moving parts to designate one person as a spokesperson at this time."

Replying by email, the Association of Crime Stoppers Programs of Saskatchewan, which represents all five programs, said they are currently "working to understand the scope of this breach in Saskatchewan" and "through legal counsel, we are pressing Navigate360 for the information we need."

"The need for Crime Stoppers has not gone away. We are working hard to ensure people can submit tips in a safe and confidential way. We have asked Navigate360 repeatedly for the information we need…. Once we have it, we can assess the scope and impact of this breach across Saskatchewan's programs."

On Monday, two more Crime Stoppers chapters in Northern Ontario added their names to the growing list of organizations pulling away from the anonymous tip program.

Near North Crime Stoppers — which encourages North Bay residents to report crimes anonymously — published a notice on its website saying it has "paused the acceptance of new tips through our telephone line, website, and mobile app following a cybersecurity breach."

WATCH | More on the investigation: Over a million Canadian tips leaked from Crime Stoppers database | Duration closed caption 1:52 A CBC News investigation found more than a million tips submitted to Crime Stoppers in Canada over the past 25 years were exposed in a massive data breach. About half the leaked Canadian tips obtained by CBC contained personal information.

"This temporary pause has not been an easy decision, but we believe it is necessary while the situation is assessed and appropriate safeguards are established," the public notice said.

Sault Ste. Marie Crime Stoppers also published a note on its website explaining that "it is currently unable to accept or forward tips intended for Sault Ste. Marie Police Service and Anishinabek Police Service, which have paused its participation in the program."

Association advises chapters to 'not provide interviews to CBC'

To date, the chair of the Toronto Crime Stoppers chapter is the only one to have spoken publicly about the decision to suspend the program. Meanwhile, the overwhelming majority of chapters — 49 of the 64, according to CBC's tally — with tips compromised in the leak have yet to acknowledge the breach publicly, whether they were prompted to by CBC or not.

An internal memo obtained by CBC News dated Oct. 22 — the day after the publication of our initial investigation — suggests answers as to why that could be.

"Do not provide interviews, statements, background or 'off the record' comments to CBC or any other outlet, including local media," writes David J. Forster, president of the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association, adding that "If contacted, please let them know they can reach out to the Canadian Crime Stoppers Association, and provide our contact information."

The memo continues by asking that local chapters who are asked questions about the breach by their "law enforcement partner" — meaning the police unit covering their territory — also direct them to the association.

Without speaking publicly, at least one local chapter has made a discreet change to its website that suggests it is aware of the breach's now very public disclosure.

Calgary Crime Stoppers, which has not replied to CBC's request for comment, added a banner to its website that reads: "DO NOT SUBMIT PERSONAL DETAILS. Self-identification compromises your legal right to anonymity under Canadian Law."

World.title: First Nations-first ministers' meeting brings funding announcements and mixed reviews
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The premiers said they were there to listen and the prime minister said he was there to act. But one chief said history will judge them by a different measure.

"History will not remember us for gathering in a room, taking photographs, making speeches," Chief Sheldon Sunshine of Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation in northern Alberta told Canada's premiers and prime minister on Monday morning.

He paused for dramatic effect before adding: "History will judge us by what we change."

And thus began the first Indigenous-focused first ministers' meeting in 21 years — and the first such meeting in 119 years to focus solely on First Nations issues.

The group convened not on opposing sides but in a circle behind closed doors in Ottawa at the John G. Diefenbaker Building on Sussex Drive, where there was no shortage of calls for change.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew surprised reporters by holding up his Indian status card as he called to abolish the Indian Act. Prairie chiefs joined former national chief Matthew Coon Come demanding Canada revisit the 1930 Natural Resource Transfer Acts that handed control over resource development from the federal to provincial governments.

WATCH | Prime minister addresses First Nations leaders: Carney seeks to 'commit to action' at historic First Nations-first ministers' meeting | Duration closed caption 0:50 Prime Minister Mark Carney said it was 'sobering' to realize first ministers and First Nation leaders have not met together in over two decades. 'Let's seize this opportunity,' Carney said, adding that the government 'will act' both today and in the upcoming budget.

"If this first ministers' meeting succeeds, it must come up with strong, concrete measures for next steps. If they don't do that, then this is another meeting of just talks," Coon Come told reporters.

Chiefs from Ontario called for constitutional amendments that would recognize First Nations as distinct orders of government. Grassroots activists protested outside, while inside Assembly of First Nations (AFN) leaders and Canada's first ministers debated the country's future.

As the meeting wrapped, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced both financial and political commitments. He said he shares Kinew's view that the time has come to reform or even abolish the Indian Act and would direct his ministers to work with First Nations on a path forward.

WATCH | Carney and Woodhouse Nepinak on future of the Indian Act: Carney 'very open' to abolishing Indian Act | Duration closed caption 3:35 Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'there's many reasons' to move on from the Indian Act, speaking after Monday's meeting between First Nations leaders and first ministers. Carney said the solution 'could be moving beyond, it could be reforming, it could be abolishing' the 1876 law in order to establish a modernized relationship.

He said he will instruct his finance minister to work with First Nations to develop new revenue-sharing mechanisms, including a potential sovereign wealth fund, which the AFN sought in one of its position papers circulated ahead of the meeting.

Carney also announced some proposed new spending, likely foreshadowing the Nov. 5 federal budget. This includes more than $2.5 billion over five years for emergency preparedness in First Nations communities across the country, and more than $630 million over four years for First Nations and Inuit policing.

In televised opening remarks earlier, Carney called it "sobering" that two decades have elapsed since the last such meeting, held when Paul Martin was prime minister in 2005. That meeting in Kelowna, B.C., yielded an agreement dubbed the Kelowna Accord.

"This is an important opportunity, yes, to share perspectives, to listen, to learn, but above all to commit to action," Carney said.

But the meeting unfolded under a cloud of skepticism, the absence of three premiers and concerns from some chiefs that the Carney government is using the meeting as political cover for its streamlining of major infrastructure projects.

The day included a blunt address from the Algonquin Nation on whose unsurrendered land Parliament Hill now sits.

"Our nation is still waiting for justice," Verna Polson, grand chief of the Algonquin Anishinabeg Nation Tribal Council, told the group.

In her opening remarks, AFN National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said nation-building "can't just be about ramming through major projects" as fast as possible.

"The national interests must also include the proposals, law and policy reforms that First Nations seek," she said. "We have been persistent and patient, but we cannot afford to wait many, many years for results and implementation."

WATCH | National chief opens meeting: 'Our rights must be taken seriously': AFN national chief | Duration closed caption 1:35 Speaking at the opening of a historic First Nations and Canadian first ministers' meeting, Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak says Indigenous rights 'can't be respected after the fact.'

Around 40 people gathered outside to protest AFN participating at all because it's a federally funded national advocacy body elected by chiefs and not rights-holding grassroots people.

Russ Diabo, spokesperson for the Truth Before Reconciliation Network, told CBC News the Carney government is on the wrong track.

"What [Carney] should be doing is changing the way he's interacting with First Nations and Canada and not using these administrative bodies that he controls like the Assembly First Nations," Diabo said.

Reviews were mixed coming out of the meeting.

WATCH | Carney says he's open to abolishing the Indian Act: Carney ‘very open’ to abolishing the Indian Act | Duration closed caption 2:11 Speaking at the Assembly of First Nations, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he is open to reforming or abolishing the Indian Act and has asked his ministers to work in partnership with First Nations to ‘chart that path together.’

Cody Diabo, grand chief of the Mohawk Council of Kahnawà:ke, left early, denouncing the meeting as all about "butterflies and rainbows" and not dealing with big-picture substantive issues. Hereditary Chief Na'Moks of the Wet'suwet'en Nation in B.C. felt the meeting was about finding "cheerleaders" for the federal agenda.

Others were more optimistic. Abram Benedict, AFN's Ontario regional chief, said he felt good about the investments and potential creation of a wealth fund, but there was no firm pledge to hold these meetings annually, as the AFN requested.

"There seems to be a willingness, but there was no commitment," Benedict said.

Carney said the right timeline for the next meeting is probably two years. Woodhouse Nepinak told reporters she was happy with the day and the tangible commitments secured.

World.title: Excitement 'beyond Hope' as B.C.'s next premier promises to bring rural, northern perspective to top job
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

For the first time in decades, British Columbia will have a premier from north of Metro Vancouver following a general election victory.

Though he was born in New Westminster and raised in Surrey, Lorne Doerkson moved to the B.C. Interior as an adult, working for newspapers in Salmon Arm, Prince George and 100 Mile House before settling in Williams Lake in 2001.

And he isn't shy about making his love for the region known.

"I love Cariboo-Chilcotin," he enthused in his election night victory speech, calling Williams Lake home while also giving specific mention to key northern and Interior cities, including Fort St. John and Quesnel.

WATCH | Doerkson promises to bring rural perspectives to premiership: WATCH IN FULL: New premier-designate answers questions after historic victory in B.C. snap election | Duration closed caption 28:17

"For a very long time, a lot of British Columbians have felt like Victoria forgot about them, like the map maybe stopped at Hope," he said, referencing the community often referred to as the unofficial border between southern B.C. and the rest of the province.

"But tonight the whole map counts."

The last party leader from north of Vancouver to win an election was Bill Bennett, who left office in 1986.

Dan Miller served as premier and interim leader of the B.C. NDP for six months while representing the North Coast, but he never led his party in a campaign.

An incoming premier from "beyond Hope" has others expressing optimism for the future of the region, too.

"Having someone from the Cariboo step into this role is a proud moment for our city and region," Williams Lake Mayor Surinderpal Rathor wrote on Facebook.

"I look forward to ensuring the priorities of Williams Lake remain part of the provincial conversation, including health care, public safety, infrastructure and a strong local economy."

"Alex Fraser is smiling tonight," said incoming Quesnel mayor Coralee Oakes, referencing the former B.C. transportation minister, who represented the Cariboo region from 1969 until 1989 and was responsible for many infrastructure projects in the region.

Former B.C. Conservative Party leader Trevor Bolin, now preparing for his first term as mayor of Fort St. John, said he "couldn't be more proud" to see a rural premier-designate getting ready to be sworn in.

Doerkson resides in Williams Lake in B.C.'s Cariboo-Chilcotin region, known for events like the Williams Lake Stampede. (Simon Charland/CBC)

Challenges ahead

Doerkson delved further into what perspective he would bring to the job during a media scrum Sunday morning, directly addressing voters in "rural and northern British Columbia, the Interior, the Peace, the Island and the coast."

"It has been a long time since you've had a premier from where you live," he said.

"I know what it means when the mill closes, when the ER shuts at night and when there's fire on the ridge. Under this government, you will never be an afterthought to the public service."

Speaking as part of the CBC Daybreak North political panel Monday, former B.C. Liberal MLA Shirley Bond, who lives in Prince George, said Doerkson's challenge would be delivering on the message of change he's promised.

"Keeping emergency rooms open, I don't think [anyone] is going to disagree on that," she said. "The question is, how do you get there?"

Likewise, University of Northern British Columbia political scientist Jason Morris said Doerkson would still have to pay attention to the population centres in southern B.C.

LISTEN | Former northern MLAs on B.C. electing a premier from the region: Daybreak North 15:17 Post-election northern B.C. political panel Jennifer Rice, Shirley Bond, and Blair Lekstrom on the new B.C. Conservative majority.

"The role of a premier is to be a formal symbol of the province that is expected to effectively engage with and listen and represent citizens from all parts of the province," he said.

"The balance of the population in British Columbia is concentrated in the metropolis areas of Vancouver and the southern tip of Vancouver Island, and that is always where a significant amount of power and influence is going to be held."

Doerkson has made sure to connect his message to southern B.C. as well, praising businesses in Vancouver and Surrey and stating "a mine opening in the north keeps a port busy in Delta."
