The Bajío region is Mexico’s main data center hub, attracting billions in investment in recent years. ZACATECAS: Miguel Ángel Varela Pinedo, mayor of Zacatecas city and a former federal deputy. Zacatecas is currently governed by Morena under the leadership of Governor David Monreal.

The PAN has not yet named its presumptive gubernatorial candidates in Aguascalientes, Baja California, Campeche, Colima, Guerrero, Nayarit, Nuevo León, Quintana Roo, San Luis Potosí, Sinaloa or Sonora. It is possible that the PAN and the Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) will nominate common gubernatorial candidates in some states. The PRI has not yet named any presumptive gubernatorial candidates.

Morena completed the selection of its 17 “state coordinators for the transformation and national sovereignty” last month. The party founded by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador is currently in office in 23 of Mexico’s 32 federal entities.

With reports from El Financiero, SDP Noticias, Expansión, Político MX and El Economista

World.title: Government turning to AI to solve the acknowledged problem of medication shortages
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum has introduced an Advisory Council for the Digital Transformation of the Health Sector, aimed at improving control, storage and distribution of medications.

The move was in response to supply shortages publicized during recent mobilizations by Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) workers. The president has acknowledged the legitimacy of the complaints.

According to an announcement made during Sheinbaum’s morning press conference on Friday, the council will be divided into two groups of experts.

The first group will be the Advisory Board composed of four researchers specializing in logistics, engineering, information systems, and resource distribution, while the second group — dubbed the Youth AI Team — will be made up of five individuals specialized in Artificial Intelligence.

The project will use digital tools and AI to detect medication shortages, track warehouse inventory and expedite delivery to public hospitals and health centers.

“What we want is to modernize the system to ensure that the entire process — from procurement, warehousing and arrival at the hospital pharmacy, to distribution across various hospital departments and delivery to patients — is automated, so that we know the exact traceability of every medication,” Sheinbaum said on Friday.

Members of the council are expected to present their initial projects in November. The federal government plans to begin implementing the new system in January 2027.

Deputy Health Minister Eduardo Clark said the program aims to identify medication needs in real time, improve inventory management, and optimize distribution routes to reduce both time and costs. If a medication is unavailable at one pharmacy, healthcare staff would be able to determine whether it is in stock at another health facility or warehouse and arrange for its delivery.

The scale of the program’s challenge, however, is considerable.

According to figures presented by Clark, the health sector uses approximately 3 billion units of medicines and medical supplies each year. The products must be distributed among more than 1,000 hospitals and nearly 15,000 health centers and primary care units.

Sheinbaum explained that the lack of medication does not always stem from non-procurement. She noted that there are instances when medications have been purchased but fail to reach medical facilities on time, due to difficulties in the processes of storage, distribution and delivery.

Also, Sheinbaum’s administration recently said it has identified practices in which medications from the public sector end up being sold privately and, in some cases, outside of hospitals.

With reports from Latinus, Eje Central, La Silla Rota and Infobae

World.title: Mining giant Grupo México plans to expand its US copper operations to the tune of US $4-6B
World.content:
The mining and transportation conglomerate Grupo México announced on Thursday plans to double down on its investments in its U.S. copper mining unit, Asarco.

Grupo México plans to spend between US $4 billion and $6 billion over the next three years on Asarco projects, to expand the Ray and Silver Bell mines in Arizona and restart the Hayden smelter and refinery, the head of the mining division, Leonardo Contreras, told analysts on a call.

The investment is far higher than recent spending on the unit, which totaled just $101 million in 2024, and marks a significant expansion in the U.S. market.

It follows news of a 2% fall in copper output during the third quarter due to lower production in the U.S. and Peru. Even so, the firm’s profits grew by 56% during this period to a net profit of US $2 billion, owing to robust base metal prices. Overall revenue increased by 38% to $6.33 billion, surpassing consensus estimates from analysts polled by LSEG.

Corporate leadership has revised the company’s copper production target downward to 1.026 million metric tonnes in 2026, from the previously targeted 1.034 million tonnes.

Contreras emphasized that work is continuing on expanding the Ray facility as feasibility studies are conducted. In addition, the company is “increasingly optimistic” about the restarting of Hayden, which has an annual processing capacity of 1.4 million metric tonnes of copper concentrate.

“That would represent almost 350,000 metric ⁠tonnes of contained copper,” Contreras said. “If that feeds into our refinery, we could be looking at 500,000 metric tonnes of copper.”

The Silver Bell project is also in the feasibility stage, according to Contreras.

Grupo México plans to assess the potential to integrate Mexican concentrates and U.S. copper scrap into U.S. operations, according to Itaú analysts.

Grupo México’s focus on Peru

Grupo México will also continue expanding operations in Peru.

Its long-term growth focuses closely on its Peru operations through its Southern Copper subsidiary, with the delayed flagship Tia Maria project expected to finally come online in the first half of 2028.

Southern Copper is developing two other projects in Peru — Los Chancas and Michiquillay, both of which are expected to commence operations in 2032 and are expected to produce 130,000 and 225,000 metric tonnes of copper a year, respectively.

With reports from Reuters, Mexico Business News and Mexico Now

World.title: Morelia festival wraps 24th edition; ‘Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building’ takes top honors
World.content:
A childhood memory reshaped into fiction won big at the recently concluded Morelia International Film Festival, with “6 meses en el edificio rosa con azul” (“Six Months in a Pink and Blue Building”) taking both the judges’ top prize and the audience award.

The double win — the Ojo for best Mexican feature and the audience award in the same category — marked a meeting of jury and moviegoer tastes that the newspaper El Universal described as rare on the festival circuit.

Trailer de Seis meses en el edificio rosa con azul (HD)

Watch this video on YouTube

The 104-minute Spanish-language drama is the first fiction feature by Bruno Santamaría Razo, a documentary filmmaker born in Mexico City in 1986.

Planned for a 2027 theatrical release in Mexico — with no streaming dates yet announced — the film follows an 11-year-old boy discovering his feelings for his best friend as his family confronts his father’s HIV diagnosis in 1990s Mexico City.

Reconstructing family memories through imagination rather than strictly retelling events, the film premiered at Cannes Critics’ Week, becoming the first Mexican feature to compete in the section in 20 years.

The 24th edition of the Morelia International Film Festival (FICM) was held in the Michoacán capital from Oct. 16 through Sunday.

For its 25th anniversary next year, FICM officials are promising a landmark edition with major guests, bold retrospectives and a stellar lineup — and it will move the dates to the week immediately before the Day of the Dead.

This year’s festival included 96 Mexican films in competition, alongside international screenings, retrospectives and tributes.

The guest list was strong, as usual, with appearances by directors Guillermo del Toro (“Pan’s Labyrinth”) and Alfonso Cuarón (“Roma”), along with “Y Tu Mamá También” stars Diego Luna and Gael García Bernal — underscoring Morelia’s standing as a gathering place for Mexican cinema.

International guests included U.S. director James Gray, who presented “Paper Tiger,” which competed for the Palme d’Or at Cannes this year. The winner at Cannes, “Fjord,” also played in the FICM.

Festival president and Cinépolis CEO Alejandro Ramírez described this year’s event as a particularly Mexican celebration.

Mexican Nicolás Pereda won best director for “Lo demás es ruido” (“Everything Else Is Noise”), an absurdist comedy about a musician preparing for her first television interview. Its star, Teresa Sánchez, also a Mexican, won best actress.

Sam Louwyck of Belgium took best actor for playing a gay hairdresser in Mexican Nathalia Acevedo’s “Salón de belleza” (“Beauty Salon”).

Mexican Joaquín del Paso’s “El jardín que soñamos” (“The Garden We Dreamed”), about a Haitian family traveling north, earned a special mention and the cinematography award.

Mexican Fernanda Tovar received the first-time director award for “Chicas tristes” (stylized as “Sad Girlz” in translation), about two teenage girls supporting each other after one is sexually abused. Pablo Vaca’s “Forensita” won best Mexican documentary feature.

With reports from El Universal, Variety, Animal MX and Proceso

World.title: 4 new international air routes announced, including a direct flight from Italy to Cozumel
World.content:
Mexico is set to expand its international connectivity this coming winter with a new route between Milan and Cozumel operated by the Italian airline Neos, and three new connections from Mexico City to the United States offered by Aeroméxico.

The flight between Milan’s Malpensa Airport and Cozumel will begin operations on Dec. 24, with weekly Thursday flights operating onboard a Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft.

Quintana Roo Governor Mara Lezama referred to the new service as the island’s first direct air connection with Europe.

“We continue to open new doors to the world so that more visitors — travelers of all kinds— can discover the beauty of Cozumel, the ‘Island of the Swallows,’ and everything our Mexican Caribbean has to offer,” Lezama said.

She highlighted the expansion of Cozumel’s airport, which includes a new terminal. According to local media, the airport reported 65% completion in July and is expected to be operational by early 2027.

Aeroméxico’s expansion in the US

Aeroméxico has scheduled daily flights from Mexico City International Airport (AICM) to Santa Ana/Orange County, California; Fort Lauderdale, Florida; and Portland, Oregon.

According to the global aviation analytics company Cirium, cited by Aviation Club Center, the services are set to begin on January 10, 14, and 21, 2027, respectively, using Boeing 737 aircraft. These dates are subject to change before operations commence.

The expansion follows the U.S. Department of Transportation’s decision on Oct. 16 to lift restrictions that had prevented expanded operations from AICM and AIFA. The dispute centered on the allocation of airport slots and the relocation of cargo flights to Felipe Ángeles Airport.

Aeroméxico’s three new services will bring the airline’s total to 21 weekly departures to the U.S.

With reports from Quequi, Aviation Club Center, El Financiero and López Dóriga

World.title: National Electoral Institute president resigns as corruption questions mount
World.content:
Amid allegations of corruption, the president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), Guadalupe Taddei, announced her resignation on Sunday.

“After deep reflection, I have decided to present my resignation tomorrow, Oct. 26, to the Chamber of Deputies of the Congress of the Union,” Taddei said in a statement.

#BoletínINE 📄 | Mensaje de la Consejera Presidenta del Instituto Nacional Electoral, Guadalupe Taddei Zavala. 👇 Los detalles de la información en el enlace. 🔗 https://t.co/KZDmM4qKfV https://t.co/syPTgTYKPn — @INEMexico (@INEMexico) October 25, 2026



“… This decision reflects my conviction that protecting the [National Electoral] Institute and allowing it to continue fulfilling its constitutional mission, must always take precedence over any temporary or personal interest,” she said.

It is the first time since the Federal Electoral Institute (the INE’s predecessor) was founded in 1990 that a president of the electoral authority has resigned. Luis Carlos Ugalde, a former chief of the electoral authority, told Bloomberg Línea that both allegations of corruption against an electoral chief and Taddei’s resignation as INE president are “unprecedented.”

Taddei’s announcement came after Mexican media outlets, including Reforma, El Universal and Latinus, reported last week on alleged irregularities in INE contracts and her ties to businessman José Alfredo Hernández Casillas. The outgoing INE president reportedly has a close personal relationship with Hernández, whose family’s companies have received lucrative INE contracts.

In an article published on Monday under the headline “Taddei is leaving,” the newspaper Reforma noted that it documented how Hernández — who is linked to various electoral materials suppliers — “obtained [electoral authority] contracts since Taddei presided over the electoral organization of Sonora” between 2014 and 2021.

Taddei’s “closeness” to Hernández allowed the latter to obtain contracts awarded by high-ranking INE officials, Reforma reported. The newspaper also reported that Jonathan Navarrete Torres, an employee of Hernández, was on the INE’s payroll as Taddei’s chauffeur without actually working in that role.

In addition, Reforma reported on Monday that it had “revealed” that seven INE suppliers remained under investigation by the federal government’s Financial Intelligence Unit for money laundering and “simulation” in bidding processes. The allegation is that seven companies linked to Hernández and his brother feigned competition for contracts awarded by the INE and the State Electoral Institute in Sonora under Taddei’s leadership.

Reforma also noted that video footage had emerged showing Taddei and two of her children socializing with Hernández.

“One video filmed by the businessman shows a son of Taddei [Jorge Francisco Piñeda Taddei] enjoying a stay at the most expensive hotel in Paris,” Reforma reported. “‘Paris at your feet, young man,’ the businessman says in the video, boasting about the gift.”

The ASF launches an investigation

In light of the various media reports about alleged corruption at the INE, the Federal Auditor’s Office (ASF) announced on Friday that it had begun an investigation into allegations regarding the “improper use of public resources.”

In a statement, the ASF said the investigation “covers” the INE, state-based electoral authorities, companies, public servants and suppliers “that are related to each other.”

The ASF said there is “already evidence … related to irregularities in several contracts” as well as conflicts of interest, collusion and triangulation of resources.”

It said it would investigate allegations involving the INE with “complete independence, objectivity and technical rigor.”

“A Mexico without corruption is possible,” concluded the ASF statement.

Taddei: ‘Each allegation must be examined with evidence’

In her statement on Sunday, Taddei acknowledged the accusations that have been leveled against her.

“I am aware of the allegations that have circulated in the media and on social media in recent days, including rumors, fabrications, leaks and accounts whose authenticity, context and purpose — as in all cases — must be verified and corroborated,” she said.

“… Each allegation must be examined with evidence and through institutional channels,” Taddei said.

In a separate statement on Saturday, she said that “no hiring process, public servant or supplier is above the law.”

Taddei also said that some high-ranking INE officials had been stood down, but she didn’t name them.

The outgoing INE president said on Sunday she was resigning “with calmness and dignity” after dedicating 33 years of her life “to electoral service in Mexico.”

Taddei said her decision “does not relieve anyone of the duty to clarify, with transparency, rigor and due process, the events that must be investigated.”

The 63-year-old Sonora native began what was supposed to be a nine-year term at the INE in early 2023. Mexico News Daily reported at the time that Taddei had family links to both the federal government and the ruling Morena party.

The opposition National Action Party (PAN) said at the time that it was “completely unacceptable that the person who seeks to preside over our electoral umpire is clearly linked to Morena.”

The PAN had called for Taddei’s resignation in light of the corruption allegations outlined in various media reports.

“If contracts were rigged, we are very concerned that elections will be rigged as well,” said PAN national president Jorge Romero.

Sheinbaum endorses Taddei’s decision to resign

At her Monday morning press conference, President Claudia Sheinbaum described Taddei’s decision to step down as INE president as “good.”

“… Obviously, an investigation has to be carried out. … There has to be an audit in order to review the suspicions or the allegations there have been regarding abuses or privileges within the INE,” she said.

Sheinbaum stressed that there will be no interruption to the INE’s work despite Taddei’s decision to resign. One of the INE’s electoral councilors will head up the electoral authority until the Chamber of Deputies appoints a new president.

The INE’s main focus is currently the federal, state and municipal elections that will be held on June 6, 2027.

With reports from EFE, Reforma and Bloomberg Línea

World.title: Blockades reported in Oaxaca, central Mexico and Veracruz as truckers protest insecurity, steep fees
World.content:
Truckers from around the country are protesting and blocking roadways to demand greater security, primarily disrupting traffic at points of entry to the Mexico City Metropolitan Area and in the states of Veracruz and Oaxaca.

Most protests are partial blockades, although a total blockade has been reported along national highway 135D between Tehuacán and Oaxaca.

Over the weekend, national trucking associations said the indefinite national strike could involve as many as 1 million trucks, while warning the public of potential disruptions to the supply of goods and fuel.

Industry representatives have sought to explain the reasons for their strike action, telling the media they “are not seeking to harm families, but rather want answers to their legitimate demands.”

Truckers face what they describe as a “double imposition” — paying steep taxes and high private toll fees, only to receive low-quality, dangerous highway infrastructure in return.

The truckers also object to proposed changes to the toll tax incentive, urging President Claudia Sheinbaum to review the proposal in the 2027 federal budget.

The budget submitted by the Finance Ministry last month would slash fiscal incentives for the freight transportation sector by lowering the annual corporate revenue limit required to qualify for the highway toll tax credit from 300 million pesos down to 250 million pesos.

The lower threshold would impact mid-to-large freight and transport companies making between 250 million and 300 million pesos annually by locking them out of the incentive program.

The National Chamber of Freight Transportation, the largest trucking association in Mexico, claims that the sector is already suffering due to soaring diesel costs and high toll fees. They warn that removing the toll tax safety net will dramatically increase operational costs for dozens of companies, potentially forcing some into bankruptcy.

They also argue it is unfair for the government to strip away tax credits while treating organized crime’s grip on transport routes as “an acceptable condition of doing business.”

Through September, the sector has recorded 1,105 cargo truck robberies and 15 driver fatalities this year.

Truckers previously blockaded highways in April to highlight the need for stronger road security, teaming up with farmers demanding fairer conditions for agricultural producers. They also staged similar actions in November 2025, again teaming up with farmers citing rural sector grievances.

With reports from La Silla Rota, El Financiero, Eje Central and The Latin Times

Sheinbaum also pointed to electronics production as a growth driver.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Sheinbaum’s Monday press conference came a day after Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won the presidential run-off election in Brazil, Latin America’s most populous country.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@claudia_shein)

Lula’s surprise victory over Flávio Bolsonaro, son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, halted a right-wing wave that has recently swept over Latin America.

Sheinbaum made it abundantly clear that the triumph of the 80-year-old incumbent Brazilian president pleased her. She said she would speak with Lula at midday Monday to congratulate him.

Lula’s victory in Brazil after finishing behind Bolsonaro in the first round earlier this month means that the Sheinbaum administration retains an important ideological ally in the region at a time when various other Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia and El Salvador, are ruled by right-wing governments.

At today’s mañanera, Sheinbaum also commented on another significant development on Sunday — Guadalupe Taddei’s announcement that she would resign as president of Mexico’s National Electoral Institute (INE).

Taddei decided to leave the role she has held since 2023 amid corruption allegations related to the INE’s awarding of lucrative contracts to companies linked to José Alfredo Hernández Casillas. According to recent media reports, Taddei has a close personal relationship with Hernández.

Sheinbaum celebrates Lula’s victory in Brazil

“We are happy!” Sheinbaum declared at the very start of her mañanera as she made an L sign with her thumb and index finger.

“We’re very happy with Lula’s triumph in Brazil,” she said.

“Many congratulations to President Lula and the people of Brazil. It’s a breath of fresh air for Latin America and the Caribbean. We’re very, very happy,” Sheinbaum said.

Later in the press conference, she described Lula’s victory as “very important.”

“It’s the triumph of a president, of a people’s movement, of a government that represents its people,” Sheinbaum said.

“It’s the defeat of a rightist movement,” she added.

🇧🇷 La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum expresó su gran alegría por el triunfo electoral de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva en Brasil, calificándolo como “una bocanada de aire fresco” para América Latina y el Caribe. Destacó que esta victoria representa el triunfo de un movimiento popular sobre uno de derecha y reconoce el trabajo del pueblo brasileño para revertir el resultado de la primera vuelta. Asimismo, mencionó que sostendrá una llamada telefónica con Lula para felicitarlo y que evaluarían el momento oportuno para retomar proyectos conjuntos, incluyendo la colaboración entre PEMEX y Petrobras. Más información: https://t.co/JnS6s9oW56 #VideosLaJornada — La Jornada (@lajornadaonline) October 26, 2026

Sheinbaum described Lula’s administration as “similar” to hers before saying that “it makes us feel very happy that a movement like the one Lula represents in Brazil won.”

Sheinbaum endorses Taddei’s decision to resign

Sheinbaum described Taddei’s decision to step down as INE president as “good.”

She noted Taddei made her decision amid allegations of corruption.

“Obviously, an investigation has to be carried out. … There has to be an audit in order to review the suspicions or the allegations there have been regarding abuses or privileges within the INE,” Sheinbaum said.

She subsequently reiterated the view she expressed on Friday, saying that there must be “no hint of corruption” at the INE.

Sheinbaum stressed that there will be no interruption to the INE’s work despite Taddei’s decision to resign. The electoral authority’s main focus is currently the federal, state and municipal elections that will be held on June 6, 2027. The “electoral process” ahead of those elections officially began last month.

Sheinbaum touts strong economic growth in August

Sheinbaum said that year-over-year economic growth of 3.5% in August was “very good news.”

The national statistics agency INEGI reported the growth rate last Friday. It also reported that Mexico’s economy grew 0.6% in August compared to July. Earlier last week, INEGI published preliminary data showing that Mexico’s economy expanded 3.7% year-over-year in September.

Sheinbaum noted that construction, including housing and public infrastructure projects, is helping to drive growth. Construction activity increased 7.9% in August compared to the same month of last year, according to INEGI.

Sheinbaum also noted that the production of electronics is providing momentum to Mexico’s economy. Mexico’s export revenue has surged this year, in large part due to a sharp increase in the shipment to the United States of AI servers and other computer and electronic equipment. However, much of the content in such products is sourced from Asia, particularly Taiwan, limiting Mexico’s share of their total value added.

World.title: Mexico Expects Slower Growth in Friday Data
World.content:
Mexico: Economy

Key Facts When. INEGI, Mexico’s national statistics agency, publishes its first estimate of third-quarter growth on Friday, 30 October.

Forecast. Economists expect about 0.5% growth on the previous quarter, down from 1.4% in April to June.

Clue. INEGI’s own early tracker points to September activity 3.7% above a year earlier.

Peso. The peso trades near 18.56 per US dollar going into the release.

Mexico’s economy has to show on Friday that its summer rebound was more than a one-quarter burst. The number matters well beyond Mexico City, because most of the country’s exports go to the United States.

What Mexico Reports on Friday

INEGI will publish a “flash estimate” of gross domestic product (GDP, the value of everything the economy produces) for July to September. It is an early reading, issued about a month after the quarter ends and before the full accounts.

Two numbers matter. One is growth against the previous quarter, which shows momentum, and the other is growth against the same quarter a year earlier, which shows the broader trend.

Why Economists Expect a Slowdown

The second quarter set a high bar. INEGI’s revised figures show GDP grew 1.4% on the previous quarter and 1.9% on the year in April to June.

Monthly data since then has stayed firm. INEGI’s monthly activity index, known as the IGAE, rose 0.8% in July and 0.6% in August, according to INEGI.

For September, INEGI’s early indicator, which estimates activity before the final data arrive, points to growth of 0.1% on the month and 3.7% on the year. Its confidence range, the band in which INEGI expects the true figure to fall, is wide, from 2.6% to 4.9%, so the final September figure could land well away from that midpoint.

Against that backdrop, forecasters expect a calmer quarter. The consensus in the economic calendar of RT, a financial data provider, is about 0.5% growth on the previous quarter.

Why It Matters for Readers in the United States

Mexico sells most of its exports to the United States, so its growth is a read on demand for American goods and on factories across the border region. Investors holding Mexican bonds or peso positions also watch the figure for hints about interest rates.

A toll plaza on the Mexico City–Puebla motorway. (File photo) Photo: Luisalvaz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A result near 0.5% would fit the picture of steady, unspectacular growth. A reading well below it would raise doubts about the rebound, while a stronger one would back the case that the economy is gathering pace.

The peso, at about 18.56 per US dollar on Tuesday (RT), is the first place a surprise would show. Traders often react within minutes of INEGI’s release.

For earlier context, see our reports on Mexico’s August economic activity and inflation in early October. Our calendar of key market events this week lists the other releases, and the USMCA trade pact between Mexico, the United States and Canada sets the trade backdrop.

More is in our Mexico coverage.

What Is Not Known

A flash estimate can change when INEGI publishes the full quarterly accounts. We found no prediction market on Mexican growth, so there is no market-implied probability to show.

The release also lands in the same week as other major data from the United States and Latin America. That can blur the market’s reaction to Mexico’s number.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Mexico publish third-quarter GDP?

INEGI, Mexico’s statistics agency, publishes its flash estimate on Friday, 30 October 2026. It covers July to September.

What do economists expect?

The consensus in the RT financial-data calendar is about 0.5% growth on the previous quarter. The second quarter grew 1.4%.

World.title: Slovakia Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
SLOVAKIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — Government Prime Minister Robert Fico leads a coalition of his own party Smer-SD, Hlas-SD (a centre-left party) and the nationalist Slovak National Party, SNS.

— President Peter Pellegrini, head of state, refused on 21 October to appoint SNS nominee Filip Kuffa as environment minister.

— Russia Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár led talks in Moscow on 26 October that held the first session of a Russian-Slovak economic commission since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

— Local votes On 24 October Bratislava’s mayor Matúš Vallo won a third term with a preliminary 64.36%.

— Next election Parliamentary elections are due by autumn 2027.

Who Holds Power in Bratislava

Robert Fico, the populist prime minister, holds power in Slovakia, and the live story is a coalition under strain just as his government reopens formal talks with Moscow. Slovakia is a NATO and European Union member of about 5.4 million people, so its choices matter beyond its size.

This guide is part of The Rio Times series on European politics. See also our guides to Spain and Germany’s AfD debate.

For US readers, the country is a test of how much Washington’s European allies can drift on Russia and defence. A single veto from Bratislava can slow EU sanctions and aid to Ukraine.

Slovakia is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister runs the government, and the president is head of state with limited but real powers over appointments.

How the System Works

The National Council, the one-chamber parliament, has 150 seats, and a government needs 76 votes to survive. Voters elect it every four years under a proportional system.

Fico’s party Smer-SD (Direction, Social Democracy) won the 2023 election with 42 seats. It formed a coalition with Hlas-SD (Voice, Social Democracy) on 27 seats and the Slovak National Party, SNS, on 10, giving the three 79 seats at the start.

Since then the majority has become thinner. Several lawmakers have left the SNS and Hlas-SD parliamentary groups, and the coalition’s working margin is now harder to read.

President Peter Pellegrini, a former Hlas-SD leader elected in 2024, appoints and dismisses ministers on the prime minister’s proposal. He has shown he will use that power.

The Fight Over the Environment Ministry

The environment ministry has been vacant since 30 September. On that day Pellegrini dismissed minister Tomáš Taraba, a nominee of the SNS, a day after parliament passed a no-confidence vote in which SNS lawmakers joined the opposition.

Fico then took over the ministry temporarily. The SNS, led by Andrej Danko, proposed its state secretary Filip Kuffa as the replacement.

On 21 October Pellegrini said he would not appoint Kuffa because of a criminal investigation, and he asked Fico for a new name. The investigation concerns suspected procurement manipulation and handling of criminal proceeds, which Kuffa has not been convicted of.

Fico says the coalition agreement obliges him to put forward the partner’s candidate, and he sees no reason to withdraw the nomination. Danko argues the president must act on the presumption of innocence.

A Cabinet Reshuffle and a Shaky Majority

The same week Pellegrini appointed Culture Minister Martina Šimkovičová, an SNS member, as deputy prime minister. The coalition agreement gives each of the three parties that post, and the SNS had lost it with Taraba’s dismissal.

The Taraba vote was one of the most serious crises since the coalition formed in 2023. It showed that a partner can side with the opposition when it feels ignored.

The opposition is led by the liberal Progressive Slovakia, which has challenged Smer in recent polls. The government’s critics say the Kuffa case shows a double standard on ministers under investigation.

Russia, NATO and the EU

On Monday 26 October Blanár led a delegation to Moscow for the 22nd session of the intergovernmental commission on economic and scientific cooperation, with Russia’s science minister Valery Falkov as co-chair. The body had not met since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

The agenda covered energy supplies, nuclear fuel, culture and restrictions on Russian athletes. Opposition parties criticised the trip while the war continues.

Fico has long called for a policy in all directions. On 18 September he said he does not want Slovakia drawn into a military conflict because of ‘some Article 5’, the NATO clause that treats an attack on one member as an attack on all.

The remark drew sharp criticism at home and abroad, including from Czech President Petr Pavel, a former NATO military chief. Slovakia has not formally changed its alliance policy.

At the same time Fico has announced joint government talks with Ukraine in Lviv in early November. Bratislava is trying to keep both channels open.

Budget and Economy

Slovakia is a major car-making centre and one of Europe’s largest producers per head. Its economy has slowed, and the government is cutting spending to bring down a high deficit.

In April 2026 the credit agency S&P Global cut Slovakia’s rating from A+ to A with a stable outlook, citing slow progress on public finances. The independent Council for Budget Responsibility has said the deficit remains above levels typical of an A+ country.

Voters will feel the effects before the 2027 election. Tax rises and cuts are the government’s biggest domestic vulnerability.

Local Elections as a Signal

Slovakia held regional and municipal elections on Saturday 24 October. Preliminary results show Vallo won a third term in Bratislava with 64.36%, against 32.32% for his main challenger, Jozef Raž Jr.

Local votes are a weak guide to a national election. They still show how much support the opposition holds in the cities.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, Slovakia’s euro-area bonds and car-parts supply chains tie it to US companies in Europe. A political crisis would show first in the budget and in the rating.

On security, Fico’s Article 5 comment and the Moscow talks matter to a US government that wants allies to cut energy ties to Russia. Slovakia remains in the Schengen travel area, and nothing in these disputes changes entry rules for US citizens.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether Pellegrini will accept a new nominee, or whether Fico and the SNS will name one. The commitments made in Moscow, especially on energy and nuclear fuel, have not been published in full.

The coalition’s exact number of reliable votes in the National Council is unclear. Nor is it clear how much the local results will shape the 2027 contest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Slovakia’s prime minister in October 2026?

Robert Fico, leader of Smer-SD. He heads a coalition with Hlas-SD and the nationalist Slovak National Party.

When is Slovakia’s next parliamentary election?

It is due by autumn 2027. Slovakia held regional and municipal elections on 24 October 2026.

Why did the president refuse Filip Kuffa?

Pellegrini cited a criminal investigation into Kuffa and asked Fico for another candidate. Fico and the SNS have not withdrawn the nomination.

What happened in Moscow on 26 October?

Slovak and Russian officials held the 22nd session of their economic commission, the first since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Slovakia says it will cooperate where EU sanctions do not apply.

Sources: Government of the Slovak Republic; President of the Slovak Republic; National Council of the Slovak Republic; Statistical Office of the Slovak Republic, election results; Ministry of Foreign and European Affairs of the Slovak Republic; Council for Budget Responsibility.

World.title: Serbia Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
SERBIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — Result The Student List, a movement born in the 2024 protests, won about 53.4% and a projected 140 of 250 seats, with 97.6% of polling stations counted.

— Loser United Serbia, the list of Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), took about 39.7% and a projected 103 seats.

— Turnout About 68.8% of voters took part, roughly ten points more than in 2023.

— Acting head of state Ana Brnabić, the parliamentary speaker, has been acting president since Vučić resigned in late September.

— Next step Parliament must meet, elect a government and an election for president must be held within about three months.

— Prediction markets Kalshi, a prediction market regulated in the US by the CFTC (the federal derivatives regulator), prices a Student-backed candidate at 69% for the next presidential election (27 October, 1:35 a.m. ET).

This story is part of our coverage of the Serbia election 2026. The live odds, the polls and every report on the 25 October vote are in our Serbia election dossier. Latest: Serbia’s Students Celebrate Win in Belgrade

File photo: the House of the National Assembly of Serbia in Belgrade, seat of the 250-member parliament. (Photo: kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Holds Power Today

Serbia’s government is in transition. The Student List, a movement of protest candidates led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanović, has won a parliamentary majority, while Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is on its way out after 14 years.

This guide is part of The Rio Times series on European politics. See also our guides to Spain and Germany’s AfD debate.

For US readers, this matters because Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership, a buyer of Russian energy and a country under American sanctions pressure. A change of government in Belgrade could shift all three at once.

How the System Works

Serbia is a parliamentary republic. The National Assembly, a single chamber with 250 seats, elects the government, and a party needs 126 seats for a majority.

The president is head of state and is elected directly for five years. The prime minister is head of government and runs daily policy, which is why Vučić resigned the presidency to seek that post.

The 25 October Election

Voters went to the polls on Sunday 25 October in a snap election. The Republic Electoral Commission (RIK), the state body that counts the vote, reported the Student List on about 53.4% with 97.6% of polling stations counted on 26 October.

United Serbia, the list led by Vučić’s SNS, had about 39.7%. The projected seat split is 140 for the Student List, 103 for United Serbia and 7 for minority parties, so the students need no coalition partner.

A Defeat Conceded

Vučić conceded defeat on election night, saying a sample-based projection made clear his list had lost. Celebrations followed in Belgrade and other cities.

Turnout was about 68.8%, which is roughly ten points above the 2023 parliamentary election. Figures are preliminary until RIK publishes final results and the new Assembly is formally constituted.

Vučić, Brnabić and the Presidency

Vučić resigned as president in late September to run as SNS candidate for prime minister. Under the constitution the speaker of parliament, Ana Brnabić of the SNS, took over as acting president.

Under the constitution a presidential election must be held within three months, so by about late December. Until then the head of state is a Vučić ally, while the parliamentary majority belongs to his opponents.

Where the Students Came From

The movement grew from protests after a concrete canopy fell at the railway station in Novi Sad on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. Students blamed corruption and weak oversight for the disaster and demanded accountability.

The Student List is largely leaderless and has not named its candidate for prime minister. Its figurehead Srdanović is a professor at the Medical Faculty of the University of Novi Sad.

Serbia, the EU, Russia and Washington

Serbia has been a candidate for EU membership for years but has not joined Western sanctions on Russia. The Student List has stressed independent courts and anti-corruption reform, which are core EU demands, but has said little detail about foreign policy.

Serbia does not recognise Kosovo, which declared independence in 2008, and the movement has not signalled a change. Serbia is not a NATO member and relies on Russian gas.

Energy and the Economy

The central energy issue is NIS, Serbia’s national oil company, whose majority owner is Russia’s Gazprom Neft, an oil producer. The US Treasury sanctioned it in October 2025, and a US licence for talks on selling the 56.15% Russian-held stake to Hungary’s MOL, an oil and gas group, runs to 30 October 2026.

Whoever runs the new government inherits that deal and the refinery at Pančevo, Serbia’s only one. The outcome affects fuel supply and the country’s standing with the US.

What Prediction Markets Say

Kalshi, a prediction market regulated in the United States by the CFTC (the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator), prices a Student-backed candidate at 69% to win Serbia’s next presidential election. An SNS-backed candidate is priced at 1%, and 6,593 contracts have traded.

These prices are bets, not polls, and they were read on 27 October at 1:35 a.m. ET. They show what traders expect, not what any government has promised.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, the question is policy continuity. Serbia is a manufacturing and logistics base for European supply chains, and a government with a clear majority could speed up legal and anti-corruption reforms that foreign companies have wanted.

For security and travel, no disruption to flights or borders has been announced, and the transfer of power is so far peaceful. US readers should watch the NIS sanctions decision and whether Belgrade moves closer to the EU or keeps its balancing act between Brussels and Moscow.

What Is Not Known

It is not yet known who will be prime minister or which ministers will lead the police and security services. The Student List has not named a candidate, and it is unclear whether a movement with no single leader can hold together in office.

Final RIK figures, any complaints and the date of the Assembly’s first session are not yet confirmed. Nor is it known whether Vučić will take any formal role or whether the SNS will contest the presidency again.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who won Serbia’s October 2026 election?

The Student List won about 53.4% and a projected 140 of 250 seats, according to preliminary Republic Electoral Commission figures. Vučić’s United Serbia list took about 39.7%.

Who is Serbia’s head of state now?

Ana Brnabić, the parliamentary speaker, has been acting president since Vučić resigned in late September. A presidential election must be held within three months of his resignation.

How many seats are needed to govern?

The National Assembly has 250 seats, so a majority needs 126. The Student List is projected to hold about 140.

Who will be Serbia’s next prime minister?

That is not yet known. The Student List has not named a candidate, and parliament must first convene and vote on a government.

What sparked the student movement?

The collapse of a station canopy in Novi Sad on 1 November 2024 killed 16 people. Protests over corruption and accountability followed.

Sources: Republic Electoral Commission of Serbia; National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia; Government of Serbia; President of the Republic of Serbia; US Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control.

World.title: Croatia Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
CROATIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — Government Andrej Plenković, prime minister and leader of the centre-right Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), has governed since 2016.

— Latest vote On 21 October parliament rejected a no-confidence motion by 79 votes to 55; 76 were needed to topple the cabinet.

— Trigger Illegally dumped hazardous waste near Gospić, a town in Lika, a region of central Croatia. Remediation is planned for at least 44,000 tonnes.

— Head of state Zoran Milanović, a former Social Democratic prime minister, is the directly elected president with limited powers.

— Next election Parliamentary elections are due by spring 2028; the last was on 17 April 2024.

File photo: the Sabor, Croatia’s parliament, on St Mark’s Square in Zagreb. (Photo: Croativ, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Holds Power in Zagreb

Croatia is a parliamentary republic, so real power sits with the prime minister and the cabinet. Andrej Plenković has led the government since 2016 and heads the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), the country’s dominant centre-right party.

This guide is part of The Rio Times series on European politics. See also our guides to Spain and Germany’s AfD debate.

The president, Zoran Milanović, is elected directly and commands the armed forces. He is a former prime minister of the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and often clashes publicly with Plenković.

How the Sabor Is Divided

The Sabor, as Croatia’s single-chamber parliament is called, has 151 seats. After the April 2024 election the HDZ and its partners hold 61, while a coalition led by the SDP holds 42.

The Homeland Movement (DP), a nationalist party led by Ivan Penava, has 14 seats and is Plenković’s coalition partner. The conservative Most party has 11, the green-left Možemo platform has 10, and eight seats are reserved for national minorities.

The No-Confidence Vote of 21 October

On Wednesday 21 October the Sabor rejected a no-confidence motion against the government, with 79 votes against and 55 in favour. A total of 136 deputies took part, and 76 votes were needed to remove the cabinet.

The SDP, led by Siniša Hajdaš Dončić, filed the motion. According to reports, it was the 44th opposition attempt to unseat Plenković in a decade.

The Gospić Waste Scandal

The motion followed revelations about hazardous waste illegally dumped near Gospić. The opposition says institutions knew of the problem since 2022 but failed to act or warn residents.

Croatia’s anti-corruption prosecutor, known as USKOK, published an expert report on 6 August. It found so-called forever chemicals (PFAS) in groundwater below the site at 200.5 nanograms per litre, twice the 100 nanogram drinking-water limit used in Croatia and the EU.

The Clean-Up Plan and the Blame Game

The government has presented a remediation plan covering at least 44,000 tonnes of waste. About 33,000 tonnes of it is buried waste, a mixture of hazardous and non-hazardous material.

The first phase would remove about 4,500 tonnes of scattered hazardous waste within 12 months for nearly €9 million (about US$10 million). The conversion uses EUR/USD 1.1167 on 27 October.

Coalition Strains and Fresh Appointments

The governing HDZ answered the opposition by pointing to the Jakuševec landfill in Zagreb, which is run by the opposition-led city administration. Nikola Grmoja, a Most party MP, said the government fell the day it let Lika be poisoned, as the debate grew heated.

The Homeland Movement voted with the government. On the same day deputies elected Dražen Miočić director of the public broadcaster HRT and made Armin Hodžić, a deputy of the Bosniak minority, vice-president of the Sabor.

Croatia in the EU and NATO

Croatia joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013. It adopted the euro and entered the Schengen travel zone on 1 January 2023.

Plenković has kept Zagreb firmly aligned with Brussels and Washington. His government’s positions on security and trade rarely diverge from the EU mainstream.

What It Means for US Readers

Croatia is a NATO ally and a euro-area economy on the Adriatic, so its political stability matters to US investors and security planners. A government that survives repeated confidence votes points to policy continuity on EU funds, defence and energy.

Americans travelling to Croatia face no change from the waste dispute, which is regional and tied to one site in Lika. Visitors should still check official travel guidance before departure.

What Is Not Known

It is not yet known whether the Gospić site has caused wider contamination beyond the groundwater findings, or who will bear legal responsibility. Prosecutors have not announced further charges in connection with the political debate.

No early election has been called, and the date of the next vote remains spring 2028 at the latest.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Croatia’s prime minister in 2026?

Andrej Plenković, leader of the Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ), has been prime minister since 2016. His government survived a no-confidence vote on 21 October 2026.

What does Croatia’s president do?

President Zoran Milanović is head of state and commander of the armed forces. He is directly elected, but executive power rests with the prime minister.

How did the no-confidence vote end?

Parliament rejected the motion on 21 October with 79 votes against and 55 in favour. At least 76 of the 151 deputies had to back it.

What is the Gospić waste scandal?

Hazardous waste was illegally dumped near Gospić in Lika. The government has presented a plan to remediate at least 44,000 tonnes.

When is Croatia’s next election?

Parliamentary elections are due by spring 2028, four years after the vote of 17 April 2024. No early election has been called.

Sources: Croatian Parliament (Sabor); Government of Croatia; State Election Commission of Croatia; President of Croatia; Ministry of Environmental Protection and Green Transition; Office for Suppression of Corruption and Organised Crime (USKOK).

World.title: Bulgaria Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
BULGARIA · POLITICS

Key Facts — Who holds power Prime Minister Rumen Radev leads Progressive Bulgaria, his party, which holds 131 of 240 seats in the National Assembly, Bulgaria’s parliament.

— Runoff Sunday 1 November 2026: Iliana Iotova, the sitting president, faces Andrey Gyurov, a former central bank deputy governor. Polls close 8 p.m. local time (1 p.m. ET).

— First round On 25 October Iotova won 34.76% and Gyurov 31.95%. Turnout was 22.93%, very low.

— Security Drone strikes on merchant ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast in October put Russia policy at the centre of the race.

— Money Bulgaria joined the euro on 1 January 2026. The government has yet to present its 2027 state budget.

— Prediction markets Polymarket, a prediction market, prices Iliana Iotova at 69.5% and Andrey Gyurov at 28.5% to win the presidency (27 October, 1:35 a.m. ET).

File photo: the National Assembly building in Sofia, seat of Bulgaria’s 240-member parliament. (Photo: Лорд Бъмбъри, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Who Holds Power Today

Prime Minister Rumen Radev runs Bulgaria’s government, backed by an absolute majority in parliament, and the live story is a presidential runoff on Sunday 1 November. For US readers the contest matters because Bulgaria is a NATO member on the Black Sea, where drones have recently hit merchant ships.

This guide is part of The Rio Times series on European politics. See also our guides to Spain and Germany’s AfD debate.

Radev is a former air force general who served as president from 2017 until January 2026. He resigned that post to lead his new party into the April election, and parliament voted him prime minister on 8 May 2026.

How the System Works

Bulgaria is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister heads the government and sets policy, while the president is head of state with mostly ceremonial duties.

The president can send laws back to parliament and names the caretaker prime ministers who run the country between governments. The president also chairs the Consultative Council on National Security and is commander-in-chief of the armed forces.

Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Parliament is the 240-seat National Assembly. At the 19 April 2026 election, Progressive Bulgaria won about 43.9% of the vote and 131 seats, an outright majority.

GERB, the long-dominant centre-right party, took 39 seats. PP-DB, a pro-Western alliance of We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria, took 37, and the remaining seats went to two smaller parties, the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (21) and Revival (12).

Voters elect the president directly for a five-year term, on a joint ticket with a vice president. Parliament serves four years, so the next general election is due by spring 2030 unless the government falls early.

The First Round on 25 October

Iotova, a former journalist and member of the European Parliament, served as Radev’s vice president from 2017 until she took over the presidency. That link explains why the runoff is read as a verdict on the prime minister’s first six months.

Iliana Iotova, who succeeded Radev as president in January 2026, won 34.76% of the vote. Andrey Gyurov, a former deputy governor of the Bulgarian National Bank who briefly served as caretaker prime minister this year, took 31.95%.

Neither passed the 50% mark, and only 22.93% of 6.64 million registered voters took part. That is far below the roughly 40% of the 2021 first round and reflects deep fatigue after years of repeated elections.

Iotova is backed by Radev’s Progressive Bulgaria and by the Bulgarian Socialist Party, the post-communist left. Gyurov is backed by the pro-Western We Continue the Change and Democratic Bulgaria alliance.

Kostadin Kostadinov, leader of the nationalist Revival party, came third with 12.5%. His voters could decide the runoff, though he has no formal power over where they go.

What Happens on 1 November

The runoff between Iotova and Gyurov takes place on Sunday 1 November. Polls close at 8 p.m. Bulgarian time, which is 1 p.m. ET, and counting begins immediately.

Iotova stresses peace through negotiation with Russia, while Gyurov stresses Bulgaria’s Euro-Atlantic ties, according to their campaigns. A Gyurov win would put a president from the opposition beside a government that holds a firm majority.

Both candidates need more votes than the other, so the winner needs only a simple majority of votes cast in the second round. The Central Election Commission, Bulgaria’s electoral authority, publishes preliminary results overnight and certified results within days.

The Black Sea and Russia

On 13 October drones attacked two merchant ships off Bulgaria’s coast and one sank. Radev said Bulgaria lacks clear and conclusive evidence to blame either side, but that “the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation”, and he summoned the Russian ambassador.

One of the ships, the HS Dignity, sank with 11 sailors reported missing. Bulgaria has not named a culprit.

Budget and Economy

Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026 and has been in the Schengen travel area in full since 1 January 2025. The 2026 deficit is about 5% of economic output on the government’s updated forecast, and Brussels has placed Bulgaria under an excessive deficit procedure, a formal review of overspending.

The 2027 plan aims for a deficit of about 4.3%. Bulgaria sent its draft budgetary plan to the European Commission, the EU executive, on 15 October.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a prediction market where US$2.2 million has been traded, prices Iliana Iotova at 69.5% to win Bulgaria’s presidential election. Andrey Gyurov is priced at 28.5%.

These prices are bets, not polls, and they were read on 27 October at 1:35 a.m. ET. They show what traders expect, not what the voters will decide on 1 November.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, Bulgaria is a euro-area member with a government that holds a stable majority, so the runoff is unlikely to change fiscal policy. The 2027 budget draft and the deficit path are the numbers to watch, since a euro-area member in a deficit procedure is a credit-quality question for bond buyers.

Bulgarian eurobonds and local banks now trade on euro-area terms, which removes currency risk that once worried US funds.For security and shipping, the drone strikes raise insurance and routing questions for vessels near Romanian and Bulgarian ports.Americans can travel in Bulgaria without a visa for short stays, and the Schengen membership means no passport checks on most European land and air links.

What Is Not Known

Nobody knows who will win on 1 November. The first-round gap was under three percentage points, and turnout was so low that a small shift among Kostadinov’s voters or the many who stayed home could change the result.

Responsibility for the drone attacks has not been officially established. When the government will present the domestic 2027 state budget, and whether that is late under the Public Finance Act, is also not settled.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who holds power in Bulgaria?

Prime Minister Rumen Radev, whose Progressive Bulgaria party holds 131 of 240 seats in parliament. President Iliana Iotova is head of state with largely ceremonial powers.

When is Bulgaria’s presidential runoff?

Sunday 1 November 2026. Polls close at 8 p.m. Bulgarian time, which is 1 p.m. ET, and the choice is Iliana Iotova or Andrey Gyurov.

What was the first-round result?

Iotova won 34.76% and Gyurov 31.95% on 25 October. Turnout was 22.93% of about 6.64 million registered voters.

Does the runoff change who runs the government?

Not directly. The prime minister and cabinet depend on parliament, where Progressive Bulgaria has a majority, but the president can return laws and appoint caretaker governments.

Is Bulgaria in the euro and Schengen?

Yes. Bulgaria joined the euro on 1 January 2026 and became a full Schengen member on 1 January 2025.

Sources: Central Election Commission of Bulgaria; National Assembly of Bulgaria; Government of Bulgaria; President of Bulgaria; Ministry of Finance of Bulgaria; Bulgarian National Bank.

World.title: Finland Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
FINLAND · POLITICS

Key Facts — Who governs Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (National Coalition Party, conservative) leads a four-party government holding 108 of 200 seats won in 2023.

— Head of state President Alexander Stubb, in office since March 2024, leads foreign and security policy together with the government.

— Next vote Parliamentary election on Sunday 18 April 2027; advance voting runs 7 to 13 April.

— Polls The opposition Social Democrats lead the latest poll for Yle, the public broadcaster, at 22.6%, with the Finns Party and Orpo’s party level for second.

— Budget The 2027 draft budget spends €92.2 billion (US$103.0 billion) and runs a €12.9 billion (US$14.4 billion) deficit.

Who Holds Power

Finland is governed by Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, leader of the National Coalition Party, a centre-right and pro-business party. The live story is a coalition that is trailing in the polls six months before a general election.

This guide is part of The Rio Times series on European politics. See also our guides to Spain and Germany’s AfD debate.

Orpo took office in June 2023 at the head of a coalition of four parties. They are his National Coalition Party, the nationalist Finns Party, the Swedish People’s Party (which represents Finland’s Swedish-speaking minority) and the Christian Democrats.

How the System Works

Finland is a parliamentary republic. The 200-seat Parliament, called the Eduskunta, makes the laws and approves the budget, and the prime minister needs its confidence to stay in office.

President Alexander Stubb, elected in 2024, is head of state and directs foreign policy jointly with the government. The Finns Party leader, Riikka Purra, is the finance minister and so owns the budget.

The Seat Count

The April 2023 election gave the National Coalition Party 48 seats and the Finns Party 46. The Social Democrats won 43, the Centre Party 23, the Greens 13, the Left Alliance 11, the Swedish People’s Party 9 and the Christian Democrats 5, with two further seats held by small groups.

The four government parties together hold 108 seats, a comfortable majority of 200. Small changes in group membership may have occurred since 2023, so readers should treat these figures as the election result, not today’s roll.

The Fight Over Money

The government’s 2027 draft budget, presented by Purra on 4 August 2026, totals €92.2 billion (US$103.0 billion). It carries a deficit of €12.9 billion (US$14.4 billion), converted at EUR/USD 1.1167.

Parliament must still pass the final budget. The size of the deficit will shape the campaign.

The Bigger Fight After the Election

A cross-party working group has calculated that Finland needs €8 billion to €11 billion (US$8.9 billion to US$12.3 billion) of savings and tax rises over the next four-year term to meet its 2031 fiscal targets. All parliamentary parties except the Left Alliance signed up to that framework, and the working group is due to review it in December 2026.

The parties now disagree on how to deliver it. The National Coalition Party and the Finns Party want most of the adjustment from lower public spending, while the Left Alliance, a left-wing party, has proposed a tax-based package of about €9 billion (US$10.1 billion).

Polls and the April 2027 Vote

The election is set for Sunday 18 April 2027, with advance voting from 7 to 13 April. In the latest monthly poll by Taloustutkimus, a polling firm working for the public broadcaster Yle, the Social Democrats lead on 22.6%.

The Finns Party and Orpo’s party are level for second place, with the gap inside the margin of error. The Centre Party, a rural-liberal party, and the Left Alliance trail behind.

Russia, NATO and Ukraine

Finland joined NATO on 4 April 2023 and shares a long land border with Russia. Security policy has broad cross-party backing, so the election is unlikely to change it.

Orpo visited Kyiv on 22 October. Finland takes part in UNIFIL, the United Nations peacekeeping force in Lebanon, until the mission ends at the end of 2026.

NATO’s High Level Group, an advisory body on nuclear policy, met in Helsinki on 21 October. The meeting shows how closely Helsinki now sits inside the alliance.

A World First in Nuclear Waste

On 22 October the government granted Posiva, the company owned by Finland’s nuclear utilities, an operating licence for the world’s first permanent disposal site for spent nuclear fuel. The site is at Olkiluoto on the west coast, where spent fuel will be sealed in copper canisters deep underground.

The licence follows a favourable safety assessment from STUK, Finland’s radiation and nuclear safety authority, on 4 August. Operations will not start at once, because Posiva and STUK must first complete commissioning.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors, Finland is a euro-area economy with a large deficit and a government under pressure to cut spending. The 2027 budget runs a €12.9 billion (US$14.4 billion) deficit, so the savings debate after April will matter for bondholders and for US firms with Finnish operations.

On security, Finland is a frontline NATO member and a close defence partner of the United States. Travel to Finland is routine, and nothing in the government’s recent announcements changes who holds executive power.

What Is Not Known

No one knows yet which parties will form the next government. The Social Democrats lead, but the poll gaps among the second to fifth parties are small, and the Finns Party and Orpo’s party are level.

It is also unclear how the €8 billion to €11 billion adjustment will be split between cuts and tax rises. The parties will publish rival programmes in the months ahead, and none has yet committed to a final mix.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Finland’s prime minister in 2026?

Petteri Orpo of the National Coalition Party. He has led a four-party coalition since June 2023.

When is Finland’s next parliamentary election?

Sunday 18 April 2027, with advance voting from 7 to 13 April. All 200 seats in Parliament are contested.

Who is Finland’s president?

Alexander Stubb, in office since March 2024. He directs foreign and security policy together with the government.

Which parties are in Finland’s government?

The National Coalition Party, the Finns Party, the Swedish People’s Party and the Christian Democrats, with 108 of 200 seats won in 2023.

Which party leads the polls?

The opposition Social Democrats, at 22.6% in the Yle poll conducted from 7 September to 5 October 2026.

Sources: Government of Finland, draft budget 2027; Government of Finland, Posiva operating licence; Ministry of Justice of Finland, elections; Parliament of Finland; Finnish Government, Prime Minister’s Office; NATO, official website.

World.title: Ireland Politics Explained, Who Holds Power in 2026
World.content:
IRELAND · POLITICS

Key Facts — Who governs Taoiseach (prime minister) Micheál Martin of Fianna Fáil leads a coalition with Fine Gael, backed by independent members of parliament.

— Head of state Catherine Connolly, an independent, is President of Ireland, a largely ceremonial role. She took office on 11 November 2025.

— Live fights Criminal defence solicitors are boycotting new legal aid rules, and the Dáil has backed a bill to scrap the UN mandate condition (the “triple lock”) for troop deployments.

— Budget Budget 2027 is worth €8.5 billion (about US$9.5 billion), including €1.5 billion (US$1.7 billion) of tax measures.

— EU role Ireland holds the rotating EU Council presidency from 1 July to 31 December 2026.

File photo: Leinster House in Dublin, seat of the Oireachtas, Ireland’s parliament. (Photo: David Kernan, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

How The System Works

Ireland is a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union. The Taoiseach (pronounced “TEE-shock”), the prime minister, holds real executive power and is nominated by the Dáil, the lower house of parliament.

This guide is part of The Rio Times series on European politics. See also our guides to Spain and Germany’s AfD debate.

The President is directly elected and mostly ceremonial. Catherine Connolly, an independent, has held the office since 11 November 2025.

The Dáil has 174 seats and the Seanad is the appointed and indirectly elected upper house. Together they form the Oireachtas, Ireland’s parliament, and no government can pass laws without a Dáil majority.

Who Holds Power Today

Fianna Fáil, a centre-right party, and Fine Gael, its traditional rival, govern together under Micheál Martin. Simon Harris of Fine Gael is Tánaiste (deputy prime minister) and Minister for Finance.
