World.title: BAROMÈTRE DU REJET : Le Pen, toujours moins rejetée
World.content:
Pour l’emporter en 2027, un prétendant à la présidence doit donc formuler un nouveau vœu : plutôt que de rêver d’être majoritaire dans le pays, se contenter d’espérer être le moins exécré des compétiteurs. Ce que mesure notre baromètre mensuel du rejet, réalisé par Cluster 17 pour POLITICO, dont la deuxième livraison montre que les grandes tendances observées en septembre s’accentuent et témoigne d’un moment de la campagne “plutôt favorable aux droites” (traditionnelle et extrême), analyse Jean-Yves Dormagen, le président de l’institut.

Logique : notre enquête a été menée du 19 au 22 octobre, juste après les casses et pillages du 17 octobre.

Cluster 17 a, de nouveau, demandé à 3 000 personnes quelle était la probabilité, sur une échelle de 0 à 10, qu’elles votent “un jour” pour chacun des candidats à la présidentielle testés — 0 correspondant à une impossibilité totale de glisser ce bulletin dans l’urne, 10 indiquant que les sondés jugent “tout à fait possible” de le faire.

Seul motif de satisfaction pour Edouard Philippe et Gabriel Attal : la priorité des Français est davantage de faire barrage au camp RN ou au camp Insoumis plutôt qu’au bloc central. | Daniel Perron/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images

Tous les candidats testés demeurent rejetés par une majorité de Français. Les plus répulsifs restent les mêmes, mais ils voient augmenter le taux de Français excluant totalement de voter pour eux. L’Ecologiste Marine Tondelier arrive ainsi toujours en tête du classement du rejet, à 71% (+3 par rapport au mois dernier) — à égalité cette fois avec Eric Zemmour, non testé dans notre précédente enquête.

Mélenchon de plus en plus repoussoir

Même logique pour Jean-Luc Mélenchon. Toujours en deuxième position des personnalités les plus rejetées, l’Insoumis l’est encore plus qu’en septembre. Les interrogés sont désormais 69% à juger inimaginable de choisir un bulletin au nom de l’Insoumis (ils étaient 66%).

Les violences du week-end des 17 et 18 octobre ont “radicalisé sur la droite un certain nombre de personnes”, juge Dormagen. Et ainsi conforté l’image négative de “JLM”, augmentant la perception de LFI comme “un mouvement radical, qui incarne une rupture brutale”.

World.title: Tobacco lobby steps up Brussels push as EU rewrites rules
World.content:
Meetings with tobacco and nicotine groups have ramped up this term as the EU seeks to overhaul several key pieces of tobacco and nicotine legislation. The EU has also proposed measures this session to curb heart disease and cancer, plans that also affect the sector.

Some MEPs have called out the tobacco industry’s access to lawmakers as they negotiate measures to prevent addiction and disease caused by the sector’s products, such as in a cardiovascular disease strategy report and cancer plan.

“I find it scandalous and shocking that there are more meetings with the tobacco industry than the NGOs and the associations that advocate for stop smoking,” Tilly Metz, a lawmaker with the Greens/European Free Alliance, said.

“When you are working on health files, it is completely incompatible to regularly meet with the tobacco industry,” she said. Metz referenced the World Health Organization’s tobacco control treaty, which says policymakers should meet with tobacco lobbyists only when strictly necessary to discuss the sector's regulation.

The tobacco industry and MEPs who regularly meet with industry say they have done nothing wrong.

British American Tobacco’s head of fiscal affairs, Simon Trussler, said that like any other business in Europe, it had legitimate experiences and arguments to put forward “because we see what's going on on the ground.”

World.title: Frontex set for new powers to deport beyond EU borders in latest overhaul
World.content:
The push comes just months after EU lawmakers approved a new “return regulation” aimed at accelerating deportations and allowing member countries to establish controversial deportation hubs outside the EU.

With the legal framework largely agreed, Brussels is now turning its attention to enforcement — and to the agency expected to help make the new rules work in practice.

Political pressure has also been mounting. In June, the leaders of 19 EU countries urged the Commission to support the establishment of return hubs outside the bloc, including through EU funding, as first reported by POLITICO.

The proposed Frontex overhaul, which is on the College of Commissioners’ agenda and is expected to be approved by the EU executive on Oct. 27, would help put that broader shift into practice by giving the agency more resources, greater operational flexibility and an expanded role in carrying out returns beyond EU borders, including transfers between third countries.

Emergency response

But deportations are only part of the equation.

The Commission also wants to transform Frontex into a force that can intervene in border emergencies within 24 hours, according to the two officials.

World.title: European defense ministers warn Putin isn’t looking for peace
World.content:
The meeting came amid a renewed U.S. effort to push Ukraine into peace talks with Russia and growing doubts about Washington's support for Kyiv.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff said last week he would offer Russia's Vladimir Putin direct talks with President Donald Trump and Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy to secure a ceasefire.

"No results whatsoever comes for those who want to negotiate with Putin," German defense minister Boris Pistoripus said. "The results are what? It doesn't lead to anything. There is no signal whatsoever that Putin is looking for peace."

The U.K.'s Wes Streeting added: "While none of us seek confrontation with Russia ... We do have to be aware of the threat posed by Russia."

While pledging "total transparency" with the U.S., France's Catherine Vautrin said the E5 members would "work together concretely," focusing on arms production and interoperability.

"Produce more, produce faster, produce equipment suited to today’s conflicts – but we must already be planning for the conflicts of tomorrow," Vautrin said. "On that, EU financial initiatives can help us move in this direction."

World.title: French government fails to convince students to stop protests
World.content:
Students have demanded up to 250,000 extra places in higher education and universities, better conditions in educational institutions, more teachers and a major overhaul of the selection process for university entry.

On Monday, the government told students it would look into reforming France’s university admissions platform, Parcoursup, which student groups consider opaque and a source of inequality, starting in 2028. It also promised more money to renovate schools, an extra 15,000 places in higher education in industry, health and technical education, and a maximum of 28 students per classroom in the first year of high school.

Those measures, widely reported by French media and confirmed by student representatives who attended the meetings, will be detailed at a press conference later this evening.

But university students are not impressed.

“Once again, the government is missing the point. If the government’s strategy is to show contempt for our demands, then we will remain mobilized in the streets and on university campuses, and we won’t back down,” university union UNEF said earlier in the afternoon, when news of the government’s proposals began to circulate.

Student demonstrations and blockades in schools and universities earlier this month were among the first expressions of broader social unrest, which later turned into protests over the cost of living and spiraled into riots two weeks ago.

World.title: 7 big questions as Britain hikes defense spending
World.content:
Even on the smaller measure, the margins for the chancellor are tight, with government spending rules and debt targets leaving little room for maneuver. Mike Martin, an MP on the House of Commons Defense Committee, told POLITICO: “They have got themselves into a straitjacket over defense spending and none of this will be resolved before the next election. This is why I think an early general election is inevitable.”

2) Will the chancellor move to funnel private capital into defense?

Britain's defense industry has long called for more direct government spending on domestic contracts. But the sector also wants more private capital flowing into U.K. firms, and will be looking to Healey to set the conditions.

The Financial Times reported last week that Healey will allocate £15.4 billion to the country’s National Wealth Fund and £5 billion to the British Business Bank — a share of which could end up with defense companies.

Two key details to watch here are whether the government claims this money counts towards its wider defense spending commitments, or whether any cash is allocated purely for defense firms. Potential reforms to and incentives for pools of private capital, such as pension funds and venture capital funds, to invest in defense would also be welcomed by the sector in this budget — but the industry may be left waiting.

One of the government officials cited above said that a Defence Finance and Investment Strategy is slated for December, with a Defense Investment Summit coming December 1.

3) Where does Healey stand on global defense team-ups?

On Sunday evening, the Treasury disclosed that it would not join the Canadian-led Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB) — a proposed multinational financial institution with its own AAA credit rating that aims to provide cheap loans for countries to invest in defense.

World.title: Deadly parasite: how fox tapeworm warns of pandemic X
World.content:
The warning about fox tapeworm is something almost everyone in Germany has heard if they have ever wanted to pick berries or collect mushrooms in the forest. The concern is that the tapeworm eggs could be stuck to them - a parasite that attacks the liver and can cause a potentially life-threatening disease.

 

This disease is one of 21 illnesses that the World Health Organization WHO has placed on its list of NTDs. These so-called "Neglected Tropical Diseases (NTDs)", known in German as "vernachlässigte Tropenkrankheiten", are regarded as a global early-warning system.

"Wherever NTDs occur, they mark the weak points in the global health system, precisely because there is no system in place there," explains Dr. Dr. Carsten Köhler from the University of Tübingen in an interview with Euronews. He heads, among other things, the Institute of Tropical Medicine, Travel Medicine and Human Parasitology and is president of the German Society for Tropical Medicine, travel medicine and global health.

NTDs can therefore show where medical care, disease surveillance and reliable data are lacking. Precisely in such places, infectious diseases may remain undetected for a long time - with consequences that can reach far beyond the regions directly affected.

Fox tapeworm: Is it still a threat?

The parasite measures only two to six millimetres but can cause severe liver disease in humans. The medical term is alveolar echinococcosis. Adult tapeworms live in the small intestine of foxes and occasionally also in the intestines of dogs and cats.

These animals are then the so-called "definitive hosts" of the tapeworms.

To explain: in biology and medicine, a definitive host is the organism in which a parasite reaches sexual maturity and reproduces. Many parasites have a complex life cycle and change their host - their "home" - during their lifetime. Example: a mouse (intermediate host) ingests the tapeworm eggs. Larvae develop inside the mouse. A fox (definitive host) eats the mouse. In the fox's intestine, the larvae develop into adult tapeworms, which then mate and produce new eggs. The fox is therefore the definitive host.

According to the Bavarian State Office for Health and Food Safety (LGL), the most important definitive host in central Europe is the red fox. Infection in humans is very rare but, if it occurs, can be life-threatening.

In 2024, 52 infections were recorded at the Robert Koch Institute (RKI); in previous years the number in humans mostly lay between 40 and 45 cases. According to the German Liver Aid, the majority of cases come from the southern federal states of Baden-Württemberg and Bavaria. Depending on the region, between 33 and 50 percent of foxes are infected with the parasite.

Echinococcosis is one of the neglected tropical diseases that occur in Germany. But according to Köhler, leishmaniases are now also knocking at the door. This infectious disease can present in different ways and is transmitted by tiny sandflies.

"Many Germans like to travel to the Mediterranean region on holiday and can then bring it back with them," Köhler explains in the interview with Euronews. According to the health magazine of the AOK health insurer, the disease is often curable if it is detected and treated early. The WHO estimates that around 700,000 to one million people worldwide fall ill with leishmaniases every year.

However, most of the 21 neglected tropical diseases occur above all in parts of the world whose health systems are less developed than Germany's.

New neglected disease identified

For example, in 2026 the state of Gabon in Central Africa submitted an application to the World Health Organization WHO to have another disease added to the list of NTDs. "Only endemic countries are allowed to submit applications," Köhler explains. In this case it concerns Loa loa disease, a so-called eye worm. According to Köhler, the WHO will deliberate on the request.

The parasite is transmitted by horseflies. The worms can move through the subcutaneous tissue and sometimes become visible under the conjunctiva of the eye. Infection may be accompanied by itching, swelling and other complaints.

In Köhler's view, the WHO should consider the application. However, in October 2026 the responsible WHO advisory committee recommended a temporary pause in adding new diseases. First, the criteria and procedures for inclusion on the list are to be fundamentally reviewed.

"NTDs occur in regions where the health system does not exist or is only rudimentary," Köhler continues. The diseases themselves are not automatically a danger to the global population. What matters far more is what they reveal about the conditions under which infections can spread: lack of medical care, inadequate monitoring and gaps in the recording of disease cases. There is also a risk that illnesses with pandemic potential may emerge and spread there.

NTDs as an early-warning system for potential endemics

So-called community health workers operate in such regions. They go from community to community, inform the population and observe the local health situation. "A community health worker who is looking out for a worm infection that itself has no pandemic potential would still notice if, all of a sudden, an entire family had died and could report that immediately," says tropical medicine specialist Köhler.

They can recognise illnesses, refer people to medical facilities and report unusual developments to the responsible authorities. "That is why we say these structures can be used as an early-warning system if such basic services have already been set up for NTDs," he explains in his interview with Euronews at the World Health Summit.

The advantage is that helpers are already present in the communities. If NTD programmes are already running in these regions, diseases with pandemic potential are likely to be detected earlier.

Emergency structures do not have to be created from scratch when a new infectious disease appears. If staff are already supporting people with neglected tropical diseases, they can at the same time observe changes that point to other health threats. The work of health workers is also about collecting data as comprehensively as possible.

For this reason, in its strategy to combat neglected tropical diseases up to 2030 the WHO is also relying on integrated approaches: measures are to be more firmly embedded in existing health systems and linked with other areas of public health.

Ebola outbreak: data gap noticed too late

The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo showed exactly how problematic missing data can be, says Köhler. "In fact we had expected an outbreak in other hotspots," explains the director of the Centre for Tropical Medicine. "Then we had to realise that the data for the Democratic Republic of Congo were out of date."

When up-to-date information from a region is lacking, health authorities may misjudge the risk. Contact tracing and the targeted deployment of medical staff and supplies also become more difficult.

Local health workers are therefore not only vital for the treatment of individual diseases; they also help to detect outbreaks earlier and to coordinate the response more effectively.

In some cases, the withdrawal of the USA from health promotion has also made data collection in affected areas more difficult. "Because funding from the USA has fallen so sharply, the community health worker structures that were built up over recent decades have collapsed dramatically," Köhler explains.

The missing funds meant, among other things, that former health workers had to give up their jobs. According to UNAIDS, as a result of US funding cuts, thousands of community health workers in Malawi were affected by contract terminations in 2025. The organisation also reported restrictions in the electronic recording of health data.

A study published in 2026 from Zambia likewise describes how cuts in international development aid undermined the work of health facilities. Staff reported lay-offs, a lack of diagnostic tests and difficulties in using electronic patient records. The result: less comprehensive health data.

The next pandemic: Disease X

A new pandemic triggered by Ebola is not considered likely, as the risk varies greatly from disease to disease. While in the case of coronavirus, for example, droplet infection was enough, Ebola mainly threatens people who come into contact with the body fluids of infected patients.

Neglected tropical diseases likewise do not automatically have pandemic potential. A high number of NTD cases is rather a possible indication that medical care and surveillance in a region need to be strengthened.

"We should prepare for the next pandemic, which the WHO calls Disease X, whatever it turns out to be," warns Köhler. It is assumed that Covid-19 will not have been the last pandemic; only the timing cannot be predicted.

Preparation therefore means not only developing vaccines and medicines. It also includes having laboratories, specialist staff, data infrastructures and international networks in place that can work together quickly in an emergency. Köhler points to the importance of European and international cooperation.

"That is why I very much hope that programmes such as the European Vaccine Hub for Pandemic Preparedness (EvH) or the European & Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership (EDCTP) continue to receive support," Köhler says in his Euronews interview. These programmes bring together research structures, laboratory capacity and experts.

"It is important to create a platform now that enables very rapid action and to have functioning cooperative structures in place when this Disease X arrives," Köhler stresses. "For that you need a network. Health has no borders, and neither do pathogens."

World.title: Europe must prepare for a 3°C warmer world, EU climate chief warns
World.content:
The European Commission will unveil new climate rules on Tuesday requiring EU governments to clarify who is responsible for protecting citizens from climate disasters, Climate Action Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra told Euronews.

 

The move comes as Brussels warns that Europe must prepare for increasingly extreme weather, including scenarios involving 3°C of global warming by 2100.

Hoekstra warned that the world is heading towards a temporary or potentially prolonged overshoot of the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming limit, making it essential for governments to prepare for more extreme heat and climate disasters, even if efforts to cut emissions succeed.

“It is up to member states to decide where they want to put that responsibility. But what we do make mandatory is that they do have to appoint and articulate where the responsibility is going to lie,” Hoekstra said.

While the EU continues to pursue emissions reductions, the costs of adapting to a hotter world are becoming harder to ignore, from rebuilding after wildfires and floods to protecting homes, roads and public infrastructure.

The Dutch Commissioner estimated the economic damage from this summer's extreme weather at more than €100 billion.

Related EU wildfire strategy falls short as southern Europe faces another devastating fire season

Asked what a 3°C rise above pre-industrial temperatures could mean for Europeans, Hoekstra pointed to heat plans for cities and the need to prepare infrastructure for a hotter future, rather than relying on historical weather patterns.

The reference trajectory is based on scientific research, including work by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change and advanced European climate modeling, he said.

The Commission's projections envisage 2°C of global warming by 2050 and 3°C by 2100 for Europe, reflecting Brussels' assessment that Europe is warming roughly twice as fast as the global average.

The trajectory is intended to be translated into national and local risk assessments, taking account of the uneven distribution of climate impacts.

“Even if we get all of this right, we have no way to avoid more summers than the one we saw last year,” the Commissioner said, arguing that readiness, resilience and preparedness must become the priority alongside emissions cuts.

The proposed legislation would require EU countries to specify whether national, regional or local authorities are responsible for preparing for climate disasters.

Governments would retain flexibility over how they allocate responsibilities, but would have to specify who is accountable — an attempt to prevent political disputes over who failed to prepare when floods or wildfires destroy homes.

The Commission also wants climate scenarios to be considered when planning new roads, bridges and neighbourhoods, recognising that infrastructure designed for past weather conditions may no longer be fit for purpose.

"We want to introduce a culture of preparedness and resilience by design, rather than dealing with the damages in the aftermath, which is often very ad hoc and doesn't always build back better," a senior Commission official said on Monday on condition of anonymity.

No new money

However, the question of how to pay for climate adaptation remains unresolved.

No new financial commitment to household support is expected from the Commission's climate resilience strategy, despite concerns that ordinary citizens may struggle to afford the investments needed to adapt.

Hoekstra pointed to the Commission's proposal to devote 35% of the EU budget to climate and nature.

But the strategy's effectiveness will depend partly on the outcome of ongoing negotiations over the EU's next multiannual budget, with climate spending competing against priorities such as defence, security, competitiveness and agricultural support.

The Commission is also counting on the recently announced €30 billion from the European Investment Bank for climate adaptation through 2030.

Nonetheless, the lack of new funding is a potential weakness in the Commission's ambition.

The Commissioner argued that preventive investment is economically worth it but did not announce a new household support scheme or explain how the EU would ensure that lower-income households could afford necessary improvements.

In an attempt to fill the bloc's climate protection gap, Brussels wants to work with the insurance sector, as Commissioner Hoekstra pointed out that many areas in Europe are underinsured against climate disasters.

According to the senior Commission official, only around 25% of assets exposed to climate impacts are insured, leaving governments and property owners vulnerable to substantial losses.

“The fact that so many areas are underinsured” is one of the issues the Commission will examine, Hoekstra said.

The strategy could therefore expose another fault line between Brussels' climate ambitions and the cost-of-living pressures facing European voters.

World.title: Blood test could reveal prostate cancer risk more than a decade before diagnosis
World.content:
Distinctive proteins in men’s blood can signal a higher risk of prostate cancer more than 15 years before diagnosis, Oxford researchers have found.

 

“Finding proteins linked to known prostate cancer driver genes in blood collected years before diagnosis gives us new insights into the earliest stages of the disease,” said Karl Smith-Byrne, corresponding author of the study at Oxford.

Prostate cancer is the most common cancer among men in the European Union and second worldwide, after lung cancer. About 330,000 new cases are diagnosed every year and about 75,000 men die of the disease annually, in the EU alone.

Researchers at Oxford University analysed blood samples collected between 1992 and 2000 from more than 2,500 men. They compared baseline samples from 982 men who went on to develop prostate cancer with those from 1,573 men who did not.

The team measured more than 6,000 different proteins in each participant’s blood plasma. Because the samples were taken years before any diagnosis, sometimes more than 15 years, the researchers could look for early chemical warning signs — changes in proteins.

Some proteins were linked to a higher overall risk of prostate cancer, while others were associated specifically with aggressive or fast-growing forms of the disease. At the same time, men with higher levels of certain immune-system proteins, like GZMK and ANXA2, showed a lower long-term risk of prostate cancer, according to the study, published in the journal European Urology

“Many prostate cancers grow slowly and may never cause harm, while others are aggressive and can be life-threatening,” said Zhe Huang, first author of the study and a postdoctoral epidemiologist at Oxford Population Health.

“Ultimately, we hope this will help us understand the biology of aggressive prostate cancer and identify markers that could improve how we assess risk in the future,” Huang said.

The findings are not yet a screening test and need further validation, the researchers noted.

“Together with existing and future genetic evidence, these findings may help us identify biological pathways that could be targeted to prevent aggressive prostate cancer”, said Smith-Byrne.

World.title: Animal panic and air pollution: Why Switzerland is set to vote on a nationwide firework ban
World.content:
Swiss citizens are gearing up for an explosive vote: whether to ban noisy fireworks.

 

Spurred on by animal welfare and environmental groups, the citizen-proposed ‘popular initiative’ will be put to the ballot on 29 November.

“For pets, wild animals, and farm animals, fireworks are not a celebration, but pure stress,” says non-profit Schweizer Tierschutz STS (Swiss Animal Protection), which is supporting the initiative.

The proposal also calls for better protection for people and the natural environment against noise, air pollution, litter, accidents and fires caused by fireworks.

An initial Swiss Broadcasting Corporation (SBC) poll released on Friday (23 October) showed promising support for the ban, with 69 per cent of voters backing it.

While the proposal proved most popular among left-wing voters, it received majority support across the political spectrum, and particularly among women.

Votes like these are common in Switzerland, where any citizen or group can launch an initiative by gaining 100,000 valid signatures from eligible voters. Recent examples include the neutrality initiative, rejected in September, and the pending nuclear disarmament initiative.

Would it mean a complete ban on fireworks in Switzerland?

The proposal seeks to “significantly restrict particularly loud and disruptive fireworks” in private settings by banning the sale of noisy pyrotechnics. Quieter alternatives would still be permitted, such as sparklers and fountain-style volcano fireworks.

It would also allow ‘cantons’ (local areas) to grant exemptions for events of “supra-regional significance”, such as 1 August (Swiss National Day) and New Year’s Eve, but still with a focus on quieter alternatives.

Currently, Swiss cantons and communes may restrict or ban the sale and use of fireworks on a local level. Age limits and licensing requirements also govern their use.

STS says the initiative, ‘For a restriction on fireworks’, would create a clear rule for the entire country.

But industry association the Swiss Fireworks Coordination Office (SFK) argues that the proposal is a “threat to Swiss tradition”, while some politicians have said that it would infringe on citizens’ personal freedoms and should be left up to the cantons to govern.

The Swiss People’s Party, the Centre Party and the Swiss Trade Association have launched a campaign to vote against the measure, warning of its impact on business owners and potential to fuel a "prohibition culture".

After initially being submitted in 2023, the proposal received over 137,000 signatures. A failed counter-proposal in summer means it will now be followed by a public vote.

If successful, it could see Switzerland follow in the footsteps of the Netherlands, where a broader firework ban came into force this summer, primarily for safety reasons but also on animal and environmental welfare grounds. Other countries in Europe have their own rules and restrictions, such as Belgium where the use of large, powerful fireworks is restricted to professionals only.

How do fireworks impact the environment?

When fireworks explode, they release tiny dust particles, which are rich in toxic metals from the gunpowder and colouring compounds they contain.

According to the Swiss Federal Office of Police, between 1,000 and 2,000 tonnes of fireworks – three-quarters of which is made up of packaging – are used annually in Switzerland, producing between 200 and 400 tonnes of particulate matter per year.

This accounts for two-to-three per cent of the country’s annual particulate matter emissions, according to the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN).

As well as contributing to air, water and soil pollution, these fine particles can be inhaled with harmful health impacts, particularly for vulnerable people with existing conditions.

Unfavourable weather conditions can heighten the harms, such as fog which can trap particles in the air for longer, or hot and dry conditions which can increase wildfire risk.

FOEN urges responsible disposal of used fireworks, which can be placed in regular household waste once cooled down, while packaging should be recycled as normal.

Fireworks trigger ‘fear, panic and disorientation’

Animal welfare groups have been vocal in their support of a firework ban.

“The sudden noise triggers fear, panic, and disorientation [in animals],” says STS. “The consequences range from flight behaviour and acute stress to injuries or even death. Protecting animals from unnecessary noise is therefore a central concern of animal welfare.”

Speaking in a campaign video for the initiative, Swiss veterinarian Maruschka Blaser says that animals hear high-pitched sounds and loud bangs more acutely than humans. Giving horses as an example, she says “things can become dangerous very quickly when they run uncontrollably because of fireworks”, either for people in crowds or other animals in fields.

“When it comes to domestic animals such as cats and dogs, they sometimes need to be given medication to calm them down days in advance” of firework displays, says Blaser. “I also know families who spend the night in an air-raid shelter with their pets, but somehow that isn’t a solution either,” she adds.

“Millions of pets live in Switzerland. For many of them, fireworks trigger stress or panic,” says Casimir von Arx, President of the Bern branch of Schweizer Tierschutz STS (Swiss Animal Protection SAP) in a campaign video. “We can only protect them if, as a society, we show consideration for one another.”

World.title: Dating costs in Europe: Which cities are cheapest and most expensive?
World.content:
Do you think about money when planning a date? And does your financial situation affect whether you feel ready to start a relationship?

 

Romance is not only about feelings. Dating also costs money. A coffee, a drink or a dinner can put pressure on your wallet. And for some people, money may affect not only where they go on a date, but whether they want to start a relationship at all.

So, how much does dating cost across Europe? The answer varies widely from city to city according to the Mapping the World’s Prices 2026 report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute.

What is included in the Cheap Date Index?

The Cheap Date Index includes one bottle of wine, one pair of jeans, one dress, two coffees, one meal for two people in a mid-range restaurant, two cinema tickets, two one-way public transport tickets and a 5km taxi trip.

As the index includes a pair of jeans and a dress, clothing can account for a large share of the total cost. So, it may not reflect only the cost of the date itself.

The prices come from Numbeo, which is not an official data source. Its prices are crowdsourced from users.

Switzerland most expensive, Turkey cheapest

Among 28 European cities, two Swiss cities rank at the top. The cost of this date basket is €407 in Geneva, and Zurich closely follows at €400.

Istanbul is the cheapest city for a date, but the basket still costs €168. It also costs less than €200 in the Italian capital, Rome (€195).

The simple average across the 28 cities is €270. The figures reflect prices in mid-2026.

Dating is also quite expensive in the Nordic countries. Oslo and Copenhagen share third place at €323. Stockholm ranks sixth at €310, while Helsinki is eighth at €296.

The UK is more expensive than other major economies

Among Europe’s largest economies, London is the most expensive city at €317. Another British city, Birmingham, is also in the top 10 at €290.

Paris is close to the European average at €279. In Italy, the date basket costs €278 in Milan but just €195 in Rome, showing significant differences within countries.

The three German cities on the list are all below the European average and very close to each other. A date costs €260 in Munich and €254 in both Berlin and Frankfurt.

The two Spanish cities are also among the cheapest. The date basket costs €219 in Madrid and €213 in Barcelona.

Among other cities, the cost is €294 in Dublin, €290 in Edinburgh, €271 in Brussels, €263 in Amsterdam, €250 in Vienna, and €225 in Warsaw and Lisbon. It is €222 in Athens and €214 in Prague.

Europe at the top

Eight of the 10 most expensive cities are in Europe. Europe also has 14 of the top 20 and 20 of the top 30. Istanbul is the only European city among the 20 cheapest.

A cheap date costs €270 on average across the 28 European cities whereas it costs €195 in the other 41 cities.

Globally, Tel Aviv-Yafo ranks third at €365 and is the only non-European city in the top five.

New York ranks eighth (€308), Los Angeles 13th (€288) and San Francisco 14th (€281). Sydney (€270) is close to Amsterdam (€263), while Dubai (€243) is close to Berlin (€254). Singapore and Madrid both cost €219.

Tokyo (€161) and Seoul (€163) are cheaper than Istanbul (€168). Hong Kong (€196) is also close to Rome (€195).

When income is considered, the rankings reverse

The nominal prices alone tell only half the story. Zurich and Geneva have the most expensive cheap dates, but they also have the highest salaries. That means a date takes the smallest bite out of pay there: 5.6% of a monthly net salary in Zurich and 6.4% in Geneva.

Luxembourg (6.6%), Amsterdam (6.7%) and Frankfurt (7.2%) follow.

The picture reverses in southern and central Europe. A cheap date in Athens costs €222. This is just over half the price in Zurich. Yet it takes 19.6% of an average monthly net salary of €1,132, the highest share among the 28 European cities. Istanbul (16.7%), Lisbon (16.3%) and Budapest (15.6%) come next.

The salary figures are city-level estimates from Numbeo cited by Deutsche Bank. Still, they are broadly in line with the shares calculated using Eurostat’s annual net earnings for a single person without children earning the average wage. Eurostat figures are national averages, rather than city-level data.

Using Eurostat data, the share of the date cost would be 7.2 percentage points lower in Athens at 12.4%. In Lisbon, it would be 12.6%, rather than 16.3% using Numbeo’s salary estimate.

Examining the link between income and readiness for a relationship using US data, Johanna Peetz and Geoff MacDonald found that the financial well-being of young adults is linked with romantic desire, perceived readiness for relationships, and actual transitioning into intimate partnerships.

Chen-Hao Hsu and Henriette Engelhardt also found that temporary employment and unemployment negatively affected the probability of union formation for single women and men in Europe.

Another study found that temporary employment and unemployment negatively affected the probability of union formation for single women and men in Europe.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | October 27th, 2026 – Morning
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Seeking guaranteed snow? These are Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions
World.content:
Choosing where to go on a ski holiday involves more than finding a great resort, especially if you have a need for speed, slopes and adventure.

 

Snow conditions, the reliability of snowfall throughout the season and whether lifts and slopes are open can make a huge difference to your ski holiday.

Although no destination can completely promise perfect conditions, Inghams Ski has analysed more than 100 popular ski resorts and regions in the Northern Hemisphere to create the “Reliable Ski Score” ranking, with scores out of 100.

The travel operator measured each resort for mountain running (35%), which looked at the average percentage of lifts and slopes operating during the core season; and for snow adequacy (25%), which looked at the percentage of core-season days with 30cm or more at the base station.

Other factors included consistency (20%), or how steady mountain running was from season to season; downside protection (12%), which is the gap between the average season and the worst one; as well as average snow depth of the mountain (8%).

Each resort and region’s historical performance was studied during the core season period of 5 January to 20 March across seven Northern Hemisphere winter seasons between 2017-2018 and 2025-2026, with the exception of the seasons impacted by Covid-19.

The results see Italian, Austrian and French destinations dominate the top 10 ranking of Europe’s most reliable ski resorts and regions.

Top 10 most reliable ski resorts and regions in Europe

How the destinations scored out of 100 in the study:

1. Pontedilegno-Tonale, Italy: 93.1

2. Obertauern, Austria: 92.9

3. Les Arcs, France: 92.2

4. Les 3 Vallées, France: 91.1

5. Alpe d’Huez, France: 90.5

6. Kitzsteinhorn, Austria: 89.6

7. Filzmoos, Austria: 89.5

8. Tignes-Val d'Isère, France: 89.4

9. Espace San Bernardo (La Rosière/La Thuile), France: 89.2

10. Damüls Mellau, Austria: 89.1

Les Arcs, France Alex Lange/Unsplash

A look at the top three most reliable ski resorts and regions

Pontedilegno-Tonale, Italy

According to the Inghams study, Pontedilegno-Tonale in northern Italy is Europe’s most reliable region for skiing.

The mountainous area between Valle Camonica in Lombardy and Val di Sole in Trentino is a standout destination for its glaciers, nature reserves and high-altitude areas. It was highlighted for its consistent performance across reliability factors, giving skiers “practically hiccup-free exploring alongside snow-sure slopes”.

The ski area is home to 46 slopes, with the highest point of the resort sitting at 3,016 metres above sea level. Ponte di Legno’s slopes take skiers through dense pine and spruce forest, while Passo del Tonale sits at the foot of the Presena glacier and the skiing area features more than 44km of slopes.

During selected dates of the ski season, Inghams recommends taking advantage of the “Alba in Quota”, or “dawn at high altitude” window of opportunity. Here, lifts open earlier for skiers to experience sunrise skiing before the slopes officially open for the day.

Obertauern, Austria

In Austria’s Salzburg region, at 1,752 metres, the Obertauern ski resort emerged as the second most reliable in Europe.

It offers beginners and advanced skiers alike more than 100km of slopes across a long season from November through to May. And, as Inghams highlighted, the area is made up entirely of ski-in/ski-out hotels, giving visitors direct access to pistes from their accommodation.

Obertauern is also replete with cross-country ski trails, with routes ranging from six to 23km, including the medium-difficulty Gnadenalm. At an altitude of 1,350 metres, the trail sits halfway between Obertauern and Untertauern, earning the name "snow basin" because of its unique location.

Les Arcs, France

Rounding up the top three is Les Arcs. The French ski resort nestled in the heart of the Alps is set amid alpine meadows, glaciers and a peak that reaches 3,226 metres.

The mountain resort features 200km of ski trails with a winter season set to start on 12 December this year and will last until 24 April 2027.

Part of Paradiski, one of the world’s largest interconnected ski areas, Les Arcs is described as an “excellent choice for both freestyle enthusiasts as well as those looking for reliable conditions”. Les Arcs is also connected to Peisey-Vallandry and La Plagne via the iconic Vanoise Express cable car. Paradiski features 425km of slopes and 258 ski runs between the three linked resorts.

World.title: Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall could make or break the next EU budget
World.content:
The fight over the European Union's next seven-year budget has entered a critical new phase, one that could make or break the deal.

 

In a striking coincidence, the heated negotiations have overlapped with the effort to fill Ukraine's €70 billion shortfall for 2027.

Brussels had long suspected that Kyiv's accounts would show a sizable gap next year, as Russia escalates its war and devastates the levers of the domestic economy. But it was not until this month's summit that the €70 billion figure was validated.

Leaders then asked the European Commission to present possible options for providing the additional financing, with joint debt immediately emerging as the most feasible path.

The bloc is expected to cover two-thirds of the request, roughly €46 billion. Other allies, such as the UK, Canada, Norway and Japan, should take up the rest.

The vast scale of the deficit prompted a change of agenda in next month's special summit, which was originally planned to focus exclusively on the draft budget.

The meeting has been extended to two days, 26 and 27 November, to accommodate discussions on Ukraine. Fresh proposals are expected on both fronts.

Technically, the two issues remain separate files. But politically, diplomats and officials say, they are becoming rapidly intertwined.

"These are the most pressing issues for the remainder of the year, definitely," a diplomat said, cautioning it was still too early to talk about one big package.

Two key reasons explain the entanglement.

First, the two are about money.

The budget battle pits the so-called “Frugals”, or “Sensible Six”, against the “Friends of Cohesion”, with the two camps clashing over which budget envelopes should be cut and by how much. The "Frugals", which happen to be the net payers, demand steep reductions across the board, while the "Friends" want to preserve bigger volumes.

Second, the two face a pressing deadline set by the French election.

Marine Le Pen, the candidate of the far-right National Rally, who is firmly ahead in polls, has vowed to cap her country's contribution to the budget at €5 billion a year and warned sealing a deal before the election would be a "democratic scandal".

The incumbent, Emmanuel Macron, told his fellow leaders that reaching a deal between January and April would be "complicated".

The same logic now applies to Ukraine. As part of her programme, Le Pen has promised to halt all French support for the war-weary country.

"This funding will stop, and it is a matter of honesty to tell (Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy) the truth," she said earlier this month.

Easier or harder?

The prospect of a Le Pen win in the spring weighs heavily on officials and diplomats in Brussels, who admit both open issues – the budget and Ukraine – must be resolved by the end of the year before the window of opportunity closes.

The closer the election, the narrower the space for high-stakes decisions.

"Our internal cohesion is fragile. If that starts to unravel, the consequences for Ukraine could be even greater than anything Trump says or does," a national official said, referring to the US president's recent shift to Russia.

"We need a structural solution for financing Ukraine. We can't keep scrambling at the end of every year under pressure. Support for Kyiv needs to be properly built into the next budget. It's good that these discussions are coming together in November."

However, it is not yet clear whether Ukraine would make it easier or harder to agree on the budget, which remains stuck in maximalist red lines from the opposing camps.

One school of thought holds that reaching a deal may be easier because the “Frugals” includes some of Ukraine's largest bilateral donors – Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands, Sweden and Germany – who have a vested interest in locking in the fresh funding.

A strong collective decision on Ukraine could make it more politically palatable for them to accept – or rather, tolerate – a bigger budget than they might have wished.

"It might be helpful to get it done," another diplomat said.

But an alternative view is that the “Frugals’” continued push to cut funding for agriculture and cohesion policies could make it impossible for some “Friends of Cohesion” to back a deal on Ukraine without triggering a backlash at home.

The Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia are signalling they will exempt themselves from any joint debt to support Kyiv. Bulgaria, a vocal critic of weapons deliveries, is expected to follow suit. All of them sit in the cohesion group.

Making matters more difficult, the talks will unfold against a bleak backdrop of elevated energy prices, high borrowing costs and public discontent across Europe.

"It would be very dangerous, and I want to make this absolutely clear, if anyone tried to link the financing of Ukraine to the budget," Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said.

"It would be a miracle if we reached an agreement in December."

World.title: Azerbaijan hijab ban exposes strain in ‘brotherly’ ties with Turkey
World.content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, a staunch advocate of Muslim rights, has been notably silent on Azerbaijan’s recent hijab ban in schools. For years, Erdogan and Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev have shared a close alliance, but the ban is putting the Turkish president in a tight spot.

Advertising

School uniform rules introduced in September in predominantly Muslim Azerbaijan, which is a secular state, have been used to bar pupils wearing the hijab. Teachers have also reported being excluded. The new rules do not explicitly mention hijabs, but prohibit clothing deemed incompatible with school uniforms or secular education.

With Turkish social media awash with videos of Azerbaijani children wearing hijabs and pleading to be let into their schools, the ban has sparked outrage among Turkey’s religious conservatives.

Yet Erdogan, a vocal defender of Muslim rights both at home and on the world stage, has remained silent on the issue.

"He's unusually muted because Azerbaijan and Turkey, of course, had this extremely good relationship,“ said Turkish political analyst Sezin Oney. "If it were another country, he would have had a harsher reaction.”

‘We're fighting a daily battle': Iranian women dare to shed hijab in public

Baku's response

Erdogan, who is religiously conservative, rose to political prominence in the 1990s by challenging a similar ban in Turkish universities, and went on to become a global advocate of Muslim rights.

Oney predicts his silence on Azerbaijan will damage this reputation.

"[It's] a far cry from the days when Erdogan could stand up against the powerful of the world. That was the image he projected, and now he cannot even stand up to Aliyev."

Aliyev has publicly dismissed criticism of the hijab ban by one of the Turkish president’s advisors and Baku has issued international arrest warrants for several prominent Turkish Islamist and conservative figures, along with banning others from entering the country after similar criticism.

Azerbaijani officials accuse the critics of threatening its sovereignty and national security.

Shifting status

Aliyev and Erdogan have enjoyed close ties for more than two decades, built on economic and defence cooperation, with the mantra of ‘two states, one nation’.

“Erdogan and Turkey [still] see Azerbaijan as a little brother,” explains Tbilisi-based defence and security expert Eugene Kogan.

“I think that's not the perspective that comes from Baku because they say quite clearly that their relationship is no longer between a big brother and a little brother, and their relationship is now of equals.”

He added: “I think this phrase 'equal' is not fully accepted in Ankara. So that puts a strain on bilateral relations between the two countries."

Energy-rich Azerbaijan is growing in economic importance, in comparison with Turkey’s struggling economy. It is also among Turkey’s largest foreign investors.

Earlier this month, the two countries signed arms agreements worth more than $500 million. Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR says it has invested around $19.5 billion in Turkey.

“SOCAR is the flagship of investments in Turkey – it's huge," said Turkish analyst Atilla Yesilada of Global Source Investments.

“Turkey has a chronic deficit in plastics and petrochemicals. In fact, there are plans to establish a huge petrochemical complex in the Adana or Antalya area with a cost of $10 billion. I don’t think domestic capital has that kind of funding. Eventually, if Turkey wants to cover its petrochemical deficit, it needs SOCAR to get involved."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

Relations with Israel

Azerbaijan’s deepening relationship with Israel, despite its Turkish ally’s condemnation of Israel’s war in Gaza and broader escalating tensions, is another source of friction with Ankara.

International media reported that Azerbaijan signed a $235 million arms deal with Israel’s Elbit Systems this month, although neither side has commented on the reports.

Azerbaijan also remains a key oil supplier to Israel, with oil piped through Turkey and shipped from the Turkish Ceyhan port. In 2024, Erdogan moved swiftly to suppress mounting protests against these exports – protests led largely by religious conservatives who form a crucial part of his political support.

However, Kogan believes Israel will not try to exploit any rift between Baku and Ankara. “The stability of relations between Ankara, Baku and Tel Aviv is very, very important for Tel Aviv,” Kogan said.

Turkey-Azerbaijan alliance strained by opposing stances on Israel

Baku last year hosted talks between Turkey and Israel aimed at defusing tensions over Syria.

'[Isreal] understands that it could come to war [with Turkey] and Baku can still act as a meeting point for both countries. I cannot really think of another meeting point between Ankara and Tel Aviv at the moment,” Kogan said.

With Turkey the main export route for Azerbaijan’s oil and gas, mutual dependency remains a powerful means to contain any tensions.

Gasimov suggests the current rift is part of a learning process.

“I wouldn’t read it as reshuffling or rebalancing, but rather as a new chapter that may have opened up now, if the two sides learn from it and are ready to accept these kinds of differences."

As Turkey wrestles with mounting financial and economic woes, Erdogan is expected to look for ways to smooth things over with his affluent neighbour. But the full impact on their ties of this dispute remains to be seen.

World.title: Israel election: Israelis vote for 1st time since October 7 terror attack
World.content:
There's a lot at stake in this election: The fallout and questions of political accountability for the attacks of October 7, 2023; mandatory military service for ultra-Orthodox men and sharing the burden of national defense; along with Israel's standing in the international community.

Nowhere can the division within Israeli society be more felt than in debate over Benjamin Netanyahu.

For the past four years, Israel's long-standing prime minister has led what has been described as the most right-wing government in the country's history. He broke with political convention by forming an alliance with ultranationalist politician Itamar Ben-Gvir.

Many Israelis want to see an end to this government. They blame it for the failures surrounding Hamas' terror attack and for the country's growing isolation internationally. Many are placing their hopes in Gadi Eisenkot, who has emerged as a leading opposition figure to challenge Netanyahu.

World.title: Brazil elections: Merz, world leaders congratulate Lula on his win
World.content:
The Kremlin said on Monday it welcomed Lula's victory and praised what it said were his efforts to cultivate Brazil-Russia ties.

"We welcome Mr. Lula's victory. He does a lot, not only for the development of bilateral relations but also for advancing processes within the framework of BRICS," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.

He said Russia hoped for more of the same.

Lula himself has possibly put Brazil in the Kremlin's good books by not joining Western sanctions on Russia over Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and calling for a negotiated peace.

However, he has called on all nations to adhere to the principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity enshrined in the UN Charter, thus implicitly condemning Russia's aggression.

Brazil and Russia are both members of BRICS, an international cooperation group founded in 2009 along with India and China, with South Africa joining a year later, and taking all those countries' first initials to make up its name.

It has since then been expanded to include 10 member nations in all, with a number of "partner countries" also invited in 2024.

World.title: Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire for aid mission
World.content:
Around 2,000 people remain stranded in the city of Oleshky, facing severe shortages of food and medicine. The Russian-occupied town has been devastated by fighting and flooding since Moscow's invasion in 2022.

Russia and Ukraine began a localized ceasefire early Tuesday to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.

Both sides confirmed that the truce took effect at 3 a.m. local time (0100 GMT), following an agreement brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.

Russia's Defense Ministry said its forces had stopped shelling in the Kherson sector to prepare for the humanitarian operation.

Ukraine's human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets also confirmed that Kyiv was observing the agreement.

"As head of the Ukrainian negotiating team, I confirm that the Ukrainian side is honoring its commitments," he wrote on Facebook.

However, it could not be independently verified whether fighting had decreased.

What is the humanitarian situation in Oleshky?

Around 2,000 people, including up to 50 children, remain trapped in Oleshky, according to Ukrainian and US estimates. The town had about 24,000 residents before Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

The United Nations says residents face severe shortages of food and medicine. Mines and drone attacks have made it difficult for them to leave.

International media have limited access to Oleshky, making it difficult to independently assess conditions in the town [FILE: September 22, 2026] Image: Ukrainian 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/AP Photo/picture alliance

Former residents told news agency AFP earlier this year that people remaining in the town were starving, sometimes hunting pigeons or surviving on food grown in their gardens.

"They've forgotten what bread is. You need flour for bread, and there's not even flour left," said Olga, who was in contact with two families still in Oleshky.

Oleshky lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson.

Floodwaters submerged large parts of Oleshky in June 2023 after the collapse of the Kakhovka dam on the Dnipro River [FILE: June 10, 2023] Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

Russian troops captured the town during the first days of the invasion in 2022. It suffered further destruction in June 2023 when the collapse of the Kakhovka dam caused widespread flooding.

What role did Melania Trump play in the ceasefire?

The White House said last week that Melania Trump had helped secure the agreement after holding talks with civilian negotiators from Russia and Ukraine.

Her office said the first lady had also met United Nations officials who briefed her on conditions in Oleshky.

Announcing the agreement on Friday, Trump said civilian officials from both countries would visit residents to assess their needs.

US first lady Melania Trump has taken on an unusually prominent diplomatic role in efforts to address the humanitarian crisis in Ukraine [FILE: October 19, 2026] Image: Mark Schiefelbein/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Doctors, food, drinking water and medicine are expected to reach the town before evacuation corridors are opened.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.

Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing residents from leaving, an allegation Moscow denies.

Neither side has provided details about who will monitor the ceasefire. Reports have also differed over its duration, with one account saying it could last through Saturday.

What happened in Kyiv after the ceasefire began?

Russian missile attacks continued elsewhere in Ukraine as the localized ceasefire began.

Explosions shook Kyiv shortly after 3 a.m. local time Tuesday, according to witnesses, while air raid alerts sounded across several regions.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the attacks had damaged the Southern Bridge and associated subway infrastructure. City authorities said traffic on the bridge had been suspended.

Buildings in Kyiv were damaged by Russian missile strikes, which also left several people dead or injured Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

On Monday, a Russian missile attack on Kyiv killed at least one person and injured 10 others, including students at a dormitory. Further attacks caused casualties in Kharkiv and Pavlohrad.

"It is important that the world sees that Russia is showing nothing but a desire to kill and continue waging war," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote after the attacks.

Could the Oleshky ceasefire help revive Ukraine peace talks?

The limited truce in Oleshky comes ahead of another round of US-mediated peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv, expected in November.

Negotiations have been effectively frozen since the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in February.

The last trilateral peace talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US took place in Geneva in February 2026, ending without a breakthrough [FILE: February 17, 2026] Image: Yekaterina Chesnokova/ITAR-TASS/IMAGO

Previous attempts to establish ceasefires have repeatedly failed amid deep mistrust between Russia and Ukraine.

More than four and a half years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, hundreds of thousands of soldiers and civilians have been killed, while millions have been forced to flee their homes.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: US seeks new charges against former FBI chief James Comey
World.content:
The Trump administration accuses the former FBI director of leaking classified information a decade ago. Comey denies wrongdoing, while his lawyers argue the case is legally invalid and comes too late.

The US Justice Department has launched a third attempt to prosecute former FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of illegally disclosing national defense information in 2016.

Court documents unsealed on Monday reveal allegations that Comey directed a subordinate to share classified information with a journalist.

The case marks another escalation in President Donald Trump's long-running conflict with the former FBI chief, who has denied wrongdoing.

What are the latest allegations against James Comey?

The case centers on an October 2016 New York Times article about a secret US surveillance order involving internet company Yahoo.

The order reportedly required Yahoo to scan emails for messages potentially linked to a foreign terrorist organization. It had been issued by a secret intelligence court.

Prosecutors allege that Comey instructed a staff member to contact a New York Times journalist to correct inaccurate information published by news agency Reuters the previous day.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly accused former FBI director James Comey of wrongdoing, while Comey has denied the allegations Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance

According to the Justice Department, this resulted in the illegal transfer of classified national defense information to an unauthorized person.

However, the allegations have already been investigated twice.

Federal authorities began examining the disclosure in 2017. Prosecutor John Durham recommended against bringing criminal charges in December 2018, according to Comey's lawyers.

A second investigation, launched in 2019 under the code name "Tropical Vortex," was also closed without charges in February 2020.

How are Comey's lawyers fighting the new charges?

The Justice Department filed a legal document known as a "criminal information" in early October, shortly before the 10-year deadline for prosecuting the alleged offense.

Unlike an indictment, a criminal information does not require approval from a grand jury or judge.

Prosecutors say the filing allows them to extend the statute of limitations, which determines how long authorities have to bring criminal charges.

A courtroom sketch shows former FBI director James Comey alongside his lawyer Patrick Fitzgerald during his arraignment in 2025 [FILE: October 8, 2025] Image: Dana Verkouteren/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Comey's lawyers dispute that interpretation. They argue that federal law explicitly requires an indictment within 10 years and that the government's filing does not meet that requirement.

They have asked a judge to dismiss the case. A ruling is still pending.

Comey's attorney, Patrick Fitzgerald, also pointed to the two earlier investigations.

"Both times the Government determined that no charges should be brought against anyone," he said.

Responding to the latest allegations in a video posted on Substack, Comey condemned the prosecution.

"It would almost be funny if it weren't such an appalling abuse of the Department of Justice," he said.

"I'm still innocent. I'm still not afraid of these people, and I still believe in the independent federal judiciary."

What other criminal cases does James Comey face?

The latest case is the third criminal proceeding brought against Comey since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025.

In September 2025, prosecutors charged him with making false statements to Congress and obstructing a congressional proceeding.

A federal judge dismissed the case after finding that the Trump-appointed prosecutor who brought the charges had been unlawfully appointed.

Former FBI director James Comey testified before the Senate Intelligence Committee in June 2017 about his dismissal by Trump and the Russia investigation [FILE: June 8, 2017] Image: Andrew Harnik/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

In April 2026, Comey was indicted again, this time over an Instagram photograph showing seashells arranged to form the numbers "86 47."

The Justice Department interpreted the numbers as a threat against Trump, arguing that "86" referred to killing someone and "47" identified Trump as the 47th US president.

Comey denied threatening Trump's life and has sought to have that case dismissed.

Why has Trump targeted former FBI director Comey?

Comey was appointed FBI director in 2013 by Democratic President Barack Obama.

His relationship with Trump deteriorated shortly after the president took office in 2017.

Comey resisted Trump's request to pledge personal loyalty during a private dinner.

Trump fired him in May 2017 while the FBI was investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election and possible connections to Trump's campaign.

Donald Trump and James Comey initially appeared to have a cordial relationship before the president fired the FBI director in May 2017 [FILE: January 22, 2017] Image: Andrew Harrer/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

The investigation was subsequently taken over by special counsel Robert Mueller. It established that Russia had interfered in the election but found insufficient evidence to prove criminal coordination between Moscow and Trump's campaign.

The two men have remained bitter political opponents. Trump has repeatedly accused Comey of treason, while Comey compared the president to a mafia boss in his 2018 memoir.

Edited by: Wesley Dockery

World.title: England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane wins Ballon d'Or
World.content:
The England captain ends his country's 25-year wait for the prestigious award after scoring 73 goals for club and country last season, beating competition from Lamine Yamal and Kylian Mbappe.

England captain Harry Kane won the men's Ballon d'Or for the first time on Monday, becoming the first English player to receive the prestigious football award since 2001.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker was honored at a ceremony at the London Palladium after scoring 73 goals in 65 appearances for club and country last season.

The Ballon d'Or, awarded by French magazine France Football, is one of football's most prestigious individual honors, recognizing the world's best players.

The last English player to win the award was former Liverpool striker Michael Owen, who claimed the prize 25 years ago.

Why did Harry Kane win the 2026 Ballon d'Or?

Kane's remarkable goalscoring record helped Bayern Munich secure a German league and cup double last season.

The former Tottenham Hotspur forward also led England to the World Cup semifinals, the country's best finish since winning the tournament in 1966.

Harry Kane also received the Gerd Müller Trophy, awarded to the season's top goalscorer, after netting 73 goals for Bayern Munich and England Image: Matthew Childs/Action Images/REUTERS

Kane has finished as the Bundesliga's leading scorer for three consecutive seasons. He was also Europe's top club goalscorer during the 2025-26 campaign.

At Monday's ceremony, Kane thanked his Bayern Munich teammates for their support.

"Without you guys (his Bayern Munich team-mates) and the rest of the team it wouldn't be possible, the way you guys push me, the way we compete. So thank you very much," he said.

Kane also paid tribute to his former club Tottenham Hotspur, which he joined at the age of 11, as well as his England teammates and family.

"To my wife Kate, my best friend. We've been through ups and downs. You are my biggest support and I felt like you wanted this more than me," he said.

Barcelona's Lamine Yamal was among Harry Kane's strongest rivals for the Ballon d'Or, alongside Kylian Mbappe Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Reflecting on his career, Kane encouraged young footballers to pursue their ambitions despite setbacks.

"I hope my journey, it wasn't straightforward, I didn't go straight to the top, I had to experience a lot of loan moves and fight my way to get to where I am now. I hope that can give you inspiration."

Kane faced strong competition from Barcelona's Spanish teenager Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid's French forward Kylian Mbappe.

He joins Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen among the English players to have won the award.

Who else won at the 2026 Ballon d'Or awards?

Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas claimed the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career, having previously won the award in 2021 and 2022.

The 32-year-old was recognized after a successful season with Barcelona, winning the treble and scoring 21 goals across all competitions.

Spain's Alexia Putellas won the women's Ballon d'Or for the third time in her career Image: Kin Cheung/AP Photo/picture alliance

Putellas also played a key role in Barcelona's Champions League triumph, contributing seven goals and seven assists during the campaign.

She joined English club London City Lionesses in July after spending 14 years at Barcelona.

Her victory ended a run of three consecutive Ballon d'Or wins by fellow Spaniard Aitana Bonmatí.

Barcelona's Lamine Yamal won the Kopa Trophy for the best young male player for the third consecutive year, while his teammate Vicky Lopez claimed the women's award for the second year running.

Barcelona coach Pere Romeu was named women's coach of the year, while Spain manager Luis de la Fuente won the men's coaching award.

Spain coach Luis de la Fuente beat Arsenal's Mikel Arteta and Aston Villa's Unai Emery to win the men's Coach of the Year award Image: Franck Fife/AFP

Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon received the men's Yashin Trophy, with Cata Coll winning the women's equivalent.

Barcelona was named women's club of the year, while Paris Saint-Germain took the men's award.

World.title: Jordan says its military struck 'militant hideouts' in Syria after deadly church attack
World.content:
Jordanian armed forces carried out strikes on "militant hideouts" in Syria that it said were linked to a deadly church attack on the kingdom last week. Syria gave a different account.

Jordan said late Monday that its air force has struck military hideouts in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to last week's deadly church attack were hiding there.

Jordanian forces said the deadly attack on a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church was linked to "terrorist groups" hiding in Syria.

Jordan's armed forces said the strikes on southeastern Syria was carried out in coordination with Damascus.

But Syria gave a different account, saying it had launched an investigation into the Jordanian attacks.

A health official told Syria's state news agency that at least five civilians, including women and children, were killed as a result of strikes carried out by Jordan, Reuters reported.

Jordanian security forces arrest 3 men in Karak province

Jordanian security forces earlier on Monday morning arrested three men in connection with last week's deadly terrorist attack at the Hammoud Church that killed nine people and injured 40 others.

Officials said the arrests took place following a dawn shootout with the armed men who were discovered hiding in an abandoned house in the Karak governorate, located some 120 kilometers (75 miles) southwest of the capital, Amman.

All three suspects were wounded in the operation, but Jordanian security forces reported no casualties.

"The security services have fulfilled their duties, resulting in the capture of those who carried out this terrorist act," said Jordanian Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya in a phone interview with state broadcaster Al-Mamlaka on Monday.

"[The suspects] put up fierce resistance but were ultimately subdued and taken into custody, having sustained severe injuries."

He added that there were "three individuals involved" who were "identified early on in the wake of the terrorist incident" and that the security services had "employed all the means at their disposal to apprehend them."

Jordan's King Abdullah called for 'iron first' response

King Abdullah II of Jordan had ordered authorities to respond with an "iron fist" against anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.

"We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated," he added in a statement on Monday, following the arrests, which relatives of the victims had said brought some relief.

"Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief — and the grief of the Jordanian people — not just for us, the families of the martyrs," one relative, himself a survivor of the attack, told Al-Mamlaka.



King Abdullah II (center) visited victims in hospital and called for Jordanian security forces to respond with an "iron fist." Image: Royal Court of Jordan/Handout/Anadolu/IMAGO

Who carried out the attack in Jordan?

There has been no claim of responsibility for Friday's deadly attack and Jordan's Public Security Directorate has not named the suspects or publicly ​identified possible affiliations with any Islamist militant groups.

Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, a relatively stable Middle Eastern state which is a close ally of the United States and which maintains diplomatic and military relations with neighboring Israel.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn and Wesley Dockery

World.title: UN sounds the alarm over Israel's West Bank military operation
World.content:
The UN has sounded the alarm on Israeli action in the West Bank city of Hebron after hundreds of families were displaced over the weekend. Israel has ordered the military to demolish homes after soldiers were killed.

The Israeli military operation in the occupied West Bank city of Hebron was met with sharp criticism from the head of the UN as well as the UN's human rights commissioner in comments made on Monday.

The criticism comes after an Israeli military operation was launched in the occupied West Bank in response to a shootout on Friday that left two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinian gunmen dead. Three more Israeli soldiers were also injured.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ordered the military to demolish buildings in the West Bank city of Hebron and to close off the West Bank. It came just days before Israel's general election on Tuesday.

What did the UN say about Israeli operation in the West Bank?

The United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres said on Monday that "settlements are expanding, evictions are unrelenting with Palestinians driven from their lands," in a post on X.

"We are seeing an increasingly coercive environment, with the spectre of ethnic cleaning looming ever larger," he wrote.

The UN Human Rights High Commissioner Volker Türk also issued a statement condemning Israeli actions, saying the "aggressive operation" has resulted in the forcible displacement of thousands of Palestinians, "demolished homes and commercial property, and deprived residents of the ability to move freely."

"Collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. Threats to empty and erase entire neighbourhoods also raise serious concerns of ethnic cleansing," he said.

Israeli army demolishes Palestinian buildings in Hebron To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A UN report, also released on Monday, that accuses Israel of committing war crimes in the West Bank , was rejected by the Israeli Foreign Ministry as "propaganda."

The ministry said that the findings were "not a human rights report but a propaganda document detached from reality, aimed at undermining Israel's right to self-defense, delegitimizing the Jewish state, and legitimizing jihadist terrorism against its citizens."

What is the Israeli operation in the West Bank?

Israeli troops entered the Deir Baha neighborhood, where the assailants lived, and ordered residents to pack up and leave.

The Hebron municipality said that more than 3,000 people, including 200 babies, were ordered to leave.

The Israeli military said at the weekend that its troops were carrying out precise, targeted and thorough searches to "locate and dismantle terrorist infrastructure and locate weapons, alongside questioning suspects" in Hebron.

The military said the operation was expected to continue "for several days" and would focus on Deir Baha.

The largescale response to the firefight in the West Bank comes in the run-up to elections in Israel on Tuesday that could bring an end to Netanyahu's premiership.

Netanyahu has frequently painted himself as the only person who can keep Israel safe but his opponents have accused him of lacking a plan.
