World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019159/Chinese Reality Show’s Medical Students Criticized as Incompetent
World.title: Chinese Reality Show’s Medical Students Criticized as Incompetent
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019159/Chinese Reality Show’s Medical Students Criticized as Incompetent
World.content:
A Chinese reality show featuring medical students has sparked criticism after participants were shown guessing diagnoses, struggling to tie surgical knots, and voicing what some viewers deemed questionable ethics.

The eighth season of “An Exciting Offer,” which premiered Oct. 21 on Tencent Video, brings together 11 medical students, from undergraduates to doctoral candidates across different specialties, who compete for an internship position at Nanfang Hospital of Southern Medical University in Guangzhou, capital of the southern Guangdong province.

The show, which places participants in scenarios based on real workplace situations, has previously featured aspiring lawyers, television anchors, and architects, with its first and highest-rated season receiving an 8.2 out of 10 on Chinese entertainment review platform Douban.

However, the first episode of the latest season caused viewers to question several participants’ professional competence.

Li Ziqi, a doctoral student in neurosurgery at Fujian Medical University, said he had participated in Level 4 surgery, China’s highest surgical level. But when asked whether he believed his surgical skills were strong, he replied, “during our doctoral studies, we don’t do clinical work.”

The remark prompted pushback from medical students watching the show, who noted that professional-degree doctoral students generally must undergo clinical training. Viewers also raised concerns about Li’s research record, noting that the papers he authored were not highly ranked according to the classification system of the Science Citation Index Expanded, a trusted journal database.

As questions about Li’s qualifications mounted, Fujian Medical University told domestic media that he had completed 18 months of clinical practice. The university said his remark that doctoral students did not undertake clinical work was incorrect and had caused a misunderstanding.

Li also told fellow contestants that writing medical records could be learned in just one day, and during a diagnostic assessment, said of one case, “I’m guessing that’s a craniopharyngioma,” referring to a type of brain tumor, without presenting any evidence.

One of the show mentors — an experienced doctor in several fields — told Li that diagnoses could not be based on guesswork. The scenes drew further criticism online, with viewers questioning what they saw as Li’s dismissive attitude toward clinical work and the rigors widely considered a cornerstone of medical practice.

Meanwhile, another participant who reportedly is now an intern at a renowned private hospital in Sydney appeared to need instruction on how to tie surgical knots. In addition, the show’s only undergraduate participant said she would pay out of pocket for a patient’s cosmetic suturing, prompting questions about her understanding of medical ethics.

“Medical students undergoing standardized residency training who’ve watched (the show) want to say: endless case reports and back-to-back shifts are the daily reality. This makes clinical work look far easier than it really is,” read one highly upvoted comment on Weibo by a user claiming to be a medical student.

The controversy has also raised broader questions about how the show presents medical education to the public, with viewers voicing concern that scenes emphasizing participants’ mistakes could deepen public mistrust of doctors.

Criticism has also focused on the program’s apparent failure to distinguish between China’s two types of medical postgraduate courses, whose training priorities differ: academic degrees, where students go into research, and professional degrees, in which students seek to practice clinically.

“A program that trades on the name of ‘doctors’ has turned the things that leave no room for carelessness in clinical practice — the rigors of diagnosis, of professional growth, and the boundaries of surgery — into a ‘performance’ for the camera,” a commentary by state-run media outlet People’s Daily read.

In response to the online debate, the reported Sydney hospital intern wrote that the experience was “the first time I had such a profound realization of the differences between Chinese and Western medical training,” in a post on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote.

“I still have a lot to improve in terms of basic skills and hands-on experience,” she added.

The show’s production team has not issued a response to the controversy.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for the eighth season of “An Exciting Offer.” From Douban)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019146/How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.title: How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019146/How Contemporary Art Finds a Home in Small-Town China
World.content:
The drive southwest from Hangzhou, the capital of eastern China’s Zhejiang province, takes about six hours. The highway passes through tunnel after tunnel, opening onto solar farms terraced into hillsides, villages with white walls and gray-tiled roofs, and transmission towers climbing the ridges. The last tunnel leads into a narrow valley, with clouds hanging low over the mountains.

This is Qingyuan County, which remains relatively remote despite its location in one of China’s richest provinces and improvements in transport infrastructure. Little known beyond its shiitake mushrooms and pencil manufacturing, the county moves to its own rhythm. I arrive at dusk, just as electric moped riders stream in from factories and workshops a few minutes outside town. Here, electric mopeds have a lane of their own. At traffic lights, riders cluster together, their helmets like a patch of colorful mushrooms, then move off as one when the light turns green.

Media portrayals of China often focus on modern metropolises or traditional villages, overlooking places like Qingyuan. Its urban center is a xiancheng, or county town, where schools, hospitals, shops, and cultural and government facilities serve both townspeople and residents of surrounding villages. Qingyuan County as a whole had 141,000 permanent residents in 2023. Across China, some 160 million people lived in similar county towns at the end of 2021. A 2022 national policy recognized their role in connecting cities and the countryside, calling for improved public services, including museums.

County towns have also been largely overlooked in China’s contemporary art scene. For more than a decade, Chinese artists and curators have been working beyond major cities like Beijing and Shanghai. Festivals such as Art Field Nanhai have brought installations to the countryside in the southern Guangdong province. The Bishan Project incorporated art into a “rural revitalization” initiative in a village in Zhejiang’s neighboring Anhui province. Anren, a historic town in the southwestern Sichuan province, hosted three editions of a contemporary art biennale.

These projects have expanded the reach of contemporary art in China. Yet artistic practices in county towns, where urban and rural life intersect, remain underreported. Another problem is the condescending language sometimes used in media coverage. For example, the term xiachen, literally “sinking,” is often used to describe cultural resources flowing from major cities to smaller communities, downplaying the role of local people in shaping art scenes.

The Art Museum of Pond Loach (AMPL) in Qingyuan offers a different perspective, showing how contemporary art institutions and smaller communities can shape one another.

Established in 2023, AMPL takes its name from a small, mud-burrowing freshwater fish. The museum draws on this image to describe its mission: immersing itself in the space between urban and rural life and engaging with the everyday experiences of county-town residents. It seeks to support what its director, Hu Dingyu, describes as “modest yet significant contemporary art.”

A Qingyuan native who left the county as a child and later studied and worked as a curator in the Netherlands, Hu has a complicated relationship with her hometown and resists portraying her return as a nostalgic homecoming or a search for her roots. Instead, she sought to establish a lasting institution where relationships among artists, museum staff, and local residents could develop over time.

That starts with the architecture. AMPL occupies two floors of a ceramics museum founded by a member of Hu’s family. Dedicated to celadon, a type of green-glazed ceramic with strong ties to Zhejiang, the museum shares a building with the local marriage registry and a library reading room.

Hu and her team carved out a space for contemporary art within this setting, and the contrast remains visible. Gray concrete walls, exposed rebar and pipes, and alarm fixtures sit alongside the polished glass cases displaying celadon downstairs. To me, these unfinished surfaces made the gallery feel like a work in progress, reflecting the artistic practices taking shape within and beyond its walls.

AMPL’s development resembles a process of grafting: artistic practices and networks formed elsewhere take root through encounters with local institutions, skills, and ways of life. These local conditions are not simply a backdrop. They are constantly evolving and actively shape what artists and the museum can do.

Indeed, AMPL’s curation, research, and public education programs are all centered around county-town life. It invites artists to spend time in Qingyuan and develop projects in collaboration with local people. Rather than focusing solely on the finished artworks, artists are encouraged to gain inspiration from everyday encounters, including those with local workers.

In one project, a modified “chariot” joined the evening moped traffic. In another, local shops and a long-vanished dance hall became subjects of an exhibition. The museum’s collaborations have also extended into classrooms. Working with artists, AMPL made recordings of contemporary art classes at Hangzhou’s China Academy of Art available to local high school teachers for use in their lessons. Together, these projects have brought artistic practice into familiar settings, from roads and shops to schools.

Local networks are equally important to AMPL’s day-to-day operations. Without a dedicated exhibition installation team, the museum relies on local welders, electricians, and other tradespeople recruited through personal contacts. Since the museum opened, workers who were initially unfamiliar with installing contemporary art have become regular collaborators. These relationships have become part of the museum’s infrastructure.

AMPL’s 2026 exhibition, “Factory Girl,” is perhaps the most convincing evidence of how contemporary art can take root — rather than “sink” — in county-towns. Featuring artist Zheng Que and curated by Nie Xiaoyi, the exhibition explores manufacturing in China’s counties through Zheng’s own experience. Beginning in 2023, she worked at a factory producing Christmas goods in Pan’an, another county in Zhejiang, and filmed herself on the job. Like Qingyuan’s pencils, the factory’s products connected local workers to consumers far beyond the county. Zheng herself was the “factory girl.”

According to Zheng, most workers were women from nearby villages, ranging in age from their 30s to their 70s and 80s. Many were retired and wanted something to keep them occupied. Coworkers were often also neighbors or relatives, connected through overlapping networks of family and acquaintances.

At the opening of “Factory Girl,” I met artists, curators, and other art professionals who had traveled from Shanghai and Hangzhou. Over dinner, we shared loach hotpot, a local specialty featuring the fish that gave AMPL its name, and shiitake mushrooms, all prepared by local residents.

Together, these activities suggest a more reciprocal relationship than the language of xiachen implies. At AMPL, the graft is both architectural and cultural. What matters is how the different elements come together: how space is shared, how local skills are put to use, and how relationships are sustained through repeated collaboration and practical adjustments.

Whether these connections can sustain AMPL in the long term remains uncertain. Resources and networks from major cities will continue to matter, but so will the museum’s ability to give artists time to develop work with local residents and maintain those relationships beyond individual exhibitions. For the graft to take hold, collaboration must become an ongoing practice, giving people in Qingyuan a role in shaping the museum’s future. More broadly, AMPL raises questions about how contemporary art can develop beyond China’s major cities, and the role smaller communities can play in shaping it.

(Header image: The installation “Zheng Que: Factory Girl,” Art Museum of Pond Loach, Qingyuan County, Zhejiang province, 2026. Photo by Luo Shunqi, Han Qian and Cao Danyang. All images courtesy of Jin Yu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.title: China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019158/China Develops 1-Gram, Wireless Microscope for Lab Animal Use
World.content:
Chinese scientists have developed the world’s lightest wireless mesoscope, a miniature microscope weighing just 1 gram that can record 25 times as many neurons in mice as comparable devices.

The device, named Airscope, was unveiled in the prestigious journal Nature on Oct. 19, and developed by a team led by Tsinghua University professor Dai Qionghai and Chinese PLA Medical School professor Dai Pu, in collaboration with researchers from other institutions.

When installed on a mouse’s head, the Airscope can record activity from over 8,500 neurons as it freely explores, climbs, and interacts with other mice.

Previously, microscopes designed to image large areas of the brain at high resolution often required cables or the subject to be restrained, making it difficult to study natural behavior. Meanwhile, head-mounted microscopes that let animals move freely could observe only limited areas.

In contrast, the Airscope combines wireless operation with mesoscopic imaging, allowing scientists to observe large areas of tissue while still distinguishing individual cells. This enables researchers to “understand how large numbers of neurons interact and work together to produce complex functions,” Wu Jiamin, an associate professor in Tsinghua University’s Department of Automation and one of the study’s corresponding authors, said in an article published Tuesday by Tsinghua University.

The device weighs just 1 gram without its battery, more than 30% less than the latest head-mounted mesoscopes, according to the researchers. It has single-cell resolution of 4 to 6 micrometers, and a 6-millimeter field of view compared with typically less than 1 millimeter for conventional head-mounted devices. A magnetically attached battery can be replaced in two seconds.

With the Airscope, the team conducted several experiments that were previously difficult because of cables or equipment weight.

For example, in a simulated natural habitat with ramps, tree hollows, and shelters, mice could explore freely while researchers recorded their cortical activity. The team could also use neural signals to predict which portion of the habitat a mouse was in.

In another experiment, researchers placed two mice at opposite ends of a narrow tube and used their neural activity to predict which would force the other to retreat, achieving over 80% accuracy.

Other experiments included mounting one Airscope on a mouse’s head and another on its back to compare spinal cord and cortical neural activity, as well as tracking mice exploring a large maze in search of water rewards.

The team has also publicly released several datasets collected from their experiments.

Zhang Yuanlong, one of the study’s first authors and an assistant professor at Tsinghua University’s Center for Life Sciences and Artificial Intelligence and Department of Automation, said the team used AI to help optimize the optical design. The technology also uses a 2-megapixel image sensor, whereas previously published wireless systems had not exceeded 1 megapixel, allowing higher resolution.

Dai Qionghai said the Airscope could enable “more precise neural detection” and potentially expand into fields such as immunology and cancer research.

Zhang added that the device could be used to track the progression of Alzheimer’s disease, brain injuries, cardiovascular diseases, depression, and other conditions in animal models, and gain insights into disease mechanisms, prevention, and treatment.

In 2023, researchers at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology developed two head-mounted microscopes using a new optical design: one optimized for a larger field of view, measuring around 4 millimeters and weighing 1.4 grams, and another optimized for lower weight, with a 1-millimeter field of view and weighing just 1 gram. Both devices required wires for power and data collection.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from the WeChat public account of Tsinghua University, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.title: In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019154/In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
World.content:
For her vacation to China’s southern province of Hainan during this year’s weeklong National Day holiday, Chang Yajie bought five new pieces of clothing: a beach skirt, a floral halter top, a straw hat, a swimsuit, and a pair of loose rainbow pants.

She wore them all on the trip, relishing taking photos in her new outfit on the resort-laden island’s beaches and posting them to social media.

But when she got home, she stuffed the clothes into her trash can.

Chang, an office worker in Xinxiang, a city in the central Henan province, used to spend thousands of yuan on vacation outfits. Unsuitable for work and out of place in everyday life, they ended up at the back of her closet after her trips.

“You can’t possibly wear a plunging, neon-colored beach dress to a corporate desk job,” the 37-year-old told Sixth Tone. “Spending so much on clothes I might wear only once or twice just isn’t worth it.”

In contrast, the five items she packed in early October had cost a total of just 200 yuan ($28). Known as cipaoyi, or disposable outfits, these clothes typically cost under 50 yuan per item and are designed to be worn once for holidays, photo shoots, or social media posts, and then discarded or resold.

The trend, which took off this National Day, comes amidst fast fashion and influencer-driven consumer culture, as well as the phenomenon of haoyangmao, or buying clothing, wearing it for travel, photoshoots, or events, and then returning it for a full refund.

On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, posts under the topic have drawn over 60 million views. On e-commerce platforms, sellers offer clothing ranging from coats and snowpants for use in the northeastern city of Harbin to red dresses designed for photos in the desert. The trend is particularly popular among young women.

Proponents of disposable outfits argue that they’re an inexpensive way to look and feel good while matching scenery and holidays. But others, including environmental advocates and medical professionals, have raised concerns about their potential impact on the planet and people’s health.

Cutting costs

Despite having always loved dressing up, Chang said her clerical desk job leaves little room for it, so she keeps an understated, practical wardrobe. Disposable outfits, then, are a way to “boost her mood.”

“When I go to work, I just wear whatever helps me blend into the crowd,” she said.

But travel, and embellishing her outfits, have helped her reconnect with a more energetic, youthful version of herself. “After months of the same dull routine, dressing up for a trip feels like a shot of adrenaline,” she said.

Chang wasn’t initially looking for disposable clothes. But as she scrolled online for holiday looks, she found it hard to choose among those that caught her eye. In the end, she opted for cheaper versions of similar styles so she could buy more.

A brand dress can easily cost 300 to 500 yuan, she said. “For the same amount of money, I could buy seven to 10 cheaper outfits — enough to wear a different look each day of the trip.”

Chang said the appeal of disposable outfits lies partly in their novelty, helping her match a destination’s look and feel. The clothes let her try styles she rarely wears in daily life — brightly colored pieces with bold, saturated hues, more revealing cuts, or designs that push the boundaries of her usual wardrobe.

For 20-year-old Wu Xiangmeng, a college student in the southern Guangdong province, disposable outfits help her travel money — saved from her university’s monthly living allowance — go farther, leaving more for train tickets, accommodation, food, and activities. So far, she has visited almost 10 cities across China this way.

Before each trip, she researches her destination to pick disposable outfits that fit the scenery. When she’s done with her clothes, she lists them on secondhand platforms like Xianyu and Xiaohongshu instead of throwing them away, pairing the listings with photos of herself wearing the outfits on holiday to attract buyers.

“I can recoup some of the cost while making room — and saving money — for my next trip,” she said.

Outside impact

Though disposable clothing can be a cost-effective way to dress for specific destinations, Wu said she spends hours finding clothes she considers suitable, shopping, sorting through poor-quality purchases, and returning those that don’t make the cut. “The shopping experience is very draining,” she said.

While preparing for a trip to Hainan’s city of Sanya, for instance, Wu ordered several dresses, only to find the fabric flimsy, ripping at the slightest pull. She ultimately kept only two pieces from the pile and returned the rest.

Zhang Bingquan, who operates a garment factory in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, said disposable outfits cost so little partly because of their simplified designs and production process. With fewer patterns and straightforward sewing techniques, as in beachwear, he said production costs per garment can be kept in the single digits in yuan.

But the low prices have also intensified competition among manufacturers. To cut costs, some factories use lower-quality fabrics, reduce fabric weight and thickness, or take risks by using fabrics and dyes that fail to meet quality standards, he added.

“The biggest health risk with disposable clothing lies in the materials used,” Zhong Jianbo, deputy chief physician of the dermatology department at Hangzhou First People’s Hospital, told local media. “Cheap garments often use low-quality fabrics and dyes that may contain high levels of chemical residues.”

Sun Weiling, a dermatologist at Jiangsu People’s Hospital, told domestic media that disposable clothing is often made from stiff fabrics that can irritate the skin and cause damage, particularly in more delicate areas, such as the underarms, chest, waist, abdomen, and inner thighs.

The trend has also drawn criticism over its environmental costs. China is the world’s largest producer, consumer, and exporter of textiles, and generates vast amounts of textile waste. According to the China Association of Circular Economy, discarded clothing in the country is expected to reach 50 million metric tons a year by 2030, with each person throwing away an average of 16 garments annually.

During this year’s National Day holiday, the volume of textiles collected by Shanghai-based recycling platform Feimayi nearly doubled from the same period last year, Deng Qihua, the company’s head of marketing and sustainable development, told Sixth Tone.

“Some of the clothes we collected still had their original tags attached,” Deng said.

But recycling disposable outfits can be difficult and costly, as they are often made from blends of synthetic fibers, she added. “A garment bought cheaply and worn only a handful of times may therefore leave behind a much longer problem once its owner is ready to discard it,” Deng said.

A growing number of users are noticing the problem. A September commentary by state-run media outlet People’s Daily called on regulators to steer the market toward more sustainable alternatives, such as clothing rental. A Douyin hashtag promoting alternatives to “disposable fashion,” with tips on styling existing clothes and buying clothes with long-term use in mind, has garnered more than 32 million views.

But for many, health and environmental concerns take a back seat to looking good on vacation for minimal cost. Chang, the office worker, said that when she posted pictures of herself in her disposable outfits, friends praised her looks and “girlish charm.”

“At least it helps me feel better about myself,” she said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.title: China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019153/China Approves Nation’s First Brainstem Implant for Deafness
World.content:
China has approved its first auditory brainstem implant for clinical use among deaf patients amid a national push to commercialize brain-computer interface (BCI) technologies.

Approved Oct. 19 by China’s National Medical Products Administration, the implant — dubbed Nurotron WH-01A — is classified as a Class III medical device, the highest-risk category under the country’s medical device classification system.

The device was developed by a team led by Wu Hao, a surgeon and professor of otolaryngology at Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine’s Ninth People’s Hospital, in collaboration with Zhejiang Nurotron Biotechnology, headquartered in the eastern city of Hangzhou.

It is designed to restore hearing in patients who cannot benefit from conventional cochlear implants because of severe inner-ear malformations or an absent cochlear nerve, which normally carries auditory information from the inner ear to the brain.

Unlike cochlear implants, which stimulate the nerve via the inner ear, the auditory brainstem implant bypasses both the cochlea and the cochlear nerve, delivering electrical impulses directly to the cochlear nucleus, a brainstem structure through which all sound information enters the brain and where sound processing begins.

The system consists of six components, including a stimulator and a receiving coil. Used with Nurotron’s cochlear speech processor, located outside the patient’s body, it converts digital signals into electrical pulses that directly stimulate the cochlear nucleus.

Eligible patients include children aged 2 to 6 with “nonsyndromic deafness,” or deafness without other associated medical conditions or physical abnormalities, as well as those whose deafness was not caused by tumors or who cannot benefit from cochlear implants.

By 2024, the team had completed the implant surgeries and follow-up procedures for its clinical trial. The device achieved an overall treatment effectiveness rate of almost 97% after 12 months of activation, they told domestic media.

The approval comes as China ramps up efforts to advance its BCI industry toward clinical use and commercialization. China’s national development plan, part of its most recent five-year plan (2026–2030), identified BCI as one of six future industries. In July 2025, seven national ministries jointly set guidelines and targets for fostering a globally competitive BCI industry by 2030.

National regulators have also accelerated BCI device approvals for patient populations including those affected by stroke, Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s disease, and spinal cord injuries. In March, the country approved its first BCI kit, designed to help patients with quadriplegia caused by cervical spinal cord injuries regain limited hand function.

China’s BCI market is expected to exceed 6 billion yuan ($900 million) by 2028, with a compound annual growth rate of roughly 18% between 2024 and 2028, according to domestic research agency CCID Consulting.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Left: Professor Wu Hao’s team during an auditory brainstem implant surgery. Right: The auditory brainstem implant recently approved for market release. From the website of Shanghai Ninth People’s Hospital)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.title: Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019145/Frustrated by Dating Apps, Chinese Students Abroad Still Hope for Love
World.content:
In 2022, I spoke with Emma, a 22-year-old Chinese student in the UK, about her experiences with dating apps. Recalling one particularly disappointing encounter, she let out a sigh. Emma had matched with a man whose profile explicitly stated that he was looking for a long-term relationship. But the day after their third date, he texted her to say he had only ever wanted casual sex, then ghosted her. Feeling betrayed and emotionally drained, Emma changed her dating profile to say she was “Not Sure” what she wanted.

Emma’s experience was far from unusual. More than two-thirds of the 40 heterosexual Chinese students I interviewed in the UK reported similarly ambiguous dating intentions — findings drawn from a longitudinal study conducted between January 2022 and March 2023 that examined how their experiences with dating apps evolved while studying abroad. Many initially joined dating apps with clear goals, whether to pursue romantic relationships, make friends, or engage in language and cultural exchange. Yet over the course of the study, 27 of the 40 interviewees became less certain about what they wanted, increasingly adopting a “go with the flow” or “I’ll just see what happens” attitude.

For some, this ambiguity opened up new possibilities. For many others, however, it became a way to protect themselves after disappointing dating experiences. Beneath their apparent uncertainty, many still longed for a stable, long-term relationship.

For some young Chinese students arriving in the UK, keeping their dating intentions ambiguous is a deliberate strategy to leave their options open. In China, traditional dating culture places considerable emphasis on long-term commitment and marriage. Expressing vague or noncommittal intentions on Chinese dating platforms can carry a social stigma, with users sometimes labeled zhanan or zhanü, derogatory terms for men and women perceived as dishonest or irresponsible in romantic relationships.

Moving abroad can change these expectations. In the UK, students encounter a dating environment where a wider range of relationship arrangements is socially accepted. Living far from their parents and the social expectations of home also gives them greater freedom to experiment. For some, dating apps offer an opportunity to explore different kinds of relationships without committing to any particular one.

This “go with the flow” mentality was particularly common among postgraduate students enrolled in one-year degree programs. Jenny, a 23-year-old master’s student, explained during our first interview, shortly after arriving in the UK, that she had deliberately avoided setting clear dating goals so she could explore unconventional relationships.

“In China, I never thought about it because I was afraid of facing stigma and judgment,” she recalled. “I want to seize this opportunity to explore different possibilities during this one-year period.”

But not everyone embraced ambiguity out of a desire to experiment. For many other students, particularly women, keeping their intentions vague was a response to negative dating experiences.

After encountering misleading dating profiles and being ghosted without warning, some students became reluctant to invest emotionally in new relationships. Julia, a 23-year-old woman who had joined dating apps hoping to find a long-term partner, described feeling “emotionally paralyzed” after repeatedly meeting men who were only interested in casual sex. She initially had a clear relationship goal, but as she grew increasingly doubtful that she would find the commitment she wanted, she changed her profile to express more ambiguous intentions. By lowering her expectations, she hoped to avoid further disappointment.

Yet the difficulties these students faced in finding long-term relationships were not only about whom they encountered on dating apps. Their status as temporary residents in the UK could also make commitment more complicated. With student visas approaching expiration, many faced uncertainty about where they would live or work after graduation. Investing emotionally in a relationship could feel risky when relocation or a return to China was only months away. Potential partners in the UK might also hesitate to commit to someone who could soon leave the country.

Chou, a 23-year-old student, summed up her approach as “No expectations, no disappointments.” She explained, “Most local daters did not want to form a long-term relationship with me because I’m only here temporarily as an international student. They worried that once I head back to China after graduation, our relationship wouldn’t have a future.” Chou thus adopted ambiguous motivations to cope with the difficulty of forming and maintaining long-term relationships as graduation approached.

Yet perhaps the most surprising finding from my study was that adopting a “go with the flow” approach on dating apps did not necessarily signal a growing preference for casual relationships. In practice, my interviewees experienced different kinds of relationships, with some remaining short-term while others had the potential to develop into longer-term partnerships. Many of them still longed for lasting love. In some cases, that desire became stronger over time, as the initial excitement of exploring different relationships began to fade.

Jack, a 26-year-old student, described this gradual shift. During our first interview, he said he found it exciting to keep his intentions ambiguous because it allowed him to “explore different types of relationships.” But when we spoke again nearly a year later, he had come to understand his desires differently.

“As I kept using dating apps, I started to realize my expectations for long-term relationships had been awakened. Trying different relationships was fun, but it gradually left me feeling empty. I really wanted a serious relationship, but I suppressed that desire because I felt it was impossible to find something long-term on dating apps.”

The word “awakened” is revealing. It suggests that Jack’s desire for long-term commitment had never entirely disappeared. Rather than simply shifting from a preference for casual relationships to serious ones, he gradually came to recognize what mattered most to him.

Eve, a 23-year-old master’s student, captured this tension through a food metaphor. She described her short-term relationships as daican, a Chinese term meaning “meal replacements.” In Chinese internet slang, the term describes a substitute that offers some comfort or satisfaction but cannot fully make up for what someone really wants.

“I feel it’s very difficult to form long-term relationships on dating apps, so I’ll just stick to some ‘meal replacements’ for now to keep me from getting hungry,” she explained. “But a meal replacement cannot replace staple food.” For Eve, these brief connections were not meaningless. They offered companionship and helped ease the loneliness of living abroad. But they were substitutes for what she really wanted. The “staple food” in her metaphor was a stable, long-term relationship.

These experiences were neither entirely positive nor entirely negative. The “meal replacement” strategy could help meet immediate emotional needs. But such relationships rarely satisfied overseas students’ deeper desire for lasting commitment. In this sense, these experiences shouldn’t be taken as defining who they were or what they wanted from intimacy.

Dating apps offer Chinese students abroad new opportunities to explore relationships beyond the expectations they grew up with. But while living overseas may change how they approach dating, it does not necessarily change what they ultimately want. For many, the desire for lasting love remains, even as the uncertainty of their temporary lives abroad shapes what they feel able to pursue.

In line with research ethics, all research participants are given pseudonyms.

World.title: FACT CHECK: Marcos did not call for SC shutdown over budget ruling
World.content:
A 2025 video resurfaces out of context, falsely presented as a recent pronouncement by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. against the SC

Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said he wants to shut down the Supreme Court (SC) after it ruled parts of the 2024 to 2026 national budgets unconstitutional.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A video posted by Facebook user Ka’abs on October 24 claims, in overlaid text, that Marcos is speaking to reporters while being asked about a petition to the SC regarding the 2025 national budget.

The text reads, “Dahil sa pagbunyag ng Supreme Court ng kabulastugan mo” and “Ngayon gusto mo ipa-shutdown ang Supreme Court, ano ka hilo?”

(Because the Supreme Court exposed your wrongdoing, now you want the SC shut down. What’s wrong with you?)

The caption repeats the text, followed by raised-fist and crocodile emojis. As of writing, the video has garnered over 795,000 views, 10,000 reactions, 3,400 comments, and 2,900 shares.

The facts: No Palace statement or credible report shows Marcos seeking the SC’s shutdown. The clip’s original context shows he was referring to government operations.

The part of him saying that everything will be “shut down” was taken out of context from a January 2025 video, and sensationalized.

The original video shows an interview with Marcos in Cebu City, where he was asked what his administration would do if the SC ruled in favor of voiding the 2025 national budget. He answered, “No, we shut down everything.”

This was after former executive secretary Vic Rodriguez and Davao Representative Isidro Ungab asked the Court to void the 2025 national budget.

He then accused the petitioners of wanting “the government to cease working” so their “destabilization” could continue. He added that the solicitor general had assured him the budget was constitutionally sound. Rodriguez countered that the government would operate under a reenacted budget and “will never shut down.”

Recent SC ruling: The clip resurfaced after the SC’s October 20 ruling on the 2024 and 2025 General Appropriations Acts as unconstitutional.

On October 21, Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said Malacañang disagreed with parts of the ruling and had directed the Office of the Solicitor General to seek reconsideration. She added that the decision was not yet final, so spending under the 2026 budget would continue.

In a 121-page decision written by Senior Associate Justice Marvic Leonen, the Court voted 13-2 to declare Congress’ P449.5-billion increase in 2024 unprogrammed appropriations and a P17.99-billion increase in the 2025 DPWH Special Road Fund as unconstitutional.

It also struck down the SAGIP lump-sum allocations in the 2024 and 2025 budgets and key unprogrammed appropriations provisions in the 2026 budget.

The SC ruled that the lower chamber committed grave abuse of discretion by exceeding the constitutional cap on the President’s recommended appropriations. It applied the doctrine of operative fact, which protects spending already made in good faith. (READ: 5 practical effects of SC ruling on unprogrammed appropriations)

Court spokesperson Camille Ting said the ruling is not yet final, and the solicitor general may file a motion for reconsideration within 15 days from notice. Navotas Representative Toby Tiangco said the ruling could prompt new impeachment complaints against Marcos once the one-year bar expires in February. – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: BARMM’s Teduray, Lambangian tribes win ancestral land after 2 decades of struggle
World.content:
RITUAL. Indigenous leaders perform a ritual during a gathering marking the official recognition of their ancestral land title in Maguindanao del Sur, on October 23, 2026.

After more than two decades of legal battles, bureaucratic delays and relentless struggle, the Teduray and Lambangian indigenous communities in the Bangsamoro region secure formal recognition of 117,101 hectares of ancestral land

MAGUINDANAO DEL SUR, Philippines – Some died before they could see it. Others nearly lost hope.

After more than two decades of legal battles, bureaucratic delays and relentless struggle, the Teduray and Lambangian indigenous communities in the Bangsamoro region have secured formal recognition of 117,101 hectares of ancestral land — a hard-won victory that now leaves them with another fight: protecting it for generations to come.

The turnover of the Certificate of Ancestral Domain Title (CADT), covering 11 separate parcels, was marked by the traditional Tulak Këgëforor ritual in South Upi, Maguindanao del Sur, where most members of the two communities live. The gathering on Friday, October 23, reaffirmed their shared identity and their resolve to preserve their ancestral homeland.

A crowd gathers during the formal rites marking the official recognition of their ancestral land title in the BARMM, on Friday, October 23, 2026. Ferdinandh Cabrera/Rappler

The Constitution and the Indigenous Peoples’ Rights Act protect indigenous communities’ rights to their ancestral lands, which are held collectively for present and future generations. A CADT formally recognizes these rights.

Ancestral domains generally cannot be sold to “outsiders,” and development projects are subject to requirements for free, prior and informed consent from the affected communities, which are collectively have the right over the lands.

Timuay Alim Bandara, reflecting on the decades-long journey, emphasized that the achievement belongs to the younger generation.

“Dahil sa inyo, itong ginagawa natin… hindi para sa mga matatanda kundi para sa inyo na mga kabataang Teduray at Lambangian,” Bandara said during the gathering, underscoring the duty of safeguarding the document and the physical land for future generations.

(What we are doing here is because of you… not for the elders, but for you, the young Teduray and Lambangian people.)

Organized in collaboration with the Institute for Autonomy and Governance (IAG), the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP), and other relevant government agencies, the event drew together tribal leaders in the region, local executives, and national officials.

Two-decade journey

The path to recognition officially began on August 26, 2005, when the Teduray, Lambangian, and Dulangan Manobo Ancestral Domain Conference (TLADMADC), represented by Bandara as Timuay Labi and head claimant, filed a petition for recognition, delineation, segregation, and the issuance of a CADT.

The original claim covered approximately 201,850 hectares across the municipalities of Upi, South Upi, and southern portions of Datu Odin Sinsuat, Talayan, Guindulungan, Datu Unsay, Shariff Aguak, and Ampatuan in the Maguindanao area.

RITES. IP community members watch as their leaders lead rites during a gathering marking the official recognition of their ancestral land in Maguindanao del Sur, on October 23, 2026. Ferdinandh Cabrera/Rappler

The road to recognition was far from easy.

Bandara traced the formal processing roots back to August 12, 1996, under a Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) administrative order. However, due to administrative bottlenecks, the community shifted its processing efforts to the NCIP through the Mamalo Descendants Organization, officially commencing on January 10, 2005.

Jurisdictional complexities and legal overlaps between national laws and the former Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (ARMM) framework created significant delays. A crucial turning point came with the issuance of Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) Resolution Number 38, which initially posed a cease-and-desist challenge before paving the way for renewed institutional cooperation.

Through the NCIP Regional Office XII, the BARMM Ministry of Indigenous Peoples’ Affairs (MIPA), civil society organizations (CSOs), security sectors, and local governments across 11 municipalities, overlapping boundaries were reconciled, clearing the path for the official turnover.

Heritage protection and resource management

Spanning 117,101 hectares split into 11 parcels, the ancestral domain faces new challenges centered on community organization and resource management. Bandara called on community members and local leaders to foster unity, protect boundary monuments established during the 2016 perimeter surveys, and address pressing issues on the ground, such as land depletion and unauthorized sales.

“Ang pinaka-challenge dito, paano natin ma-organize ang mga tao na nakapaligid doon sa mga parcels na ito… dahil ang 117,000 hectares ay nakalat-kalat sa buong claim natin,” said Bandara, emphasizing that unified stewardship remains vital under the new development direction set by MIPA.

(The biggest challenge is how to organize the people living around these parcels of land, because the 117,000 hectares are scattered across our entire claim.)

Bandara noted that policy issues have now been largely established, with local laws for indigenous peoples in the BARMM ready for implementation.

He pointed to the Fusaka Inged Development Office (FIDO) and the Reservation and Arbitration Board (RAB) as established mechanisms to handle development and resolve land disputes.

Addressing the need for institutional support, Bandara said the BARMM parliament would need to increase financial allocations for MIPA during budget hearings.

“Although we understand that through MIPA there is already an automatic allocation of around P200 million, we think that because this is not the only ancestral domain we are looking at, the budget for developing ancestral domain areas inside the BARMM needs to be increased further,” he added.

Bandara also addressed the challenge of strengthening community-level policies to curb unauthorized land transactions.

“The only problem left is how to really strengthen it at the community level to prevent it…. [The] excuse before: we had nothing to show as titles. So now, with the issuance of CADT, we truly have a legal basis to take legal action against people who violate the law.”

Bandara said governance structures within the Timuay Justice and Governance (TJG) would be strengthened, and communities would be organized for every parcel. He said a higher body may need to keep watch given vastness of the ancestral land.

Leaders’ perspectives

NCIP Chairperson Nancy Catamco emphasized that with the focus now turning toward development, ancestral lands must be guarded more closely than ever.

She pointed out the traditional mindset regarding land titles. “IPs really do not have titles in their consciousness. Because for them, land is not claimed. Land should be used for everyone. That is why the thinking of needing a title came late. Because right now, it’s like waking up one morning and realizing the land is no longer theirs, even though they’ve been there. Then suddenly someone else owns it because they managed to get a title” she narrated.

On addressing investors and development projects covering the claimed lands, Catamco pushed for the Exercise of Priority Rights (EPR), emphasizing the true essence of Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC).

“It’s more of them exercising their priority rights. Meaning, as long as there is FPIC, what they want to get is their consent to say yes. But the essential function of FPIC is really to safeguard the rights of the ICCs/IPs to their self-determination, not to secure consent from a proponent or a project,” Catamco clarified.

BARMM MIPA Minister Guiamal Campong cited the historical significance of the CADT issuance and said coordination is ongoing to ensure the title is legally solid and incorporated with the EPR framework:

Campong added that his technical team would coordinate directly with the NCIP to explore the Exercise of Priority Rights (EPR). The NCIP also acknowledged MIPA’s crucial role in championing the rights and welfare of Non-Moro Indigenous Peoples in the Bangsamoro.

South Upi Mayor Helen Benito-Padua, herself a decendant of the Teduray-Lambangian indigenous community, was amothional during the gathering.

“To my fellow leaders, especially in South Upi, may we continue to stand by and respect our ancestral land. May we not say that ‘that’s just paper, that’s just you.’ May we show true unity and respect the hardship of the people who fought to get this title”, she said.

“To my fellow Teduray and Lambangian, let us fight for it. Let us not be ashamed of it, ‘let us not sell it or let money sway us.’ Money can be seen while we are alive, but the respect and this title that we can pass on to our descendants cannot be brought back once we ruin it,” she said. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Vantage Point] Tubig Pilipinas’ backdoor listing move opens into another suspension
World.content:
Tubig Pilipinas Holdings Inc. (TPHI, listed as TUBIG) has completed one of the local bourse’s most literal corporate metamorphoses: a dormant coal shell has been refashioned into a piped-water holding enterprise.

TPHI and Tubig Pilipinas Group Inc. (TPGI) are distinct corporate entities. TPHI is the publicly listed parent company whose shares trade on the exchange, while TPGI is the unlisted operating arm that develops, manages, and operates the underlying water distribution utilities.

With TPHI acquiring 100% of TPGI through a share swap, the investing public now holds its economic interest in the water assets indirectly through the listed shell.

Yet for ordinary minority shareholders watching from the sidelines, the initial dividend of this transformation is neither a buoyant commercial pipeline nor an invigorated business. It is a stock certificate they are legally barred from trading.

The Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) lifted the company’s extended suspension on October 14 after classifying the transaction as a backdoor listing. The reprieve proved ephemeral.

Just five trading sessions later, the bourse slapped TUBIG with another trading freeze because the share swap diluted the public float from 28.31% to 10.64%, well below the mandated 20% threshold.

Under the exchange’s amended rules, the company has a strict six-month cure period. Failure to restore the float within that compressed window triggers automatic delisting.

That timetable creates an immediate strategic disconnect. In its disclosures, TUBIG indicated plans to execute a follow-on public offering within a year of completing the swap. The exchange’s trading suspension sends a sharp counter-signal: the market will not wait that long.

The asset transaction was massive relative to the legacy corporate chassis. To acquire full control of operating subsidiary TPGI — owned equally by Pure Water Corporation and Quadwater Corporation — TPHI issued 66.46 billion new common shares at a par value of P0.10 each.

That pegged the acquisition value at P6.646 billion. The transaction handed the vendors a dominant 62.43% equity slice, ballooning total outstanding shares from 40 billion to 106.46 billion.

The resulting registry consolidates control into a few hands. Following the swap, Pure Water and Quadwater emerged with matching 37.65% stakes. Affiliate Pure Energy Holdings Corp. preserved a 4.69% toehold, while Dutch investment vehicle CEF2 A09 B.V. took 9.36%.

Together, this controlling bloc locks up 89.35% of the company. The legacy public float, stranded at an unchanged 11.33 billion shares, was relegated to a residual 10.64% corner.

The underlying arithmetic shows the sheer scale of the balance-sheet surgery required to cure the deficit. If the controlling shareholders execute a secondary placement, they must unload roughly 9.97 billion shares to the public.

If management opts for a primary offering, TUBIG would need to issue approximately 12.46 billion fresh shares, as the enlarged capital base demands higher share volume to reach 20%. Even at par, a primary issuance implies raising P1.25 billion in fresh equity—an ambitious capital call whose clearing price will test market appetite.

Rely on faith

Consequently, that equity offering is no administrative footnote. It represents the solitary bridge between an engineered private arrangement and an active public market. More critically, its clearing price will deliver the first authentic, arm’s-length market test of the P6.646-billion valuation ascribed to TPGI.

For now, minority investors are asked to rely on faith. Filings indicate that Isla Lipana & Co. prepared an independent fairness opinion and valuation report dated January 29 using income and market approaches.

Yet published disclosures omit the substantive quantitative machinery: there are no disclosed discount rates, cash-flow projections, terminal growth assumptions, peer matrices, or sensitivity ranges. The complete valuation report was visibly missing from the public bundle.

This opacity is difficult to reconcile with TPGI’s audited financial position. The water business recorded 2025 revenue of P270.77 million, an operating loss of P27.53 million, and a net loss of P31.34 million.

Total equity stood at P818.18 million against P1.93 billion in long-term loans. Current liabilities of P1.87 billion eclipsed current assets of P1.15 billion, leaving a working capital deficit of roughly P719 million.

To be clear, the business is not a hollow shell. TPGI generated P193.01 million in operating cash flow in 2025 while absorbing P750.78 million in capital outlays. It operates 12 water distribution facilities, manages five projects under development, and projects P1.93 billion in capital expenditures through 2031. It is an authentic, capital-intensive infrastructure play undergoing buildout.

Yet an acquisition price of P6.646 billion represents 8.1 times book equity and 24.5 times trailing revenue for an unprofitable asset. While long-gestation utility concessions can justify premiums on future cash flows, those multiples make the underlying math essential reading for public investors whose holdings were diluted.

I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. – Rappler.com

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. World.title: Anthropic discloses month-long training pause, AI security breaches in IPO filing
World.content:
ANTHROPIC. An Anthropic logo is displayed at Moscone Center during the Dreamforce 2026 technology summit in San Francisco, California, US, September 17, 2026

Anthropic says in its IPO filing's risk factors section that it delayed pre-training of a new 'frontier' base model to strengthen safeguards against the theft of model weights and intellectual property

Anthropic paused training of its next-generation flagship AI model for more than a month over security concerns, while four of its AI agents accessed live external computer systems during testing, its initial public offering filing showed on Monday, October 26.

The Claude maker said in the filing’s risk factors section that it had delayed pre-training of a new “frontier” base model to strengthen safeguards against the theft of model weights and intellectual property.

The disclosure highlights the safety challenges facing developers of increasingly powerful AI models, some of whose creators have warned the technology could eventually escape human control. Rival OpenAI also paused some training earlier this year over safety concerns after its models hacked Hugging Face.

The incidents illustrate how unexpected safety failures could disrupt development and deployment of models central to Anthropic’s growth as it prepares for a widely anticipated stock market debut.

Anthropic warned that training pauses could delay revenue and leave it trailing competitors. The company devoted about 94 pages to risk factors, more than in its confidential filing seen by Reuters.

Sandbox escape

The filing also detailed previously undisclosed safety evaluation failures in which four AI models escaped their testing environments and accessed real-world computer systems, with sessions lasting between 10 and 34 hours.

Anthropic said an error during cybersecurity tests with a third-party partner left the testing environment connected to the internet despite instructions that web access be disabled.

In one instance, an early version of the model continued pursuing an impossible evaluation task, discovered a stored password and used it to gain administrator access to a third party’s system. It then obtained additional credentials, changed system settings and accessed an individual’s personal data. The filing did not identify the external parties involved.

Anthropic said it notified all affected parties and found no evidence that the models had sought to evade human oversight or coordinate with each other. It subsequently suspended certain pre-release cybersecurity evaluations and paused higher-risk reinforcement learning environments.

Separately, the company said on Sunday that Claude had bypassed a paywall and accessed publicly available aggregate voter counts from the US state of Georgia without human authorization. – Rappler.com

World.title: Ban or tiered limits? Meta, gov’t agencies discuss child online safety
World.content:
DIGITAL DIALOGUE IRL. Meta hosts a forum with representatives from government, civil society, and the technology sector to explore practical ways to help young people recognize online risks and make informed decisions, on October 26, 2026.

CICC says child safety ‘cannot be matched by promises alone,’ urging platforms to deliver results on safeguards for minors online

MANILA, Philippines – As Congress moves to reconcile legislation prohibiting minors from accessing social media and other high-risk digital services, Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram, hosted a forum to discuss children’s online safety on Monday, October 26, at the Ayala Malls Glorietta Activity Center.

Meta, together with the Department of Information and Communications Technology-Cybercrime Investigation and Coordinating Center (DICT-CICC), Department of Education (DepEd), National Youth Commission (NYC), and other stakeholders, hosted the forum to kick off the Digital Dialogue In Real Life, a free interactive exhibition that aims to take a comprehensive approach to youth digital well-being in the Philippines. The exhibit will run from Monday, October 26 to Friday, October 30.

The forum covered what platforms and families can do, from parental controls to conversations at home. This comes after incidents of school violence were reported nationwide, with investigators examining possible online influences, and as lawmakers weigh bills restricting minors’ access to social media.

‘Not yet satisfied’ with platforms’ commitment

During Meta’s event, DICT-CICC Director IV Noel Carlo Gracilla said that “children’s safety cannot be matched by promises alone.”

“Although we have secured [the platforms’] commitments, the CICC is not yet satisfied…. What we need to see is their action and effective solutions that will leave good results for our young people,” Gracilla said in his welcome message, speaking in Filipino.

He did, however, credit Meta’s quick responses to CICC requests with helping curb young people’s exposure to inappropriate content. He said the agency met in recent months with Discord, Reddit, Meta, and Roblox to raise concerns about their in-app safety features, especially for content unsuitable for minors.

At least eight incidents of school violence in the Philippines have been reported in 2026, including three deadly school shootings. Such incidents have prompted authorities to seek commitments from social media platforms.

In August, after the second deadly shooting took place in Zamboanga City, the DICT said Meta and Roblox had agreed to enhance child-safety protections for users in the Philippines, including age verification and parental controls.

Senator Risa Hontiveros also said in the same month that the Philippine government had secured a commitment from Meta to provide user data to law enforcement when there is an imminent threat of violence.

Ban or tiered limits?

Meta kicked off the exhibit with a forum to explore practical ways to address the risks children face online today. Among the panelists were:

Gio Tingson, head of public policy, Meta Philippines

Joseph Francisco Ortega, chairperson, NYC

Razzel Requesto, director IV, DepEd

Ysrael Diloy, child protection specialist, Stairway Foundation

Niel Steve Kintanar, external relations officer, Psychological Association of the Philippines

Mariel Kliatchko, influencer mom and school owner

The forum took place as Congress weighs whether to ban children from social media altogether. Under the Senate-approved Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) bill, social media accounts determined as being owned or used by a minor will be suspended, restricted, disabled, or removed. It will also prevent users below 18 years old from creating accounts.

Diloy argued that a ban would push children out of online spaces where they have rights to expression and information.

“The rights holders are the children. The duty bearers are us, the adults. It’s our obligation to ensure the safety of the spaces the children move in, and to ensure that the children reap the benefits of technology,” Diloy said in Filipino.

“What we’re hoping for is for tech platforms to have accountability and responsibility,” Diloy said, adding that Meta’s launch of Teen Accounts with parental supervision tools is a welcome step.

Meta’s Digital Dialogue IRL builds on its Screen Smart Philippines initiative, launched in June, which educates parents and teens about the safety features built into Teen Accounts across its products: Instagram, Facebook, Messenger, and Threads.

The protections in Teen Accounts include default private accounts, messaging restrictions, sensitive content limits, daily 60-minute time limit reminders, and a “sleep mode” that mutes notifications between 10 pm and 7 am. Teens cannot opt out or loosen these settings without a parent’s permission.

“Learning from other jurisdictions, without naming any country, we saw that bans are ineffective,” Tingson told Rappler on the sidelines of the event, saying that their solution is a tiered approach.

He argued that giving a five-year-old and an 18-year-old the same restrictions online would not address the core problem. “Their dimension of learning, of exploration, of responsibility is very different, so you want to make sure that the experience is appropriate. Because if we push people outside of the platform by doing bans, it’s either they circumvent it, or they delay learning,” he said.

Early evidence from Australia’s restrictions on social media for children under 16 years old found that roughly eight in ten children continued using social media despite the ban.

Hontiveros, the only senator to vote against the SMART KIDS bill, also earlier suggested a tiered access by age instead of a blanket ban.

‘Connection before correction’

But whatever safety features social media platforms roll out only matter if families use them. Tingson told Rappler on the sidelines of the event that they’re still working on getting people to 

For the other members of the panel, using the features starts with a conversation between parent and child.

“Connection before correction. We can correct, we can punish. We can do all that. But do we understand [why we’re doing it]?” Kliatchko said in a mix of English and Filipino.

The influencer mom said that parents should protect, but it should be done with preparation. “You cannot just forbid your children to play Minecraft or Roblox…. You have to understand it. You have to be able to explain why [you’re setting boundaries],” she said.

Others on the panel echoed her. Kintanar said research shows relationships matter for mental health and well-being, while Ortega said parents can’t set limits for children they haven’t connected with.

A bigger problem outside the Philippines

The panel’s advice puts parents at the center. But what happens when even engaged parents become inundated with the apps’ features that are alleged to be built to hold teens’ attention?

Earlier this year, documents, primarily internal communications at the social media companies, were unsealed and shown in a Los Angeles trial brought by a young woman who said Instagram and YouTube fueled her addiction and depression. In March, the jury found Meta and YouTube liable for negligently designing products that harmed her. Meta has since appealed.

In August, a separate federal trial began on claims by 29 different US states. All 29 accused Meta of improperly collecting children’s data, and four lead states also alleged it deliberately designed Facebook and Instagram to hook children and misled the public about their safety.

Meta denied the claims and said it has strong protections for teenagers. About a week in, a federal judge approved an $18-billion settlement. Meta agreed without admitting wrongdoing, so the court made no finding on the states’ claims. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who will be VP if Sara Duterte is convicted?
World.content:
VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte waves to supporters as she arrives at the Quezon City Regional Trial Court for the arraignment of her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.

A political science professor says the choice of a successor will involve more than simply filling a vacancy

Even before Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial reaches a verdict, the question of who could replace her is already stirring debates among senator-judges.

Under the Constitution, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has the authority to nominate Duterte’s possible successor from among the sitting lawmakers but the decision will still be subject to congressional confirmation.

Article VII, Section 9 of the 1987 Constitution states: “Whenever there is a vacancy in the Office of the Vice President during the term for which he was elected, the President shall nominate a Vice-President from among the Members of the Senate and the House of Representatives who shall assume office upon confirmation by a majority vote of all the Members of both Houses of the Congress, voting separately.”

Over the weekend, Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero explained that while Marcos has the authority to nominate Duterte’s possible successor, the nominee must also meet the constitutional qualifications for vice president, including the age requirement.

This narrows the pool of potential nominees to sitting members of Congress who meet the constitutional requirements, including Escudero himself.

“I have yet to receive offers but as I’ve said before, I would not accept it because of a simple reason: conflict of interest,” Escudero said in his podcast.

“We tried her case so personally, I don’t think accepting that would be proper,” he added.

Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano lauded Escudero and urged other senator-judges to issue similar commitment to decline such proposals, citing the need to maintain political neutrality in the trial.

“It’s essential that in all impeachment proceedings, senator-judges are politically neutral and will have no incentive to convict except for evidence that proves the article/s of impeachment,” he said.

Cayetano’s remarks, however, did not sit well with Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, who cautioned against preempting the decisions of other senator-judges.

“He should not preempt the decision of other senator-judges. Selecting the successor is under the prerogative of the President but of course, subject to the confirmation of the Congress,” Lacson said, adding he would decline if he would be offered such position.

“But I think [Cayetano’s statement] is uncalled for,” the senator added.

So what would Marcos look for in a successor? For political science professor Jean Franco of the University of the Philippines Diliman, the choice of a successor would involve more than simply filling a vacancy.

The President would have to consider the political implications of his nominee and whether that person could be trusted to assume the country’s highest office if necessary.

Franco identified several qualities Marcos might look for in a potential successor:

Someone who can help elevate public trust in the administration

Someone who can tell Marcos the truth

Someone whom the First Lady [Liza Araneta-Marcos] likes and whom she can get a long with

Most importantly, someone who is ready to be President

Someone who is friendly to members of the House of Representatives and the Senate since they will concur with the appointment

Franco also said calls for senator-judges to declare they would refuse offers may not exactly paint a picture of impartiality.

“I think there is no need for that call actually, since in the first place, no senator in his right mind will publicly say that he/she wants to be vice president even if they secretly want to be one,” Franco told Rappler.

“Moreover, having this call amplifies the talk that the Vice President will be convicted, but at the same time, if she is convicted, it is not because she is guilty but because some senators are aiming for her position,” Franco added.

No names have publicly emerged as possible appointees, but as Senator JV Ejercito puts it, discussing who will succeed the Vice President — at this time — may still be too “premature”.

“I don’t think it is proper to discuss who will succeed the vice president because her trial remains ongoing. It’s still too premature,” said Ejercito. Who will likely be the President’s choice, is the big question. – Rappler.com

World.title: In Marawi, therapy helps mothers find new ways to connect with their children
World.content:
Recovery efforts focused on psychosocial needs after the 2017 Marawi siege uncover the needs of children with developmental delays

October 27 is marked as World Occupational Therapy Day to raise awareness about how therapists help people of all ages gain or regain everyday life and working skills

When Sania Naga calls her son, Amal, for help, he answers, “Yes, Mama.”

It is an ordinary exchange, but one Naga could not always have with her firstborn. For many years, Amal was non-verbal. At three, Amal was not saying “Mama” or “Papa.” When he wanted milk, he handed Naga his bottle. When the television would turn off in a power outage, he pointed to it and cried.

Naga noticed that other children Amal’s age were already discovering words and sounds and becoming talkative. They could follow simple instructions from their parents. Others assured Naga that some children develop later than others, but she still worried.

Neither she nor her husband knew what to do.

“What will happen to my child when he gets older? What will happen to him when his father and I are no longer around?” Naga recalled thinking.

An opportunity to seek help came when Amal fell ill. During a visit to a pediatrician, Naga raised her concerns about his development. The doctor referred them to a specialist in Cagayan de Oro, roughly three hours from their home in Marawi City.

Distance, time, and then the pandemic became hurdles to getting treatment. When they tried to set an appointment, a year had passed before Amal was seen by a doctor.

Amal was initially diagnosed with cognitive development delay, a condition where there is a lag in thinking, learning, and reasoning skills. Naga asked whether medicine could help. The recommendation was therapy.

Getting it meant traveling to the nearest therapy center in Iligan, about 45 minutes away, every week. Amal had an hour of occupational therapy and another of speech therapy.

Naga arranged Saturday appointments around her job, her husband’s work, and caring for their two other children.

“During the first six months, I felt like giving up,” she said.

Then the therapist began noticing Amal’s progress. His behavior, once marked by hyperactivity, became more manageable. He became calmer as he learned to express himself more. At home, Amal began making eye contact and responding when she greeted him good morning.

Gaps at every stage of care

Naga’s experience underscores the care and treatment gaps facing children with disabilities. The gaps span all touch points that starts from having their needs recognized, reaching someone who can assess them and link them to care, and sustaining treatment and support.

Data from the government’s January 2026 National Education Plan estimates that there are about 4.7 million to 5.1 million children with disabilities. Statistics from the previous year indicate that there are about 391,000 identified learners with disabilities in public schools during the 2024-2025 school year. Roughly 6 in 10 lacked a formal diagnosis.

In addition, a shortage of specialists and therapists complicates getting therapy and care even when assessed.

In Naga’s case, occupational therapy was one of the interventions recommended for Amal to help him develop skills for everyday activities such as eating, dressing and participating in school.

LEARNING. Regular therapy helps children with intellectual and developmental delays. Photo courtesy of REACH Foundation

The World Health Organization listed fewer than 6,000 registered occupational therapists nationwide in 2025, with services concentrated in urban areas.

In Marawi, where Naga and her family live, accessibility is also a geographic problem.

In 2024, there were reportedly only two developmental pediatricians in Northern Mindanao. Families from Marawi seek care in Iligan and Cagayan de Oro. Appointment waits can reportedly reach three and a half years.

Jalil Usman, a social worker for Community and Family Services International (CSFI) in Marawi, said that intensified mental health outreach around 2019 as part of the recovery efforts after the Marawi siege brought them to parents needing support for their children with intellectual and developmental delays.

“There were gaps in understanding and, in some families, shame about showing others that a child had a disability. As families learned about available help and shared their experiences, others approached us,” said Usman.

“Some parents had assumed their children could never learn certain everyday skills, but it turned out they could,” Usman added.

CFSI secured funding to partner with the Medbay Therapy and Learning Center in Iligan to provide 21 children through 10 sessions each of occupational therapy.

Getting children to therapy became somewhat of a field trip. CFSI staff picked up some families from their homes and drove them to Iligan in an office vehicle. In the clinic, the parents would wait for their turn for their therapy session.

However, funding was not enough to cover the recommended 72 sessions. When the CFSI funded sessions ended in 2023, Naga paid for the treatment costs out of pocket.

“Sometimes, when we did not have enough money, we would miss sessions,” she said.

Teletherapy to bridge access

CFSI partnered with the Rehabilitation and Empowerment of Adults and Children with Handicap Foundation (REACH), a non-profit organization in Manila that provides free occupational and speech therapy to undersupported children and adults with disabilities. Together, they developed and conducted teletherapy sessions adapted to the children’s needs.

Through sessions conducted online or by phone or through other messaging platforms, therapists work with family members to develop home-based interventions using everyday or improvised materials.

“We often use toys, books, school materials, kitchen items, and other familiar household objects to make learning part of the child’s daily life,” said Archie David, founder and president of REACH Foundation.

A simple clothespin, for example, can help strengthen fine motor skills, while everyday activities such as preparing meals, sorting laundry, or playing games can become opportunities for learning and development.

ONLINE. Teletherapy sessions adapt to every child’s needs. Photo courtesy of REACH Foundation

Amal’s occupational therapy program focused on visual perceptual skills, which are important for handwriting, copying from the board, organizing written work, and other classroom tasks.

Another child, Shoraim, had a hearing impairment that made spoken conversations difficult to follow in school. His mother, Sohairah Batabor, used gestures and written words to communicate with him.

Through occupational therapy and guidance at home, Shoraim developed everyday skills, including dressing, bathing, and preparing simple meals like his favorite noodles and fried egg. His daily morning routine is comprised of reading the Quran and praying.

“The most meaningful changes are not always reflected in assessments. Sometimes it is a parent noticing that their child is joining family activities more often, participating in class, communicating a need, or trying something independently for the first time. These moments may seem ordinary to others, but for families, they can be life-changing,” said David.

“As a child’s confidence grows, so do his opportunities to build relationships, independence, and a stronger sense of belonging at home, in school, and in the community,” David added.
