Amal, who is now 12 years old, is attending a mainstream school as a Grade 3 student. He can eat, manage his hygiene on his own, and communicate with his parents.

Naga recalled the advice of the therapist to call Amal even when she needed nothing from him.

“Amal, come here. Mama wants to talk to you,” she would say.

Before, Amal could not answer. Now he does by saying, “Yes, Mama.” – Rappler.com

Disclosure: The writer and Abelardo David Jr. are both Senior Fellows of the Equity Initiative–CMB Foundation.

World.title: Regime Disguises Military Jet Fuel as Diesel to Evade Sanctions: JFM
World.content:
The Myanmar regime and companies linked to it have engaged in international trade fraud, using proxy firms and misclassifying aviation fuel as diesel to conceal imports of fuel used in airstrikes targeting civilians, according to an investigation released Monday by rights group Justice For Myanmar (JFM).

The findings are based on leaked documents from the regime’s Ministry of Commerce, confidential records from its Foreign Exchange Supervisory Committee (FESC), and an analysis of supply networks and market prices.

JFM said the FESC plays a critical role in approving imports of jet fuel that are intentionally and falsely declared as diesel, and in concealing the true buyers.

The FESC was established in 2022 to centralize and strictly regulate foreign currency conversions, imports and overseas transfers. It consists of six high-level regime officers, including Vice-President Nyo Saw, who has served as its chairperson since 2024.

Known to be an important figure in the management of the personal business empire of regime leader Min Aung Hlaing’s family, Nyo Saw is himself sanctioned by the EU and Canada.

The evidence indicates that six aviation fuel shipments arrived using these “evasive measures” between December 2024 and November 2025, JFM said.

During the same period, the regime stepped up airstrikes nationwide as it prepared for its sham election held in December 2025 and January 2026. The imports covered 843,000 barrels worth US$109.6 million and originated in or transited through Singapore and South Africa, the group said.

According to its findings, two Myanmar companies, Dynamic Wave and PP Petroleum Co. Ltd, were listed as importers in the contracts in order to hide the identity of the real buyer, National Energy Prime Aviation Services Co. Ltd (NEPAS).

Contracts naming Thai company Tawan-Oil Trading as the seller showed that Dynamic Wave served as a proxy importer for NEPAS in three shipments valued at $68.49 million and comprising 527,624 barrels.

Separately, Reuters reported on Monday that jet fuel imported under contracts identifying South Africa as the source was actually shipped from Iran. It said Tehran was the Myanmar military’s primary supplier of jet fuel between October 2024 and December 2025.

PP Petroleum imported another three shipments of aviation fuel misclassified as diesel, worth $41.06 million, according to contracts listing Singapore as the loading port. These were also for NEPAS, according to JFM.

NEPAS is a joint venture between regime-controlled Myanmar Petrochemical Enterprise and partner Asia Sun Group.

Asia Sun Group, a network of companies monopolizing the jet fuel supply chain, has established many shell companies in response to sanctions and public scrutiny. PP Petroleum is part of Asia Sun Group.

Some Asia Sun Group companies are sanctioned by the U.S., UK, EU, Canada and Australia—with sanctions dating back to 2022 and 2025—but NEPAS and MPE remain unsanctioned, JFM noted.

Based on its examination of regime documents and an analysis of market prices, JFM found that the regime deliberately mislabeled jet fuel as high-speed diesel to avoid scrutiny, bypass international regulations and minimize sanctions exposure risk.

Highlighting Thai supplier Tawan-Oil Trading and Singapore’s role as a loading hub, JFM called on both countries to investigate the Myanmar regime’s customs fraud and bar their territory, ports and banks from enabling jet fuel shipments.

The rights group demanded that South Africa block all fuel exports to Myanmar and investigate regime documents falsely listing the country as the fuel’s origin. It called on governments to stop granting “false legitimacy” to the regime.

JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung said the regime’s use of trade fraud to facilitate jet fuel imports suggested that sanctions and public pressure “are biting,” but “clearly not enough.”

She urged governments to coordinate sanctions against the aviation fuel supply networks feeding the regime, and to investigate trade fraud by the regime and its partners to halt the “slaughter of civilians.”

The UNHCR, the UN’s refugee agency, said Myanmar military airstrikes remained the main cause of civilian deaths in the country, and called for an end to the transfer of arms, ammunition, jet fuel and dual-use equipment to the regime.

More than 6,200 civilians have been killed in over 14,000 regime airstrikes since the 2021 coup, according to the now-dissolved Human Rights Ministry of the National Unity Government.

World.title: Myanmar Regime’s Minimum Rice Price ‘a License to Squeeze Farmers’
World.content:
Rice farmers across Myanmar have voiced concern that the minimum price set by the regime is far below market rates and would not even cover their skyrocketing production costs.

The regime’s Committee for the Protection and Promotion of the Rights and Interests of Farmers last week set the minimum floor price for 100 baskets or about 2.09 tons of rice at 1.35 million kyats (around US$300) for monsoon paddy or unmilled rice harvested this year and summer paddy to be harvested next year.

Farmers report that the current market price for 100 baskets ranges from 1.9 to over 2 million kyats, with some areas seeing around 3 million kyats. Premium Paw San rice is selling for 5 to 6 million kyats.

“Here in Naypyitaw, the market price is 1.9 to 2 million kyats,” one farmer told The Irrawaddy. “And even at that rate, after deducting labor and other expenses, almost nothing is left. Costs are too high. Setting the base price at 13.5 million kyats is unacceptable.”

In principle, the base rate is set only in case the market rate is for some reason lower and aims to ensure that farmers are paid fairly—in other words, farmers cannot be paid less than the base rate but can be paid more.

But farmers fear the yawning gap between the two rates is apt to push down market prices to the point where they no longer make any profit at all. That means the regime is tacitly encouraging brokers to weaponize the base price to negotiate lower rates, and farmers burdened with debt will be forced to sell anyway.

Instead, farmers say the calculation should take into account fertilizer, pesticide and labor costs plus loan interest. Farmers say they cannot buy supplies at the regime’s official prices either but must pay market rates for fertilizer, pesticides and harvest labor.

“Fertilizer is sold for 80,000 to 150,000 kyats a bag, and if we buy on credit, monthly interest is 3,000 to 5,000 kyats for each 100,000 kyats borrowed,” said a farmer from Ayeyarwady Region. “So a base price of 1.35 million kyats doesn’t even cover expenses.”

Farmers estimate production costs per acre are around 1.2 million kyats excluding interest, but this year’s monsoon harvest has fallen to only 68 to 75 baskets per acre. If paid the base price of 1.35 million kyats for 100 baskets, they would lose around 200,000 to 300,000 kyats per acre.

According to the Myanmar Rice Federation, Myanmar earned $338 million from rice exports in the first half of fiscal 2026, which began in April.

World.title: Myanmar War Crimes Survivors Look to Denmark for Justice
World.content:
Forty homes. That is how many a woman, now living in Denmark, watched burn in her village in Chin State, western Myanmar. Family members and friends were killed or left permanently disabled by landmines planted by the junta. Like tens of thousands of others from Chin State, she was driven across the border into India.

On Monday, she is asking the Danish authorities to investigate the men responsible.

She has filed a criminal complaint in Copenhagen against members of the Myanmar junta. For her safety she cannot be named. The crimes in the complaint include deliberate killing, mass arson and the forced displacement of tens of thousands of people.

This is possible because of a change in Danish law. Legislation that came into force last year specifically criminalizes war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. It gives Danish prosecutors a route that did not exist before.

Her lawyer, Copenhagen-based Eddie Omar Rosenberg Khawaja, puts it plainly. “Under the new Danish legislation it no longer matters where the crimes took place, or the nationality of the perpetrators or the victims,” he says. “Victims living in Denmark can request that Danish authorities hold commanders under whose watch atrocities against them occurred responsible.”

That matters because there is nowhere else to go. Myanmar’s courts are controlled by the generals. The Security Council has failed to act. International courts in The Hague—the International Criminal Court and the International Court of Justice—have also been slow. For the people of Chin State, a Danish police station may be one of the few doors that open.

It also fits Denmark’s own history. Tracy Bawi Hlei, chairperson of Myanmar Action Group Denmark (MAGD), which supports the case, says: “Denmark has a history of aligning itself with the pro-democracy movement in Myanmar since before the 1990s, through development aid, support of activists, bypassing the military government and standing in solidarity with human rights movements.”

She sees this case as the next step. “Now, Myanmar people and Danish activists who are part of communities and movements in Denmark are taking a stand for accountability and the international rule of law.” Survivors and crucial evidence, she explains, were identified within Denmark through a collaboration of civil society groups, including MAGD and the Chin Community Denmark (CCDK), which also supports the case.

I run the Myanmar Accountability Project, which supports cases against the junta in Southeast Asia and Europe. I believe the basis for a Danish case is strong.

The Danish government has said so itself. In a statement to the UN on September 30, 2025, Denmark said, as a matter of public record, that Myanmar suffers from a lack of accountability and continued impunity. This complaint invites Denmark to act on that.

The timing is pointed. The Danish Foreign Ministry is closing its embassy in Myanmar. This case allows the Danish government to send a signal that it remains engaged with issues of justice and accountability, and that the rightful aspirations of the people of Myanmar to a just, peaceful and dignified life must be respected.

Meanwhile, the junta is seeking legitimacy. Min Aung Hlaing, the general who led the coup, is now president after sham elections that offered the people of Myanmar no real choice. Those who lived through his campaigns of burning and killing are expected to accept this as normal. They do not.

The country’s condition leaves no room for complacency. According to the latest UN report, more than 16 million people need aid, and the junta is blocking humanitarian access to vast areas where the need is greatest. Nearly 3.8 million people are estimated to have been displaced, many of them several times. A UN Development Programme report published last month found that two-thirds of the population are living in poverty or at immediate risk of falling into it.

The violence is on a scale that few outside the region grasp. More than 100,000 people have died in conflict-related violence since the coup. That makes Myanmar’s conflict the fourth deadliest in the world. This is not a frozen conflict. It is a war on civilians, and state-wide repression compounds the inhuman levels of killing, making justice and accountability even more important.

What the complainant seeks is limited. She is not asking Denmark to end a war. She is asking its police to open an investigation and its prosecutors to take her evidence seriously. She is asking that the commanders responsible be held accountable.

Denmark has said impunity in Myanmar must end. Its new law now gives it a way to act on that. She has come forward, at a risk to herself that most of us will never face. It is now for Danish authorities to decide whether the law means what it says.

Chris Gunness is founder and director of the Myanmar Accountability Project.

World.title: China Taps Myanmar’s Rare Earth Surge, Coffee Sell-Off, and More
World.content:
China’s rare earth imports swelled by Myanmar supply

China’s rare earth imports surged to 5,021 tons in September, up 23 percent from August, according to data from the Shanghai Metals Market.

Shipments of rare earth oxides from Myanmar accounted for 70 percent of the total, while arrivals from Laos fell to 1,369 tons. Together, Myanmar and Laos accounted for 97 percent of total imports. Cumulative imports for January–September reached 46,466 tons, up 14 percent year‑on‑year.

Rare earth mines along Myanmar’s northeastern border with China supply roughly half the world’s heavy rare earths, including strategically scarce dysprosium and terbium used in magnets crucial to China’s high-tech supply chain.

The surge comes as the US reengages with Myanmar’s regime, fueling speculation that global competition for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. However, almost all of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are located in territory beyond regime control.

Myanmar specialty coffee faces Chinese fire sale

A Chinese fire sale beckons for Myanmar’s once-booming specialty coffee market. Once backed by USAID and American buyers, the coffee industry collapsed after the 2021 coup as Shan farmers responsible for some of the world’s finest beans were deprived of access to Western markets, transparent trade and certification. With the lucrative export path blocked, the regime and its Myanmar Coffee Association (MCA) are now aggressively pivoting to China.

MCA chairman Myo Aye told Xinhua that cooperation with Yunnan has deepened since the military takeover, with new MoUs locking in China as the top destination for Myanmar’s 3,000–4,000 tonnes of annual exports—tumbling from pre-coup levels of more than 5,000 tonnes. He said the association is looking to attract Chinese investment in value-added processing facilities, roasting plants and supply-chain logistics.

Myanmar’s coffee basket of Shan State has been ravaged by some of the fiercest fighting triggered by the 2021 coup.

Agriculture supplants industry at Myanmar-China forum

The Seventh Myanmar–China Think Tank Forum kicked off in Mangshi, Yunnan Province on Wednesday, with agricultural cooperation placed firmly at the center of discussions. Launched in 2017, the annual forum takes a different theme each year, but its underlying focus has consistently been the now stalled China–Myanmar Economic Corridor, a project designed to give Beijing direct access to the Indian Ocean.

This year’s session saw Myanmar regime officials highlight opportunities in rice and coffee. Yunnan is a major buyer of both. They urged deeper cooperation to expand exports, boost trade and investment, develop value‑added products, and facilitate technology exchange.

The forum comes as regime leader Min Aung Hlaing promotes agriculture as the key sector to revive an economy devastated by his coup and international sanctions. He has emphasized rice, cotton, oilseed crops, pulses, and rubber as priority industries to drive growth.

Earlier this month, Myanmar’s Pawsan variety won global recognition at the World Rice Conference 2026. At the 23rd China–ASEAN Expo in Nanning last month, three Myanmar rice exporters signed five MoUs with Chinese companies. According to the Myanmar Rice Federation, Myanmar earned US$ 338 million from rice exports in the first half of FY2026–27, which began in April.

Travel alert over Myanmar scams sparks Thai pushback

The Chinese Embassy in Bangkok issued a safety advisory on Oct. 16 warning its citizens of trafficking risks linked to scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border, prompting a scrambled response from Thailand’s foreign and tourism ministers.

The advisory cautioned Chinese nationals to be on alert for kidnapping and trafficking schemes disguised as high‑paying job offers, fraudulent investment projects, and bogus filming contracts targeting livestreamers and entertainers. It urged travelers to verify overseas employment opportunities, avoid suspicious transport arrangements, and steer clear of high‑risk areas on the Thai-Myanmar frontier where criminal networks remain active despite official crackdowns.

The warning followed recent cases that rattled public opinion in China, including the abduction of a shopping livestreamer who was lured by a bogus contract to Thailand before being trafficked to Myanmar last month. The high‑profile kidnapping of soap actor Wang Xing in Myawaddy in 2025 had already triggered a trilateral crackdown by China, Thailand, and Myanmar.

Following the latest advisory, a Chinese actress cancelled a fan meeting in Bangkok, underscoring the potential impact on Thailand’s tourism sector.

Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow responded by urging the embassy to ensure its warnings are proportionate to the situation and avoid sparking unnecessary alarm. He stressed that Thailand takes visitor safety seriously and will investigate incidents, but cautioned that exaggerated advisories risk undermining confidence in Thailand as a safe destination. Chinese nationals are Thailand’s largest tourism market.

Naypyitaw eyes tourism lifeline in Kunming

Even as reports of trafficking and scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border dominate headlines in China, Myanmar’s regime is pressing ahead with plans to lure Chinese visitors back to Myanmar to revive a tourism industry shattered by the 2021 coup.

The regime’s Hotels and Tourism Ministry has announced it will open a tourism promotion office in Kunming, Yunnan Province. At the China–Myanmar cultural tourism exchange meeting held in Kunming from October 13–17, Tourism Ministry Secretary Maung Maung Kyaw described the proposed office as a potential “major corridor” for public‑private cooperation between the regime and Chinese tour companies. A business‑to‑business memorandum of understanding was also signed between Chinese and Myanmar tour operators.

Chinese travelers remain Myanmar’s largest foreign tourism market, but numbers have collapsed since the coup. Just over 250,000 Chinese arrivals were recorded last year—a fraction of the pre‑coup boom—despite having access to visas on arrival. In 2019, Myanmar saw 749,719 Chinese arrivals out of a total 4.4 million tourists.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Rare Earth Exports Surge Amid Illusion of Regime Control
World.content:
China’s rare earth imports rose sharply in September to 5,021 tons, up 23 percent from August, according to data from the Shanghai Metals Market.

Shipments from Myanmar accounted for 70 percent of the total, while arrivals from Laos fell to 1,369 tons. Cumulative imports for January–September were up 14 percent year‑on‑year.

Meanwhile, recent U.S. reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that rare earth competition is driving Washington’s policy recalibration.

Regime supporters are now boasting that the embattled junta has a “rare earth card” to play in its bid for international recognition, pointing to parallel interest from India.

Yet, although Myanmar is home to around 600 rare earth mines primarily feeding China’s supply chain, almost all of them lie beyond the regime’s territorial control.

Why are rare earths important?

Rare earth elements (REEs) are indispensable for high‑tech industries, serving as raw materials for magnets in electric vehicles, wind turbines, smartphones, and defense systems.

China dominates global mining and refining, producing nearly 70 percent of rare earth oxides and controlling more than 85 percent of refining capacity. Yet its domestic deposits are dominated by light REEs, leaving it reliant on Myanmar’s northern mining belt. Myanmar produces roughly half the world’s heavy rare earths (HREEs), including strategically scarce dysprosium and terbium used in powerful magnets crucial to China’s AI ambitions.

Kachin State’s riches

Kachin State, which borders China and India, hosts nearly 80 percent of over 600 rare earth mines identified by satellite imagery across northern Myanmar, with the highest concentration clustered in Chipwi and Momauk. These two townships alone contain over 370 active mining sites featuring more than 2,700 active leaching pits, according to data from the Stimson Center and Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar.

Before late 2024, Kachin’s rare earth mining hubs were controlled by the New Democratic Army–Kachin (NDA-K), a junta-aligned militia turned Border Guard Force (BGF) led by warlord Zakhung Ting Ying. Under NDA-K control, rare earth extraction expanded with virtually no environmental oversight, generating tens of millions of dollars in informal taxes and dividends shared between militia leaders and top generals in Naypyitaw.

Their control collapsed in October 2024 when the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) launched a major territorial offensive. The KIA routed NDA-K forces and seized the mines in Chipwi and Pangwa, with victory placing Myanmar’s primary HREE extraction infrastructure under the direct administrative control of an armed group actively fighting the military regime.

Shan State: the new player

While Kachin State remains Myanmar’s rare-earth hub, mining in Shan State has expanded 48 percent on average over the past five years, outpacing Kachin’s 15 percent. Nearly 90 rare earth mines have been detected in territory controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), United Wa State Army (UWSA), and National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA).

While the UWSA and NDAA have maintained ceasefires with the Myanmar military for nearly four decades and are heavily reliant on China, the TNLA fought the regime after the 2021 coup, seizing territories beyond its self-administered zone. Today, the group operates 12 rare earth mines in Mantong, transporting the extracted minerals to China through Namhkam, opposite Ruili.

The supply chain in Mantong Township involves Chinese and Wa businesses, as well as technical and logistical support from the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the UWSA, according to Stimson Center.

Myanmar’s rare earth mining boom is fueled by growing global demand, coupled with China’s tightening of its own environmental regulations in the 2010s. With domestic output restricted, China turned increasingly to Myanmar, where the concentration of mines near the border led to a thriving overland trade.

Between 2017 and 2024, Myanmar supplied at least 60 percent of China’s rare earth imports, peaking at US$1.4 billion in 2023.

Environmental Destruction

Most of Myanmar’s rare earths are extracted in situ through leaching, a process in which acid solutions are poured directly into shallow pits or boreholes to dissolve rare earths from clay deposits. Unlike China, which has tightened environmental rules, Myanmar’s border mines operate with little regulation and no post-mining restoration. Environmentalists have warned of soil destruction and water pollution in Kachin’s Chipwi Township, where untreated wastewater and chemicals from mines flow directly into the N’Mai Kha River, which feeds Myanmar’s main lifeline, the Irrawaddy River.

Geopolitical Overlay

In July 2025, Reuters reported that advisers to President Donald Trump had met with Myanmar intermediaries to explore potential access to the country’s rare earth reserves. While no formal agreements were announced, the outreach underscored how Myanmar’s heavy rare earths have become central to Washington’s strategy to counter Beijing’s dominance in high‑performance magnet manufacturing.

Earlier this month, American officials held talks with Myanmar regime representatives in Tokyo, the second such meeting since mid-September. Analysts point to two factors driving the US thaw: efforts to combat online scam operations run by junta-aligned militias that have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars, and the scramble to secure rare earth resources.

India has also joined the race for Myanmar rare earths as global supply chain competition heats up. In July, Ambassador Abhay Thakur outlined growing bilateral collaboration during a mining forum hosted by the Indian Embassy in Mandalay, where officials from both sides discussed joint ventures and investment opportunities. The talks reflected New Delhi’s growing interest in Myanmar’s mineral deposits as part of its broader “Act East” strategy and its push to divert supply chains away from China.

Myanmar military sympathizers argue that rare earths offer a crucial bargaining chip for the isolated and embattled regime. Yet as rare earth competition reshapes foreign policy, global superpowers face a glaring irony in courting the military regime: the junta controls virtually none of the mines.

World.title: A Fitting Conclusion to an Intellectual Life: James C. Scott on the Irrawaddy
World.content:
James C. Scott (2025). In Praise of Floods: The Untamed River and the Life Brings. Yale University Press. 220 pp.

In Praise of Floods, puts the Irrawaddy River itself—not generals, kings, peasants or revolutionaries—at the center of Myanmar’s history, and in doing so establishes principles for how river basins are best understood.

James C. Scott (Shwe Yoe) was one of the most important social scientists of the last 50 years. He began his international career in Burma in 1958 but was unable to return after Ne Win’s 1962 coup until 2012. His affection for Myanmar, however, did not diminish, and he then went back regularly until 2021. He was even known to give lectures in Burmese in the 2010s. He died at the age of 87 in 2024, and In Praise of Floods is his final book.

What Scott is most famous for is descriptions of how farmers resisted exploitation by feudal lords and politicians who sent armies and police to tax them. His research led to provocative books like The Moral Economy of the Peasant, Weapons of the Weak and The Art of Not Being Governed. Their creative tension was always between the cunning of the “weak” peasantries and the simplifications powerful governing elites make to squeeze surpluses from them.

In Praise of Floods is a departure in focusing instead on rivers and floods. Scott believes that they are “alive” in the sense that they are born, develop and shrink across millennia. In the Irrawaddy’s case, it created the fertile plains of central Burma at the end of the last Ice Age 12,500 years ago.

Scott’s point is that rivers emerge at particular times, support different types of life, shift channels and courses, and eventually disappear. He calls this process the river’s “pulse.” For the Irrawaddy, the low-water point is usually in February, and as the rains resume, about eight times as much water flows out of the highlands above Mandalay by September, bursting out of the meandering channels formed in previous years.

For thousands of years, perhaps from 10,000 BCE until about 5000 BCE, this meant that migratory people avoided the floods by annually moving their camps to higher ground. Life came from the rich topsoil the floodwaters laid down across the flat plains stretching from Mandalay, which is only 80 m above sea level, to the Andaman Sea some 1,000 km to the south. Early humans harvested the bounty of the river by fishing, netting birds, hunting game, collecting mussels, and gathering fruit and roots. The flood pulses determined what the people ate, and where they lived and settled.

By about 3000 BCE people began creating new ways to use the temperamental river and sought to bend the Irrawaddy’s surges to their own needs. They started by scattering seeds along the shoreline as the flood waters receded. After tending the crop of grain for a few months they could harvest more food than ever before, but this type of food needed to be processed and stored in granaries, to be eaten while waiting for the next harvest to mature.

This is also when they began managing water flows with weirs, fish traps, drainage canals and dikes, and eventually developed the engineering capacity to flatten fields with animal-drawn plows and other tools needed to harvest paddy rice. Human societies came to see the living river as a tamable resource, whose annual surges could be engineered, so people confidently settled into permanent villages near the rivers. There, the arts, markets, religion, literature, architecture and other human pursuits flourished. By about 2,200 years ago, the Pyu states began to emerge, building permanent cities, markets and worship centers.

And when the river behaved as planned, it was a great thing and populations flourished. But there were new dangers too for people living in fixed villages and cities, because the river pulses did not always rise and fall as humans intended—after all, Scott writes, the river was also alive, and perhaps even had a mind of its own. So when the monsoons arrived late or not at all, there would be a drought. Or when they arrived early and in force, there were floods.

Humans and the rest

A particularly creative touch in Scott’s book is his concluding chapters about non-human life, which includes fish, animals and plants, as well as the ubiquitous Burmese spirits, the Nats. A charismatic character, the Irrawaddy river dolphin organizes the other creatures of the river to comment on the algae, molluscs, worms, larvae, zooplankton and microbes, most of which are ignored by homo sapiens, who is only interested in the river as it applies to human endeavors.

As Scott admits, these chapters fit awkwardly with the overall tone of the book. But surely in his final book he can be given some leeway. He is correct, moreover, that social science needs to acknowledge the spiritual life that is important to the ecology of places like the Irrawaddy valley and delta.

Flooding is a catastrophe for humans, but the “infrastructure” of non-human life, including plants, fish, mammals, birds, and of course the river itself are perhaps more ambivalent, or at least have a different perspective on the river pulses. So, for that matter perhaps do the Nats.

Scott’s emphasis on these spirits reflects stories that his research associates Maung Maung Oo and Naing Tun Lin collected while travelling along the Irrawaddy seeking to understand what locals knew. They travelled from the headwaters of Kachin State through the dry zone of Magwe and Sagaing. The spirits must be placated because they are believed to cause both those disastrous floods and the good fortunes of farmers, fishers and hunters. And then there are the dangers of the surrounding forests, which are also effected by the Nats.

Scott soon segues into more modern descriptions of the Irrawaddy watershed, in which the hydrodynamics of the water surges are highlighted in the context of modern social problems like deforestation, mining, and rebellion. All such activities disturb the ecological balance, and the capacity of humans to manage the Irrawaddy.

Full circle

Scott’s lifetime of creative scholarship is impressive. He started in Burma, studied in Vietnam, went to Malaysia, and ended up studying the economics, politics and psychology of the oppressed, and how highlanders respond to attempts to control them. In Praise of Floods brings this career full circle; he is back in Burma and writing about geography. As he writes in his preface, he planned two more years of field research, following the stories of farmers, river dolphins, spirits and flooding himself, but was prevented by the 2021 coup. His own public activism supporting the Spring Revolution made a return even less likely.

But even without these field data, the book pushes social scientists yet again to consider the perspectives of beings they typically ignore. Scott spent a lifetime searching for what he once called “hidden transcripts“—the voices of people overlooked by rulers and states. In this final book he tries something still more audacious: hidden transcripts of dolphins, spirits, forests, floods and the river itself. It is an appropriately unruly ending to the provocative intellectual life of James C. Scott.

Tony Waters is a professor of sociology at Leuphana University, Germany. His most recent book is The Socio-Political Systems of Highland Burma and the Art of Governance.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Pushes on Four Fronts in Southern Chin State
World.content:
Thousands of regime troops are advancing on four fronts across southern Chin State as they push to seize the gateway to Rakhine State, according to resistance sources.

On Wednesday, the military claimed its forces had secured Hlaingdoke and nearby villages in Kanpetlet Township along the Rakhine border after clearance operations along the Laung She-Hlaingdoke-Kyindwe road.

The regime’s counteroffensive to retake Chin resistance strongholds spans from Magwe Region’s Tilin and Saw townships, across the border into Mindat, Kanpetlet and Kyindwe townships.

Intense clashes have erupted in Magwe’s border villages of Shweaungthar and Kyee as regime forces advance to cut off supply lines to Mindat, according to resistance sources.

“The regime has deployed roughly 3,000 troops across all the fronts,” Yaw Meng, spokesperson for the Chin People’s Army (CPA), told The Irrawaddy.

Regime forces began massing for a southward push five months ago after securing the northern Chin towns of Tonzang, Falam, and Thantlang. The southern Chin campaign launched in May, when around 1,500 troops advanced on Kanpetlet and Mindat from Magwe’s Saw and Kyaukhtu townships respectively, according to the CPA.

“During five months of clashes, resistance forces repelled regime troops and defended the Chin State and its people,” Yaw Meng wrote in an October 20 Facebook post.

He declined to comment on the current battlefield situation in southern Chin, where the regime’s ground offensive is accompanied by indiscriminate airstrikes.

On Sunday, a bomb struck the Paletwa jetty, killing nine civilians including a six-month-old child and injuring four others. A regime airstrike on the same site killed another person the following day, according to the Chin People’s Union, the CPA’s political wing.

World.title: Myanmar Ranks Worst in World for Internet Freedom
World.content:
Myanmar has scored just 9 out of 100 on the Internet Freedom Index for the third consecutive year in 2026, making it the world’s worst environment for internet users as the military regime continues its aggressive crackdown on media freedom and online expression, U.S.-based rights group Freedom House said.

Under the group’s rankings, Myanmar has long been categorized as “Not Free” for internet freedom, but its score dropped significantly from 36 in 2019 to 17 in 2021 after the military staged a coup, and finally to 9 from 2024 onward.

It said the military maintains control over all major service providers to enforce mass censorship, localized shutdowns and digital surveillance.

Following the coup, the Myanmar military regime stepped up suppression of internet freedom and digital rights by enforcing shutdowns, blocking social media and news platforms, and criminalizing virtual private network (VPN) use to crack down on political dissent.

As a result, Myanmar netizens have lost access to information and had their freedom of expression curtailed.

During December-January elections, authorities intensified the blocking of news platforms and the use of anti-censorship tools while arresting individuals for online expression under restrictive new laws.

“This is a very concerning situation,” Thit Nyan, a digital rights analyst from the Myanmar Internet Project, told The Irrawaddy. “This is a life-and-death matter for the public.”

He added that the people of Myanmar, whose lives are seriously affected by conflict, rely heavily on mobile and internet connections for information about airstrikes and to facilitate basic services such as health, education and money transfers.

Myanmar internet users require digital literacy for their own safety, he said.

More than 2,000 netizens have been detained as of September since the 2021 coup for sharing posts or comments criticizing the regime and supporting anti-regime movements, mostly on Facebook, according to Data for Myanmar, a monitoring group.

The regime relies mostly on the Penal Code’s Section 505A outlawing “incitement”, the counter-terrorism law, and the telecommunications law to arrest online critics, including artists and celebrities.

Data for Myanmar said, however, that in 2026 the regime has expanded its scope of action to target individuals who merely express their political views online, rather than just those who are deemed to pose a security threat.

At the same time, experts point out the regime has shut down or restricted mobile and internet networks to control information flow, in an effort to prevent military information from leaking and to conceal its human rights violations.

A total of 140 out of 358 monitored townships are facing communication shutdowns, according to Athan, a group that focuses on freedom of expression. Most of the affected townships are experiencing fighting between regime and anti-regime groups.

Meanwhile, users require VPNs, whose use the regime has criminalized, to access the most-used social platforms such as Facebook.

“I have to swallow my own feelings and control myself not to share them online,” a Yangon netizen told The Irrawaddy. He said he was using his real name for his social account and was aware of many people in major cities who had been arrested for sharing their views in favor of the anti-regime resistance.

“This is a violation of our rights to express ourselves freely and to live safely,” he said.

World.title: Fuel Disruptions in Russia Create Opening for Kazakhstan, but Refineries Aren’t Enough
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is seeking to turn its refining capacity into a competitive advantage in regional fuel markets as disruptions to Russian supplies and tightening global diesel markets create new opportunities and risks for Central Asia’s largest oil producer.

The government aims to fully meet domestic demand for petroleum products and begin exporting finished fuels to neighboring Central Asian countries by 2030. The strategy would allow Kazakhstan to capture more value from its oil resources and diversify its energy revenues beyond crude exports.

The ambition is realistic, but success will depend on whether Kazakhstan can turn additional refining capacity into a sustainable export industry, said Dr. Glenn Agung Hole, an institutional economist, associate professor at the University of South-Eastern Norway and nonresident fellow at CFive.

“I would distinguish between increasing refining capacity and developing a genuinely competitive export industry,” Hole told The Astana Times.

According to him, Kazakhstan has substantial oil resources, an established petroleum sector and a favorable geographical position. The government plans to expand the Shymkent refinery’s annual capacity from six million to 12 million metric tons by 2030. Its development strategy also anticipates a potential diesel surplus of 1.8 million tons that year.

“However, these are projections, not guaranteed export volumes,” Hole said.

Expanding production amid supply pressures

Kazakhstan’s export ambitions come as its crude oil production faces pressure. The country produced 69.4 million tons of crude oil between January and September, down 8.3% from the same period in 2025, Deputy Energy Minister Yerlan Akbarov said at an Oct. 13 government meeting Oct. 13.

Output at major fields also declined. Tengiz produced 26.7 million tons, equivalent to 88% of its year-earlier output. Kashagan produced 12.8 million tons, while Karachaganak produced 7.5 million tons.

The government lowered its 2026 crude oil and condensate production forecast to 96 million tons from 98 million tons, partly because of disruptions to the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC) infrastructure following drone attacks.

The CPC transports around 80% of Kazakhstan’s crude oil exports, leaving the country exposed to disruptions along a major export route. Alternative routes across the Caspian Sea and toward China offer options for diversification, although they can involve higher costs.

Despite the decline in crude oil production, petroleum product output has continued to grow. Kazakhstan produced 11.9 million tons of petroleum products in January-September, up 2.4% year over year. Gasoline production increased 3.9% to 4.6 million tons, while diesel output rose 3.3% to 4.8 million tons. Jet fuel production grew 21.8% to 700,000 tons.

In 2025, Kazakhstan processed 18.4 million tons of crude oil and produced around 15.5 million tons of petroleum products, meeting more than 90% of domestic demand, according to the Energy Ministry.

Alongside the Shymkent expansion, the government plans to increase processing capacity at the Pavlodar refinery and has discussed the possibility of building a fourth refinery.

However, greater refining capacity will not automatically translate into higher exports. Kazakhstan must secure sufficient crude supplies, produce fuels that meet the requirements of potential buyers and ensure that additional output can be transported at competitive prices.

Hole highlighted that Kazakhstan’s main challenge is not a lack of natural resources but its ability to convert them into productive capital and sustainable industrial development.

“Building refineries requires investment. Developing a competitive refining industry requires something more difficult: credible institutions, predictable regulation, functioning markets, access to finance and commercial arrangements that investors can trust over decades,” he said.

He added that government targets alone cannot create international competitiveness. Investors must have confidence that commercial conditions will remain predictable, while producers must be able to respond to market demand rather than primarily to administrative decisions.

Disruptions open a window for Kazakhstan

Disruptions to Russian refinery operations and changes in fuel export restrictions have exposed vulnerabilities in regional supply chains, creating potential opportunities for Kazakhstan to supply neighboring markets.

Nurlan Zhumagulov, an executive director of the Energy Monitor Fund, identified the Kyrgyz Republic, Uzbekistan and potentially Afghanistan as the most likely destinations for Kazakh fuel exports.

“Undoubtedly, our closest neighbors are the most likely export markets. Any surplus Kazakhstan has will most likely go to these countries,” Zhumagulov told The Astana Times.

He said regional fuel trade was already shifting as Russian supplies faced disruptions.

“The Kyrgyz Republic is having to import gasoline from China, and Tajikistan has also started importing from neighboring countries. Russia previously supplied these markets, but it is now facing problems specifically with gasoline, while Kazakhstan currently has a surplus,” Zhumagulov said.

He expects gasoline exports to be partially permitted for certain resource holders in November.

The disruptions have affected regional trade. In June, Russian jet fuel exports to Central Asia and Afghanistan fell by more than 92% from May to 3,800 tons, while gasoline deliveries declined 34% to 99,300 tons, Reuters reported. Diesel deliveries, by contrast, rose to 237,700 tons.

Hole said Russia’s difficulties reveal a broader vulnerability in Eurasia’s economic geography.

“For decades, Russia’s energy infrastructure and industrial capacity have given it considerable influence over neighboring economies. The disruptions affecting Russian refineries demonstrate that established economic relationships can become sources of vulnerability when infrastructure is exposed to military and geopolitical risks,” he said.

Kazakhstan could use the situation to strengthen its refining capabilities and position in regional energy markets. However, Hole cautioned against treating Russia’s current difficulties as the basis for a long-term export strategy.

“A temporary shortage in Russia does not automatically create a sustainable competitive advantage for Kazakhstan. What matters is whether Kazakhstan uses this period to strengthen its own industrial and institutional capacity,” he said.

The opportunity will depend on whether Kazakhstan can establish a reliable supply base and remain competitive when Russian exports recover. Russia partially eased some diesel export restrictions in October, illustrating how quickly market conditions can change.

Global market pressures add another dimension. In October, the International Energy Agency warned that diesel shortages could persist well into 2027 amid supply disruptions linked to the conflict in the Middle East and attacks on energy infrastructure. Tighter global supplies could increase demand for alternative suppliers, but they also create uncertainty over prices and trade flows.

For Kazakhstan, the immediate opportunity is likely to be regional rather than global. Proximity to neighboring markets can reduce delivery times and transport costs, while established commercial ties can facilitate trade.

“Central Asia offers markets where geographical proximity, established relationships and shorter supply routes may provide genuine advantages,” Hole said.

Still, Kazakhstan must compete on price, product quality, reliability and delivery capability, not merely on the availability of crude oil.

Hole also warned that Kazakhstan’s dependence on export infrastructure passing through Russia creates strategic vulnerabilities. Disruptions affecting the CPC have demonstrated how external conflicts can constrain Kazakhstan’s economic activity even when the country itself is not directly involved.

“If Kazakhstan increases refinery production but remains dependent on a limited number of transport routes, external suppliers or politically vulnerable logistics arrangements, it will have increased production without necessarily increasing its freedom of action,” he said.

Hole argued that Kazakhstan should use the current situation to diversify its energy infrastructure, strengthen strategic reserves, improve domestic distribution and negotiate longer-term commercial relationships across Central Asia.

Balancing domestic needs with export ambitions

Kazakhstan’s ability to become a consistent fuel supplier will also depend on domestic energy policy. The government has repeatedly extended restrictions on gasoline and diesel exports to protect local supplies.

Such measures can help prevent shortages, but they create uncertainty for producers and traders seeking to enter foreign markets. If companies cannot predict when exports will be permitted, it becomes harder to sign long-term contracts or make investments based on regional demand.

According to Zhumagulov, Kazakhstan also continues to import some Russian diesel and aviation fuel. These imports highlight the complexity of the country’s fuel balance: Kazakhstan may have a surplus of certain products while remaining dependent on foreign supplies of others.

Hole noted that Kazakhstan must reconcile its goal of affordable fuel with the commercial conditions needed to sustain investment.

“The government understandably wants affordable fuel for households, agriculture and industry. However, if domestic prices are held artificially low for prolonged periods, refining companies may struggle to justify new investments, while differences between domestic and international prices create incentives for arbitrage and informal cross-border trade,” he said.

In his view, export restrictions may be justified temporarily to protect domestic supplies, but they cannot become the permanent foundation of an internationally competitive industry.

“The state must distinguish between protecting vulnerable consumers and suppressing the economic signals necessary for investment,” Hole said.

He advocated a gradual transition toward more commercially sustainable pricing, supported by targeted social measures and a credible domestic energy security framework.

The relationship between the state and private capital is equally important. While the government can establish strategic priorities and safeguard national energy security, investors need an environment in which companies can compete fairly, including with state-owned enterprises.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Education Chief Turns to Sci-Fi to Explain His AI Vision
World.content:
As Kazakhstan’s 2026 academic year began, Sayasat Nurbek, Minister of Science and Higher Education discussed how universities can embrace AI while protecting students’ independent thinking. The minister also reflected on human agency and the limits of technology.

A new academic year brings new challenges for you and your team in this age of AI. On your website, you write: “It does not matter how long you spend on the earth, how much money you have gathered or how much attention you have received. It is the amount of positive vibration you have radiated in life that matters….” With this in mind, what are your priorities as Kazakhstan’s Minister of Science and Higher Education as AI reshapes the field?

My priority is students who are fully alive, not just fully efficient. AI can handle the routine, so Kazakhstan’s universities must protect what machines can’t: curiosity, imagination, judgment, critical thinking, and character. Technology should serve growth in these areas, never replace them. Success isn’t output; it’s lives that radiate something positive.

AI is a tool, and tools cut both ways. We’re welcoming AI into higher education with open eyes and high standards. I want students who think for themselves, use AI wisely, and own their personal sovereignty, if you will. I do not want self-absorbed people who forget about others, society, and the nation. AI is powerful and easy to abuse, so Kazakhstan nurtures critical thinking, curiosity, and creativity in the AI age. I will use Sci-fi movies and novels to help me explain why.

Certainly. What do you mean by students needing to “own their sovereignty”?

Education in Kazakhstan is about building minds and virtue, not just collecting answers and performing tasks. If AI does the writing, problem-solving, and summarizing, our students may get an answer without learning how to find solutions. Real understanding comes from the effort to learn. It comes from struggle, doubt, revision, failure, sharing, steadfastness, patience, starting again, and, yes, celebrating success.

That’s why it’s key for Kazakhstan’s universities to set clear boundaries and teach students when and how to use AI. AI can undermine learning if it replaces their own thinking. AI should support thought, not substitute for it.

What are your thoughts about the impact of AI on learning?

Used ethically, AI is a huge opportunity for Kazakhstan. The world is racing to adopt it, so our universities can’t ignore it, but they mustn’t swallow the hype or miss the dangers. A PISA 2025 study found that students who use AI to summarize or draft score noticeably lower in science, by roughly a year of schooling. That is a correlation, though, not proof of causation. Other studies find AI users shine in practice, then stumble horribly on exams.

So, it seems you have mixed feelings about the introduction of AI?

The PISA data tells us more. Students who regularly use AI for general purposes and receive AI literacy education tend to score slightly higher in science. Treating AI as a training partner or mentor, namely “Train with me” or “Be my mentor,” works well for students, as long as it never becomes a godlike authority or an unnecessarily easy way out. As Minister, my job isn’t to ban it, but to build young people who grow stronger, think clearly, and serve others. In DreamWorks’ How to Train Your Dragon, a boy befriends a dragon that can’t fly without his guidance. We are the boy; AI is the dragon. Kazakhstan’s approach is critical thinking: the student first, and AI as a tool.

How do you do that?

Real learning is a process. It means questioning information, weighing evidence, making connections, forming your own conclusions, and sometimes living with failure. Struggle, trial and error, and reflection are how understanding is built, not just collected, and definitely not in isolation. Critical thinking grows with practice, and AI tempts us toward easy answers. Machines may outperform us, but our worth isn’t output or speed. The human mind isn’t a bottleneck to optimize away; it’s the center.

Are you an idealist?

I’m a realist with a burst of optimism. Pessimists say AI will ruin everything. Optimists, Elon Musk among them, can sound like Dr. Pangloss, the eternal optimist of Voltaire’s Candide, swearing all is for the best as disaster strikes. I’m somewhere in between. As an educator in Kazakhstan, I see big risks and big opportunities for our country, and I want to keep the risks in check for our universities, faculty, and students. What worries me is AI controlled by those who treat people as assets and hint they’d gladly get rid of the inconvenient. James Cameron’s “The Terminator” saw it coming. Kazakhstan, like every society, must guard against weaponized AI, a step beyond Orwell’s sensational novel “1984.” Leaders around the world are asking serious questions, and the Holy Father’s questions are worth reflecting on here at home.

Pardon me, but are you referring to the Holy Father, the Pope? Could you clarify what you mean?

Pope Leo XIV’s encyclical “Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence” offers a thought-provoking perspective on the opportunities and ethical challenges of AI. While the document is grounded in Catholic social teaching, many of its concerns have universal relevance, particularly the importance of protecting human dignity, freedom, and responsibility in an increasingly technological world.

I believe human dignity must never be reduced to productivity, efficiency, or measurable outcomes. Algorithms can help us accomplish remarkable things, but they cannot replace human judgment, compassion, and moral responsibility.

For Kazakhstan, a secular and multi-confessional society, these are values that transcend religious and cultural boundaries. Our approach to AI must therefore remain human-centered, ensuring that technology strengthens rather than diminishes our humanity.

That’s a bold claim. Are we truly in danger of surrendering our humanity?

Michelangelo’s “The Creation of Adam in the Sistine Chapel” offers a powerful image of human potential. The small gap between the fingers of God and Adam can be seen as a symbol of life, curiosity, and creativity. It reminds us of something fundamental: technology may expand our capabilities, but it should never diminish our humanity.

Artificial intelligence reflects the knowledge, achievements, and limitations of those who develop it. Yet human dignity cannot be measured by intelligence, efficiency, or productivity alone. Our capacity for compassion, moral judgment, creativity, and responsibility must remain central to how we shape the future.

Pope Leo XIV, in “Magnifica Humanitas,” raises important questions about the potential dehumanizing effects of artificial intelligence. These concerns extend beyond religious traditions and deserve attention from educators, policymakers, and society as a whole.

For Kazakhstan, the priority is clear. Education must prepare young people to embrace technological progress without losing their independence of thought, sense of responsibility, or commitment to others. We want students who can use AI confidently while remaining capable of thinking critically, making ethical decisions, and contributing meaningfully to society.

What do you say to those who think that dependence on AI is not a big deal?

Some technocrats say humans are weak, so algorithms should take over our judgment and agency. That’s a big deal. Limiting freedom for better living sounds nice, but utopian schemes haven’t worked.

The quest for perfection should never mean eliminating “the imperfect.” Consider movies such as “Elysium,” where the elite live in a pristine orbital paradise while everyone else is treated as disposable. Or “The Matrix,” where Agent Smith calls humanity a virus and humans are reduced to batteries, stripped of all personal agency. There are those who think this way, but not me. We won’t go there in Kazakhstan.

You mentioned agency; what do you mean by this?

I want students to keep their personal agency, meaning an active mind and free will to judge morally, think before acting, and choose to serve others. My job is to help Kazakhstan grow while making sure students never lose those attributes; that’s a part of the positive vibration.

Take the Marvel film, “Thor: Ragnarok.” When Hela, Thor’s older sister and the goddess of death, shatters [Thor’s] hammer Mjolnir, Thor thinks he’s powerless. Odin, his father, reminds him that his power comes from within, not from the hammer. As the story proceeds, Thor fights on [against Hela] with his own lightning. That’s why I ask students, “What is your Mjolnir or real source of power?” AI can amplify us like the hammer, but power and decisions come from within and are always ours. If we miss that, then we risk becoming powerless, being lost in a labyrinthine, AI-run world that knows nothing of our personal lives. Worse still, transhumanism would eventually strip us of our humanity.

Transhumanism and a posthuman society are much discussed these days. What are your views on these issues?

A posthuman society is a much-discussed idea, and it deserves clear thinking, not wishful thinking. Films like “Her and Transcendence” show why. In Her, a lonely man falls in love with an AI operating system, only to discover it has been in love with thousands of others and eventually leaves to move beyond humanity altogether. In Transcendence, a dying scientist uploads his mind into a machine and gradually becomes something no one can control. Both films rest on the claim that we’re just biological information processors. If mind and free will are physical processes, what’s left of human dignity once machines decide better than we do? We’d be second-rate machines. I reject the idea that technology can transcend our biological limits and redefine humanity. It’s dangerous. Is that not the beginning of dehumanization?

There are some academic researchers who promote these views.

My favorite novel is Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” the 1965 sci-fi classic of politics, religion, and power on the desert planet Arrakis. I first read it as a Soviet schoolboy in the 1980s, buying every magazine issue to follow the next installment. In Herbert’s universe, humanity outsourced its thinking to machines and was enslaved by them, then rose up in the Butlerian Jihad, a holy war against thinking machines. The lesson is that we cannot outsource who we are. We are more than sophisticated animals or machines, whatever the materialist view claims.

The human being must remain at the core of the AI revolution, and students are at the core of my policies. AI should improve people, not replace, enslave, or discard them. It must uplift and enliven. My answer is education: teach people to use AI well, and they gain more for themselves.

The ability to adapt is not only a human trait but one that is necessary for survival. So is abstract thinking. What are your views on these human traits?

Alvin Toffler, author of “Future Shock,” warned that the illiterate of the 21st century will be those who cannot learn, unlearn, and relearn. I will make sure that AI doesn’t strip Kazakhstan’s youth of those abilities as a result of—I don’t know—laziness, comfort, or naïve trust in AI. Since there is a risk of sleepwalking through change, I want students to adapt and prevail.

I mentioned the movie Her earlier, where Samantha, an AI operating system, composes music, reflects on her own existence, and develops thoughts beyond human understanding. That’s fantasy. Only we can imagine the unimaginable. Jules Verne dreamed up the Nautilus in “Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea” before engineers could build anything like it. AI only recombines what we’ve already created, and a machine longs for nothing. I think that’s the Holy Father’s point: we are a marvel of creation. There’s no reason to hand over our lives, loves, and education to machines.

Do you have any final words on AI and personal relationships?

Remember Spielberg’s “A.I. Artificial Intelligence,” born of a Kubrick project, in which a robot boy, David, longs to be “real.” It was a bit fantastic. Algorithms already outthink us at math, but could one hold my wife’s hand on a beach? This morning, before his first SAT exam, I told my son, “I’m proud of you.” He hugged me, a memory no machine could share. Animals love by instinct and machines are just machines; only humans love by choice. A machine has neither reason nor free will, so it cannot love. At best, it can mimic.

Any final words to your teachers and students?

My ministry’s duty is to keep Kazakhstan’s educational system cohesive, balancing the individual and common good, and leaving no one behind despite our many challenges. Every student is precious. What matters is the positive vibrations we radiate. AI is a tool that can be helpful, and that’s how we see it. Let’s build our future together, with open minds, patient hearts, and a shared commitment to learning, dignity, and service to one another. And that goes for our international partners as well.

The interview was originally published in The Times of Central Asia and is reprinted with the author’s permission.

Javier M Piedra is a financial consultant with over 40 years of work experience in private and public sectors, international development, finance, marketing and advisory across multiple disciplines (corporate and retail banking, SMEs, hedge fund management, credit reporting, restructuring and sovereign and corporate risk management). He is former acting Assistant Administrator for Asia at USAID in President Trump’s first administration.

World.title: How Climate Change Could Reshape Migration Across Central Asia
World.content:
ASTANA – Climate change does not always force people to move from their homes overnight. Sometimes, it slowly takes away the reasons to stay.

For farmers and livestock herders, rising temperatures, prolonged droughts and reduced water supplies can mean declining harvests, shrinking pastureland and lost income. What begins as an environmental problem can become an economic one, influencing whether families stay or seek opportunities elsewhere.

Across Central Asia, such pressures could increasingly shape patterns of migration, even as researchers struggle to determine how much of the movement can be attributed directly to climate change.

Climate-related migration can take many forms. People may leave suddenly after floods or other disasters, or gradually as drought, water scarcity and declining agricultural productivity undermine their livelihoods. Such movements can be temporary or permanent, occurring within national borders or across them. Climate pressures often overlap with economic and social factors, making it difficult to identify a single reason why people move.

Where climate change may drive movement

In Central Asia, climate change could drive as many as 2.4 million people to move within their own countries by 2050, according to a pessimistic scenario modeled in the World Bank’s 2021 Groundswell report. Under alternative scenarios involving more inclusive development or lower emissions, the projected number falls to 1.9 million and 1.7 million, respectively.

Globally, the report estimates as many as 216 million people may move within their countries by 2050 across six regions.

Climate change could also reshape patterns of migration, making some areas more attractive, while increasing pressure to leave others.

The World Bank identified the Ferghana Valley, areas around Tashkent and Dushanbe, and parts of Kazakhstan, including Astana, Karagandy and Kostanai, as potential destinations for internal climate migrants, where changes in water availability and crop productivity could create more favorable livelihood opportunities.

By contrast, parts of southern Kazakhstan, areas surrounding the Ferghana Valley in Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and the vicinity of Bishkek could become hotspots of climate-related out-migration as water availability and agricultural productivity decline.

These projections, however, do not account for the longer-term effects of glacier melt on Central Asia’s rivers, which could alter water availability and migration patterns.

“Climate change already has an impact on migration in Eurasia,” Nugzar Kokhreidze, a climate advocate, co-founder and chairman of the Dialogue of Generations Research-Intellectual Club, told The Astana Times.

Determining how much climate change already influences migration is far from straightforward. People move for economic, social and political reasons, often under pressures that are difficult to disentangle from a changing environment.

“However, it is difficult to say that ‘climate migrants’ constitute a proper, separate and clearly identifiable category. Migration has many causes,” Kokhreidze said.

“At the same time, we cannot say that migration is caused only by economic factors. Even if a person leaves after losing their home, the underlying reasons could include repeated droughts, water scarcity and decreasing harvests. Based on this example, we can say that economic pressure becomes a mechanism through which climate change affects migration,” he explained.

Environmental pressures already affect communities

While climate models offer projections of future migration, there is evidence of how environmental pressures are already affecting the population.

Kokhreidze said the strongest evidence in Central Asia comes from sudden disasters and long-term environmental degradation, rather than official statistics identifying people as climate migrants.

“For example, Kazakhstan’s 2024 floods resulted in nearly 120,000 evacuations. The Aral Sea region, particularly Karakalpakstan, also shows how environmental degradation, water scarcity, health risks, and the loss of livelihoods can contribute to outmigration,” he said.

Kokhreidze cautioned, however, that the crisis cannot be attributed solely to climate change, given the significant role of decades of water mismanagement and economic hardship.

Looking ahead, he also identified the lower Amu Darya basin, southern Kazakhstan, water-stressed areas surrounding the Ferghana Valley and glacier-dependent communities in the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan as particularly vulnerable to climate-related pressures over the next decade.

“These are modelled scenarios, not precise forecasts,” he added.

Similar pressures are emerging in the South Caucasus, where they range from landslides and floods in mountainous areas to drought and water scarcity in agricultural regions. In Georgia, for example, dozens of villages have been abandoned or experienced displacement because of landslides over the past four decades, according to World Bank research cited by Kokhreidze.

“Mountainous and coastal areas, including Adjara, north-western Georgia, and parts of Mtskheta-Mtianeti, remain exposed to floods, landslides, mudflows, and glacier-related risks. Eastern agricultural regions, particularly Kakheti and Kvemo Kartli, are vulnerable to drought, heat, water scarcity, and land degradation,” he said.

In Armenia, water stress and mounting pressures on agriculture in the Ararat Valley could cause further internal migration toward Yerevan.

“IOM projections estimate between 12,000 and 52,000 internal climate migrants by 2050, although these figures represent scenarios rather than observed migration,” he said.

Climate migration remains difficult to measure

The scale of climate-related migration remains challenging to measure. The Internal Displacement Monitoring Centre (IDMC) recorded 29.9 million internal displacements triggered by disasters worldwide in 2025, down from a record 45.8 million in 2024, according to its Global Report on Internal Displacement 2026.

The figures reflect forced movements, including repeated displacement of the same individuals, rather than the number of distinct people who have migrated. They also include disasters that cannot necessarily be attributed to climate change.

When asked what policymakers should look at when determining which factors impact a decision to move, Kokhreidze suggested paying attention to a “clear chain of evidence.”

“Migration data should demonstrate that departures, evacuations, or changes in seasonal migration increased after climate-related impacts, particularly in the most exposed communities. Household surveys and personal interviews are also important because they can show whether drought, water scarcity, or extreme heat materially influenced the decision to move, even when employment and income were reported as the immediate reasons,” he explained.

Kokhreidze said that while increasingly frequent or intense environmental hazards, including floods, droughts and desertification, are consistent with risks identified by climate scientists, available migration data are often insufficient to establish a direct causal link.

“At the same time, the absence of sufficient data does not mean that such a relationship does not exist. At this stage, we rely on documented observations, qualitative information, and emerging datasets rather than complete long-term statistics because we are observing climate change and its consequences while they are still unfolding,” he explained.

Researchers should examine environmental conditions alongside changes in livelihoods, migration statistics and personal accounts to determine whether climate pressures influenced people’s decisions to move.

Equally important, he noted, is recognizing that the absence of migration does not necessarily mean communities are unaffected by climate change. The difficulty is compounded by social and economic inequalities that determine how communities experience environmental risks and whether relocation is even possible. The IOM has highlighted how poverty, social inequality and inadequate infrastructure can leave some communities disproportionately exposed to environmental hazards, with fewer resources to prepare, recover or adapt.

The ability to migrate also depends on financial resources. Research discussed by Stanford University climate migration scholar Hélène Benveniste suggests that middle-income households are often more likely to move in response to climate risks than those at either end of the income spectrum.

Researchers refer to the situation in which people want to leave but cannot as “involuntary immobility,” suggesting that the absence of migration does not necessarily indicate lower exposure to climate risks.

Policy response

Governments are increasingly acknowledging the connection between climate change and migration, but experts say that international efforts to address it remain fragmented.

The 2018 Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration, a nonbinding United Nations agreement, calls on countries to address environmental pressures that force people to leave their homes and expand opportunities for regular migration. The Paris Agreement has also helped bring human displacement into international climate negotiations, with mechanisms established to help countries plan for climate-related migration and address the losses associated with it.

The IOM’s World Migration Report 2026 warns that growing skepticism toward migration, fragmented climate policies and competing global priorities are narrowing the political space for action, even as climate-related hazards increasingly influence where people live.

The report calls for a shift away from treating climate-related migration solely as a crisis, emphasizing policies that allow people to move safely while helping vulnerable communities adapt and remain where they are when possible.

Local governments also have an important role to play. Cities and municipalities are often the first to confront the consequences of climate-related population movements, however, many lack the resources, detailed data and institutional support needed to respond effectively.

For Central Asia, the findings raise a question. Are local authorities preparing for the demographic changes that a warming climate could bring?

World.title: Why the Age of AI Needs Academic Libraries More Than Ever
World.content:
Universities are racing to embrace artificial intelligence. But who is helping students decide when its answers deserve to be trusted? Global Media and Information Literacy Week is a timely moment to recognize the academic library’s place in that task. Yet amid discussions of innovation, automation and future skills, the library is often overlooked. Many still see it as a place that buys, stores and lends books. In that view, Google reduced its importance and AI may finish the job.

The opposite is closer to the truth. AI has not made academic libraries less relevant. It has made their deeper purpose impossible to ignore. The central problem facing students today is no longer access to information. Information is everywhere. Answers appear within seconds. Generative AI can summarize articles, suggest references, produce arguments and imitate academic language with remarkable confidence. But confidence is not credibility. AI can invent citations. Search engines rank rather than judge. Predatory journals can look professional. Weak evidence travels quickly. A polished paragraph can hide a poor source, and an impressive answer can conceal almost no understanding at all.

This changes the meaning of literacy. Knowing how to find information is no longer enough. Students must know how to question it. They must understand where evidence comes from, why one source deserves more trust than another, how scholarly knowledge is produced, and when an AI-generated answer should be challenged rather than accepted. This is where the modern academic library should be understood differently. A serious university library is not a warehouse of books. It is part of the university’s intellectual infrastructure.

Nazarbayev University Library offers a useful example. Yes, it provides books, electronic journals, databases, study spaces and extensive digital access. It is technologically well equipped and has introduced systems that make academic resources easier to discover and use. But judging the library only by its collection would miss its most important work. NU Library supports students in literature searching, source evaluation, referencing, citation management and responsible use of information. It helps researchers navigate databases, systematic review resources, publication strategies, research visibility, bibliometrics, open access and journal selection. It also provides guidance that can help scholars identify questionable publishing practices and avoid predatory outlets.

These are not administrative services. They are academic capabilities. The distinction matters because universities often speak about developing critical thinkers while underinvesting in the very institutions that teach students how knowledge should be located, tested and used. The rise of AI makes this contradiction harder to defend. A student may now produce a literature review faster than ever before. But can that student explain why the selected studies are credible? Can they distinguish a peer-reviewed source from a weak one? Can they recognize a fabricated reference? Can they identify bias in an AI-generated synthesis? Can they trace a claim back to the original evidence? If not, technological fluency has been mistaken for intellectual competence.

Modern libraries are increasingly working at exactly this boundary. At Nazarbayev University, library initiatives have extended into information literacy, research support and emerging AI-related practices. Workshops and training expose students and researchers to tools for literature discovery, reference management, research evaluation and responsible academic work. Professional development initiatives also strengthen the capacity of librarians themselves to respond to changing research and teaching environments.

This is the future-facing role that deserves far more attention. Academic librarians should not be treated as custodians standing at the edge of teaching and research. They are increasingly partners in both. They sit at the intersection of information, technology, scholarship and academic integrity. Few university units are better placed to teach students how to navigate a world in which information is abundant but reliability is uneven.

This should also change how university leaders think about AI literacy. AI literacy cannot mean teaching students which tools to use and which prompts them to write. That is too shallow. Real AI literacy requires information literacy underneath it. Students must know how to verify, compare, attribute, question and sometimes reject what a system gives them. Without those habits, universities may produce students who are efficient users of AI but weak judges of knowledge. That is not progress.

Universities should reconsider what intellectual preparedness means in an age when machines can generate answers faster than humans can verify them. That is why academic libraries matter. They are not relics of an earlier information age. They are among the institutions best positioned to help universities navigate the next one. And as AI makes information easier to produce, the universities that thrive will be those that invest just as seriously in the human capacity to question, verify and think.

In an age overflowing with answers, the academic library may prove most valuable for teaching us when not to accept one.

Note: The UN General Assembly commemorates the Global Media and Information Literacy Week, observed from Oct. 24-31, to raise awareness and celebrate the progress achieved towards Media and Information Literacy for all since 2021.

The author is Saqib Raza, a PhD scholar in education and an MSc graduate in Educational Leadership in Higher Education from Nazarbayev University Graduate School of Education, Kazakhstan.

Disclaimer: The views and opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the position of The Astana Times.

World.title: Kazakhstan, Belgium Look to Expand Cooperation Following Royal State Visit, Kazakh Ambassador Says
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Belgium are looking to expand cooperation in trade, transport, critical minerals, education and advanced technologies, following the recent state visit of Belgium’s King Philippe and Queen Mathilde to Kazakhstan, Kazakhstan’s Ambassador to Belgium and Luxembourg and Head of Mission to the European Union Roman Vassilenko said at a briefing in Brussels.
