Tel Aviv: Israelis have begun voting in an election widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s almost two decades in power, with the prospect of a return to war with Iran dominating the final days of the campaign. Voting began early on Tuesday in Israel (4pm AEDT) in the first national elections since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, a day that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil. A television campaign  on a bridge featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, and his main rival, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the election. AP Photo/Oded Balilty Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but the polls have shown a close result between the two blocs, and it may take time before clear results are known. Israeli media reports passed by the official military censor and published in the final days of the campaign have stated that Netanyahu pressured his military chief to provoke a confrontation with Iran ahead of the elections, suggesting high-level leaks from within the defence establishment. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz denied the reports.



US President Donald Trump told Fox News on the weekend he was deciding whether to “make a deal” with Iran or “finish it off”, adding: “It’s getting to be decision time.” Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict These voters could hold the key to Netanyahu’s demise. Why are they being shunned? Netanyahu posted an alarming AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv and spoke about using cryptocurrency to avoid international sanctions in the final days of the campaign. Some disunity broke out within the opposition bloc before polls closed over the question of whether anti-Netanyahu voters should vote for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party or spread their votes among the four parties in the bloc. Eisenkot has been pursuing a so-called “big party” strategy in recent days, designed to give him the upper-hand in post-election negotiations by scoring a lead over Netanyahu’s Likud in the final seat tally.



“The ‘big party’ campaign is a mistake,” Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats party, said. “It’s a dangerous lie designed to weaken us. I urge people not to fall for the ‘big party’ narrative.” What happens on election day? Benjamin Netanyahu took to social media to post an apocalyptic AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb being dropped in the middle of Tel Aviv. Voting in Israel is voluntary, not compulsory. Even so, turnout is usually high, reflecting the level of political engagement in society. In the last elections, 4.8 million of the country’s 6.8 million eligible voters showed up at the polls – a turnout rate of 71 per cent. Even more people are expected to vote this year, reflecting the heightened stakes. Unlike in Australia, where postal voting has become increasingly popular in recent elections, Israelis must vote in person on election day. (Only those serving their nation overseas, like diplomats and defence personnel, can vote in advance by mail.)



When will we know who won? It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear. The first strong indication of the results will come at 10pm (6am Wednesday AEDT), when Israeli TV channels begin airing exit polls. The official election results will then start coming in. A clear picture may emerge quickly, but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.



The final tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4. Why is it so complicated? Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be ​held every four years, but early elections have been frequent. Crucially, voters vote for party lists rather than individual candidates. The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25 per cent of the national vote to secure seats.



About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time. The key number to aim for is the 61 seats required to form a government, though leaders prefer a more substantial buffer to create a more durable coalition. It is possible to govern in minority, but such a government would be even more fragile. What happens after the results are published? After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.



That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘It is ours’: The far-right Israeli settlers who want to build homes in Gaza No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition ​of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts, and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers. If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present cabinet staying on as a caretaker government. Read more on Israel’s election:

World.title: One is the race that stops a nation. The other will make you an instant $30 million
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup One is the race that stops a nation. The other will make you an instant $30 million Danny Russell October 27, 2026 — 5:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Chris Waller has an uncanny way of putting things into perspective when it comes to summarising two of the biggest races of Melbourne Cup week. The winner of one, he says, will become a household name. James McDonald riding St Gotthard and Jye McNeil aboard Steel Will at Flemington trackwork on Tuesday morning. Getty Images The winner of the other will be worth a lot more money. The champion trainer was talking, of course, about a sprint and a staying test – the $2 million group 1 Coolmore Stud Stakes (over 1200 metres) for three-year-olds on Saturday, compared to the $10.2 million Melbourne Cup (3200m) three days later.



Waller has runners in both. Related Article Melbourne Cup First look at the Melbourne Cup form – we rate the top 24 horses “The horse that wins the Coolmore on Saturday is probably going to be the most lucrative or expensive horse at the end of the carnival,” Waller said on Tuesday. “So, a Melbourne Cup winner – everybody wants it. They become a household name. “But in terms of a stallion or a filly, it passes that value on to the siblings, and if you’re a stallion, you can cover mares, and obviously that turns into a very lucrative scenario as well.



“The winner of the Coolmore will be worth upwards of $30 million.” Waller speaking to the media at Flemington earlier this month. Getty Images Waller has long understood the value of winning Saturday’s stallion-making race – a 1200m dash down the Flemington Straight on Derby Day. He has snared six of the past 13 editions. On Saturday, he could make it seven in what is shaping as a family affair. The race’s third favourite, St Gotthard, to be ridden by James McDonald, is a full brother to Waller’s 2024 winner Switzerland – both are by super sire Snitzel out of mare Ms Bad Behaviour.



“He’s the younger sibling who is ready to make a name for himself,” the Sydney trainer said. Related Article Spring racing carnival Record-breaking trainer’s warning for punters on Melbourne Cup favourite Waller’s other runner, longshot Steel Will, shares the same mother as his 2020 winning filly September Run. Steel Will is by I Am Invincible, out of Pittsburgh Flyer, while September Run is by Exceed And Excel, and also out of Pittsburgh Flyer. “That’s probably something quite unique. Hopefully, they’ve got the genetics and can quinella the race,” Waller said of his two runners. There are heightened expectations that come with racing an expensive colt such as St Gotthard, which was bought for $2.7 million by world-renowned breeding and racing operation Coolmore at the Inglis Easter Yearling Sales in April last year. But Waller has been there before.



Chris Waller keeping a keen eye on his horses at Flemington. Getty Images “You learn not to worry about price tags and not to worry about the pressure of it,” Waller said. “I guess it’s like a footy coach – once you’ve been to a couple of grand finals, or been in the final season a few years in a row, it does help. “We’ve also got a great team that have been with me for a long time. The horses, they all get looked after the same, regardless of the price tags.” Waller might have dominated the Coolmore Stud Stakes in recent years, but the Melbourne Cup has been a different story.



A renowned trainer of sprinters and middle distance horses, his sole winner was Verry Elleegant in 2021. He is unlikely to add to that tally this year. “It wouldn’t be our strongest year,” he said. Asterix, part-owned by Kiwi cricket great Mark Greatbatch, is an outsider, while Soul Of Spain ran second in the Sydney Cup before an eighth in the Caulfield Cup. Perhaps his best chances are still to make the cut-off. Gai Waterhouse (right) with Francesca Cumani at the launch of the Melbourne Cup carnival on Monday. Wayne Taylor



Up-and-coming stayer Pinhole needs at least four horses to withdraw before next Tuesday to gain a start, while 2023 runner-up Soulcombe – owned by a group of premiership Tigers including Tom Lynch – needs to finish in the top three in Wednesday’s Bendigo Cup to pass the ballot clause. Hall-of-fame trainer Gai Waterhouse will also be sweating on the Bendigo Cup result – she needs The Euphrates to win to be assured a Melbourne Cup start. “He was off the scene for two years, so this is a big step for him,” she said. “Tomorrow is a vital race for him, and if he can run really well or win it, then we are in.” Waterhouse and her co-trainer Adrian Bott are guaranteed at least one Cup runner.



Vauban is lining up for his fourth start in the race that stops the nation, having previously finished 14th, 11th and sixth. They took over training the Irish import from Willie Mullins at the end of 2024. “I love this gelding, I really do,” Waterhouse said. “He’ll be going in with only one run under his belt, which is a bit unorthodox. But, you know, why not roll the dice a different way?” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Albanese confirms bolstered security for MPs after Haines attack
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Albanese confirms bolstered security for MPs after Haines attack Natassia Chrysanthos and Paul Sakkal Updated October 27, 2026 — 5:24pm ,first published 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Politicians will receive a security boost that could include a wider use of emergency alarms in their offices, as the government treats last week’s attack on independent Helen Haines as a turning point for MPs’ safety. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told the Labor caucus on Tuesday morning that the government would speed up an existing security review that had been due to report next year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen “Last week was a turning point, and people have been putting up with this growing threat environment for too long,” he told his MPs. “More can and should be done. I understand you want to feel safe when you’re in the community and have better security at your office and your home. There are a series of options you have raised including duress alarms, and we are looking at all of it.”



MPs of all stripes attended briefings with intelligence agencies following the attack on Haines. Many aired their ongoing frustrations about how long it took for their security requests to be actioned, and several MPs also made requests about duress alarms. Related Article Workplace culture ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud This masthead revealed last week that the government was examining a major round of security upgrades for MPs’ homes, as well as swifter upgrades for offices and more proactive threat assessments from the AFP. Albanese said the government had already taken steps recently to step up resourcing for politicians’ safety and the Australian Federal Police, but recognised more could be done. He has asked for the security review recommendations to be fast-tracked, and requested Special Minister of State Don Farrell, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke work together on delivering a “swift government response”.



“I know so many of you have experienced an increase in aggressive and threatening behaviour online and in person. There have been vile threats towards you and your family and damage to your electorate offices,” Albanese said. Related Article Haines attack The cardboard cockatoo, the empty seat and a parliament’s reckoning with rage “This is particularly acute for women members of the caucus, who often receive vile and misogynistic threats to their safety and increased hatred online, often of a violent and sexual nature. “I know how hard every single one of you works each day to ensure that we are accessible to our community and that people can speak to us... We need to do more to combat these threats.” Last week’s four-wheel-drive attack on the independent MP has exposed long-running tensions between federal parliamentarians and the authorities responsible for protecting them.



Elected officials claim security agencies are too reactive and need to modernise their communication with MPs to ensure politicians and their staff feel safe. But authorities have also expressed frustration with MPs who fail to follow protocol when flagging high-risk events or reporting incidents. Opposition leader Angus Taylor also addressed the security concerns of MPs in a joint party room meeting of Coalition MPs on Tuesday morning, saying it was important to “get that right”. On Monday evening independent senator Fatima Payman stunned a parliamentary hearing by asking whether Albanese was waiting for a Haines-style attack against her to provide her with comparable staffing levels to other senators. Payman refused to withdraw her comments unless provided additional staff. Payman has long petitioned the prime minister for additional staffing, and was one of four independent and crossbench MPs to tell this masthead their staff were suffering under a deluge of vitriol coming into their offices. World.title: The documentary we didn’t need? The One About Matthew Perry plays it too safe
World.content:
★ ★ CultureTV & radioReview The documentary we didn’t need? The One About Matthew Perry plays it too safe Kylie Northover October 27, 2026 — 6:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The One About Matthew Perry ★★ When an “authorised” celebrity docuseries boasts exclusive access to private archives and immediate family, we can be confident it’s going to lean towards hagiography, and this three-part series about Matthew Perry does just that. It’s less a deep dive and more a surface skim that provides little insight into the Friends star, who died of a drug overdose in 2023, aged 54. Directed by filmmaker Emmy Award-winner Mary Robertson (whose most recent series include Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV and The Fall of Diddy), The One About Matthew Perry follows the well-worn path of celebrity documentaries that are afraid to offend. While pitched as a “celebration of Perry’s life”, in reality it’s a fawning, straightforward biography that stretches back to his childhood, mostly told by his half-sister Mia Perry Bowick, and two of his longtime mates, David Pressman and Roger Castillo. Perry as Chandler Bing, with Courtney Cox as Monica Geller in Friends. NBCUniversal via Getty Images We get the requisite childhood photos and footage, memories of Pressman, Castillo and others (among them Hank Azaria), but intriguingly, none of his castmates from Friends – Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Lisa Kudrow, David Schwimmer and Matt LeBlanc – take part. Perry’s sister puts this down to it being still too painful and raw for them to publicly revisit his death, but we’ll obviously never know.



By the end of the three-episode series though, it’s hard not to wonder if this is because perhaps they didn’t have only glowing things to say about the late actor. It’s not until past the two-hour mark that a negative thing is uttered, when a former girlfriend reveals Perry had been cheating on her for a year. Related Article Review What to stream this week: Connie Britton’s weird comedy-thriller, plus five more picks For fans of Friends, there is very little of the sitcom that made Perry a star. There’s a telling quote from Perry early on (and which he wrote about in his 2022 memoir, Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing) in which he declares he asked God to “make me famous. You can do anything you want to me; just make me famous”. This invocation obviously came true with the role of Chandler Bing – and the rest of his life. We’re told Perry was “complex” and flawed” but given nothing below those surface descriptions. Even his addiction, we’re told, is caused by the opiates he was prescribed after a jetski accident; it’s not until the final episode that his struggle with depression is mentioned, his reason for using the Ketamine that would end his life.



There is his opiate-induced colon perforation, which almost killed him, his successful addiction advocacy, and a slew of former girlfriends and other talking heads, most of whom tell us that Perry was the comedic genius of his generation. Perry with Mia Perry Bowick, who presents much of the docuseries. Courtesy of Netflix But for fans who have read Perry’s memoir – by all accounts a much less unctuous account of his life – there are not many revelations. Unless you count the fact that his Friends castmates held hands as they walked to his coffin at his funeral, which sounds straight from the hands of the sitcom’s scriptwriters, frankly. But there are some shocking statistics. Perry reportedly spent more than $7 million on 15 stints in rehab throughout the years, 30 years in therapy, and attended some 6000 AA meetings. This series is one for the hardcore fans, but I venture even they might find the three-hour duration at least an hour too long. The One About Matthew Perry is now streaming on Netflix.

Getty Images “Sam has been great around the camp, he trained well on Tuesday. You wouldn’t know what’s happening on the outside with his contract situation. “[As for Dearden], I saw a bit from Tommy in the first game when he came on as a half to replace Mitchell [Moses] and I liked the way he played.



“He was five-eighth last week, he played well and had some good moments, but this week I feel like it was the right time to give him an opportunity at No. 7.” Walters, meanwhile, confirmed he had flirted with the idea of using James Tedesco on the wing after handing the No.1 jersey back to Reece Walsh for Saturday’s clash. Sam Walker and James Tedesco are out of the Australian starting side to play against the Cook Islands. Getty Images Walsh was a standout at fullback against New Zealand, while Tedesco returned serve on Sunday against Fiji when he set up several tries in the Kangaroos’ victory and kept the players calm when it looked like a boilover might be on the cards early in the second half. “I’ve gone back to Reece, it’s for this week,” Walters said. “I thought about trying to find a slot for ‘Teddy’ maybe on the wing, but that would have been an injustice to him.



“He hasn’t played a lot there, and we’ve already got two good wingers here. I didn’t want to change that. He’ll be in the squad, and if required, he’ll play a role off the bench. Teddy is a pretty good guy to have on the bench; just his energy and the way he plays, there’s nobody more competitive than him in the team.” Ethan Strange will be the only debutant for Australia, with the Canberra playmaker named in the No.14 jersey. Hours after making his debut for Australia on Sunday night, Sam Walker’s talks over re-signing with the Roosters broke down. Getty Images Melbourne hooker Harry Grant, one of 11 Kangaroos set to become free agents on Sunday, said his contract situation would not prove a distraction. Grant said more players than usual were prepared to test their value on the market because of the uncertainty around the size of the salary cap when the new broadcast deal kicks in from 2028, and the addition of two clubs in the shape of the Perth Bears and PNG Chiefs.



Penrith back-rower Liam Martin, another Kangaroo yet to sign an extension with his club, said the players were teasing each other about which areas they were looking at on real estate sites. “It’s good to have that banter,” Martin said. “What the group does well is not let it distract us, once we’re training, we’re on and focused on the job at hand, but during downtime, we can have that laugh.” Martin said his preference was to remain at Penrith. “Fingers crossed I can work out a deal and stay,” he said. “I absolutely love being there – it’s still my No. 1 choice to stay.” Walker’s Roosters teammate Salesi Foketi, meanwhile, said he hopes the Tricolours can find a way to keep the star halfback. Up to seven clubs are said to be circling Walker, with the 24-year-old set to become one of the hottest players on the market from Sunday, while the Roosters may even opt to let him go next season if he can find a deal for 2027.



Related Article Rugby League World Cup ‘There was no refund’: Why Ethan Strange was happy to trade Thai villa for Kangaroos camp Foketi on Tuesday said that would be a sad development. “The club’s very good and Sammy’s very good,” Foketi said after Tonga World Cup training in Sydney. “Sammy goes out and competes and that’s just the kind of person he is on and off the field.” Asked if it would be a disaster for the Roosters to lose their premiership-winning half, Foketi replied: “Disaster? Jeez, that’s a big word. “Yeah, honestly, I’m not too sure. I’m just focused on the World Cup at the moment and taking it day by day, as I do,” he said. ”Everyone’s irreplaceable. Everyone plays the game in their own way, everyone’s unique in that way.”

World.title: V’landys subpoenas former NSW minister in bid to unmask his critics
World.content:
NationalNSWDefamation V’landys subpoenas former NSW minister in bid to unmask his critics Chris Barrett Updated October 27, 2026 — 5:38pm ,first published 4:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. NRL boss Peter V’landys has launched an extraordinary bid to uncover what critics of his have said about him privately by having a subpoena served on former NSW government minister Brad Hazzard. The sports administrator is attempting to get his hands on confidential submissions to the so-called Hazzard report into racing as part of his defamation battle against an Australian racing website. Peter V’landys (left) and Brad Hazzard. Jamie Brown A retired former state attorney-general and health minister, Hazzard interviewed dozens of participants in the $3.3 billion racing industry after being commissioned by the Minns government to undertake a review. He has now been brought into V’landys’ bitter legal dispute with racing site The Thoroughbred Report and its owner Vicky Leonard over an article that questioned whether his stewardship of the NRL was distracting him from his long-time job as chief executive of Racing NSW.



The subpoena issued to Hazzard directs him to turn over any communications he had with Leonard and associates of hers about V’landys as well as submissions made to him that mention V’landys. The move could potentially have major ramifications for other government reviews if the names of people who spoke to the former minister are revealed in the court action. Vickey Leonard is defending defamation proceedings brought against her and her website by V’landys. Renee Nowytarger A furious Hazzard is challenging it, as is the state government, who were represented by separate lawyers during a brief appearance in the NSW Supreme Court on Tuesday. Hazzard told this masthead the integrity of his review was based around an expectation that the identities and comments of those who took part would be protected.



“As a former NSW health minister and attorney-general, I agreed to undertake a review of the Thoroughbred Racing Act for the NSW government. At all times, the review process was predicated on those making submissions feeling confident that their submissions would be treated confidentially,” he said. “I expected and believed that the process would be respected by all in the industry and until receipt of the subpoena I believe that is precisely what had happened.” V’landys has transitioned from racing to running the NRL full-time. Oscar Colman V’landys is overseas and declined to comment. V'landys viewed the story in The Thoroughbred Report as a call to arms against him because it included a link at the bottom encouraging readers to have their say on Hazzard’s review.



He claims in the defamation suit that it contained misinformation about the shape of the racing industry under his leadership and wrongly suggested the time he dedicated to running rugby league was taking away from his responsibilities. Leonard herself subpoenaed the Australian Rugby League Commission in pursuit of documents relating to V’landys and also sought access to his medical records, before being forced to abandon those efforts in May. Brad Hazzard was NSW health minister during the COVID-19 pandemic. James Alcock Hazzard was appointed by the government in August last year, three months after the proposed sale of Rosehill Gardens racecourse for housing was voted down, and tendered his report in July. It is yet to be made public.



Hazzard said it was up to the government to decide when to release it but said he was now “concerned that what was a respectful review has been dragged into somebody else’s defamation proceedings”. V’landys’ subpoena to Hazzard does not call for the ex-minister to provide the court with his full report. Jockey Chad Schofield rides Tempted to victory this month in The Everest, the showpiece of Sydney’s spring carnival. Getty Images There has been much speculation within racing about its contents, as well as about who is paying for V’landys’ defamation proceedings, which prominent barrister Sue Chrysanthou SC is fronting for him. Racing Minister David Harris has been asked in parliamentary hearings whether Racing NSW was footing the bill.



“Personally, I don’t know,” Harris said when asked in a hearing in August. Upon further questioning, he added that such issues were matters for the board of Racing NSW, which operates independently of government. Related Article Wests Tigers Court bid launched to blow up Wests Tigers power base The serving of Hazzard with a subpoena comes nearly a year after this masthead revealed that V’landys had become aware of aspects of a confidential meeting between the former minister and members of the NSW Trainers Association. An angry V’landys subsequently turned down an invitation to a barbecue from NSW Trainers Association chairman, businessman and Melbourne Cup-winning owner Richard Pegum, who he put on the board of the NRL-owned PNG Chiefs team. Hazzard said at the time he would never break the trust of those he gathered information from, stressing his independence.



His report could have implications for Racing NSW’s wide-reaching commercial and regulatory powers, which are underpinned by state legislation. V’landys has been on long-service leave from Racing NSW since July, when he stepped in as acting NRL chief executive to replace the departed Andrew Abdo. He will officially leave racing in five weeks after 22 years in charge, having become full-time executive chairman of the Australian Rugby League Commission last month. World.title: Data centres create a people power surge the industry didn’t see coming
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaData centres Editorial Data centres create a people power surge the industry didn’t see coming The Age's View Editorial October 27, 2026 — 5:37pm

October 27, 2026 — 5:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The growth in data centres has become a case study in power: corporate, government and the will of people. The rise of artificial intelligence and the data centres that deliver it have been spectacular, both in financial terms and in its potential to fundamentally change life on this planet. In this new world order, a centuries-old law of science should also be invoked – Newton’s Third Law of Motion: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. This has been clearly demonstrated recently – two companies NextDC and Firmus have been battered in two very different ways. Jemena has been installing enormous poles on Melbourne streets to transfer power to NextDC’s M3 data centre. Joe Armao Firmus’s investors throttled back their enthusiasm for the company’s aspirations, prompting the withdrawal of its plans for a multibillion-dollar listing on the ASX. It was a local symptom of a very global scepticism around the boomtime spruiking of AI companies. NextDC was upended not by traders, not initially anyway, but by people whose lives would be directly affected, and were being affected, by data centre development.



For NextDC, suburban resistance transformed ripples of rebellion on Melbourne nature strips against new power poles into a watershed market moment. A collapse in its share price wiped $3 billion off the company’s valuation, almost halving its market value. Related Article AI AI darling NextDC announces board and pay purge after Melbourne power disaster This, in turn, prompted the stalling of its data centre expansion on 10 hectares at West Footscray. That centre was already a focal point for those who felt the industry was riding roughshod into neighbourhoods. Two results of all this have been a shake-up of the board with chairman Douglas Flynn to stand for re-election at its annual meeting with investors next month but then retire once a replacement is found, and chief executive Craig Scroggie to forfeit millions in bonuses. The power needed for West Footscray meant energy infrastructure company Jemena had to replace standard wooden electricity poles with 15-metre-high concrete ones carrying 66,000 volts in West Footscray and Yarraville. Enter suburban resistance. Jemena has halted putting the power poles up until at least February and NextDC is now looking at alternative routes or even burying the cables. These delays mean dollars. The NextDC data centre sits on five hectares, and was planning to double its footprint, having applied to Planning Minister Sonya Kilkenny under the government’s fast-track Development Facilitation Program. A decision has now been delayed until after next month’s election.



As premier, Jacinta Allan welcomed data centres to Victoria with open arms. The state wanted to attract “as many as we possibly can” and offered a fast-track approach. With little requirement to deal with local communities, companies like NextDC have clearly not done the work necessary to bring those communities with them, failing to extend even basic courtesies to explain what’s happening in their streets. The industry now has too few supporters because it hasn’t cultivated them as it enthusiastically embraced the government’s consultation carveouts. That meant there is little community buy-in, from the inner city, to large projects such as NextDC’s proposal for Geelong or Syncline’s 350-hectare, 2.4-gigawatt development in Plumpton, in Melbourne’s outer north-west. The industry was thus caught very short when the wind changed. A month ago, Premier Ben Carroll announced measures to put a stricter regulatory framework around data centres’ growth in an attempt to lessen the impact on communities.



The centres will be banned from residential areas, a 150-metre buffer zone between a centre and homes will be put into place, and they will need to supply their own electricity and use non-drinking water. Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has yet to announce her party’s views. Many residents, we would proffer to say, would like to know. The shadow attorney-general James Newbury last month noted that residents were “deeply concerned” at data centres being approved in inappropriate areas. “We back communities having their say, keeping their character. No wonder the community is upset about it. Community should be at the centre of decisions.” Perhaps residents also should be concerned that the opposition has not given them a policy on the matter. This pushback has resulted in data centre projects being shelved from Western Australia to NSW and to US states such as Wyoming, where one centre was going to cover almost 500 hectares.



A Resolve poll in The Age this week found 32 per cent of respondents supported data centres in Australia, 33 per cent were opposed and 35 per cent were unsure. However this division into thirds is interpreted, one conclusion cannot be denied. When a people’s amenity will be affected by a development then they must have a say in what is being proposed. We said this a month ago, we say it again now. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

Police on Sydney’s northern beaches are appealing for information after reports of a man trying to lure children into his vehicle.

The first reports came last Thursday after a man approached and attempted to speak with a child at an oval in Manly Vale just before 5pm.

Warnings shared among parents said a man approached a child in the car park at David Thomas Reserve and told the boy his mum and dad had asked him to get into his car to go home. The boy ran back to the field, where his mother was, and the incident was reported to police.
