World.title: Four things to know as Israel’s polls open in defining test for Netanyahu
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastWorld elections Four things to know as Israel’s polls open in defining test for Netanyahu Matthew Knott Updated October 27, 2026 — 5:27pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tel Aviv: Israelis have begun voting in an election widely seen as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s almost two decades in power, with the prospect of a return to war with Iran dominating the final days of the campaign. Voting began early on Tuesday in Israel (4pm AEDT) in the first national elections since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, a day that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil. A television campaign  on a bridge featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, and his main rival, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the election. AP Photo/Oded Balilty Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but the polls have shown a close result between the two blocs, and it may take time before clear results are known. Israeli media reports passed by the official military censor and published in the final days of the campaign have stated that Netanyahu pressured his military chief to provoke a confrontation with Iran ahead of the elections, suggesting high-level leaks from within the defence establishment. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz denied the reports.



US President Donald Trump told Fox News on the weekend he was deciding whether to “make a deal” with Iran or “finish it off”, adding: “It’s getting to be decision time.” Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict These voters could hold the key to Netanyahu’s demise. Why are they being shunned? Netanyahu posted an alarming AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv and spoke about using cryptocurrency to avoid international sanctions in the final days of the campaign. Some disunity broke out within the opposition bloc before polls closed over the question of whether anti-Netanyahu voters should vote for former military chief Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party or spread their votes among the four parties in the bloc. Eisenkot has been pursuing a so-called “big party” strategy in recent days, designed to give him the upper-hand in post-election negotiations by scoring a lead over Netanyahu’s Likud in the final seat tally.



“The ‘big party’ campaign is a mistake,” Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats party, said. “It’s a dangerous lie designed to weaken us. I urge people not to fall for the ‘big party’ narrative.” What happens on election day? Benjamin Netanyahu took to social media to post an apocalyptic AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb being dropped in the middle of Tel Aviv. Voting in Israel is voluntary, not compulsory. Even so, turnout is usually high, reflecting the level of political engagement in society. In the last elections, 4.8 million of the country’s 6.8 million eligible voters showed up at the polls – a turnout rate of 71 per cent. Even more people are expected to vote this year, reflecting the heightened stakes. Unlike in Australia, where postal voting has become increasingly popular in recent elections, Israelis must vote in person on election day. (Only those serving their nation overseas, like diplomats and defence personnel, can vote in advance by mail.)



When will we know who won? It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear. The first strong indication of the results will come at 10pm (6am Wednesday AEDT), when Israeli TV channels begin airing exit polls. The official election results will then start coming in. A clear picture may emerge quickly, but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer.



The final tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4. Why is it so complicated? Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be ​held every four years, but early elections have been frequent. Crucially, voters vote for party lists rather than individual candidates. The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25 per cent of the national vote to secure seats.



About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time. The key number to aim for is the 61 seats required to form a government, though leaders prefer a more substantial buffer to create a more durable coalition. It is possible to govern in minority, but such a government would be even more fragile. What happens after the results are published? After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government.



That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘It is ours’: The far-right Israeli settlers who want to build homes in Gaza No single party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, so governments are formed by a coalition ​of parties, and negotiations on forming a government often take weeks. Every Knesset seat counts, and small parties can have a big impact by becoming kingmakers. If the nominee fails, others can get a chance to try. If no government emerges, another election is called, with the present cabinet staying on as a caretaker government. Read more on Israel’s election:

World.title: One is the race that stops a nation. The other will make you an instant $30 million
World.content:
SportRacingMelbourne Cup One is the race that stops a nation. The other will make you an instant $30 million Danny Russell October 27, 2026 — 5:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Chris Waller has an uncanny way of putting things into perspective when it comes to summarising two of the biggest races of Melbourne Cup week. The winner of one, he says, will become a household name. James McDonald riding St Gotthard and Jye McNeil aboard Steel Will at Flemington trackwork on Tuesday morning. Getty Images The winner of the other will be worth a lot more money. The champion trainer was talking, of course, about a sprint and a staying test – the $2 million group 1 Coolmore Stud Stakes (over 1200 metres) for three-year-olds on Saturday, compared to the $10.2 million Melbourne Cup (3200m) three days later.



Waller has runners in both. Related Article Melbourne Cup First look at the Melbourne Cup form – we rate the top 24 horses “The horse that wins the Coolmore on Saturday is probably going to be the most lucrative or expensive horse at the end of the carnival,” Waller said on Tuesday. “So, a Melbourne Cup winner – everybody wants it. They become a household name. “But in terms of a stallion or a filly, it passes that value on to the siblings, and if you’re a stallion, you can cover mares, and obviously that turns into a very lucrative scenario as well.



“The winner of the Coolmore will be worth upwards of $30 million.” Waller speaking to the media at Flemington earlier this month. Getty Images Waller has long understood the value of winning Saturday’s stallion-making race – a 1200m dash down the Flemington Straight on Derby Day. He has snared six of the past 13 editions. On Saturday, he could make it seven in what is shaping as a family affair. The race’s third favourite, St Gotthard, to be ridden by James McDonald, is a full brother to Waller’s 2024 winner Switzerland – both are by super sire Snitzel out of mare Ms Bad Behaviour.



“He’s the younger sibling who is ready to make a name for himself,” the Sydney trainer said. Related Article Spring racing carnival Record-breaking trainer’s warning for punters on Melbourne Cup favourite Waller’s other runner, longshot Steel Will, shares the same mother as his 2020 winning filly September Run. Steel Will is by I Am Invincible, out of Pittsburgh Flyer, while September Run is by Exceed And Excel, and also out of Pittsburgh Flyer. “That’s probably something quite unique. Hopefully, they’ve got the genetics and can quinella the race,” Waller said of his two runners. There are heightened expectations that come with racing an expensive colt such as St Gotthard, which was bought for $2.7 million by world-renowned breeding and racing operation Coolmore at the Inglis Easter Yearling Sales in April last year. But Waller has been there before.



Chris Waller keeping a keen eye on his horses at Flemington. Getty Images “You learn not to worry about price tags and not to worry about the pressure of it,” Waller said. “I guess it’s like a footy coach – once you’ve been to a couple of grand finals, or been in the final season a few years in a row, it does help. “We’ve also got a great team that have been with me for a long time. The horses, they all get looked after the same, regardless of the price tags.” Waller might have dominated the Coolmore Stud Stakes in recent years, but the Melbourne Cup has been a different story.



A renowned trainer of sprinters and middle distance horses, his sole winner was Verry Elleegant in 2021. He is unlikely to add to that tally this year. “It wouldn’t be our strongest year,” he said. Asterix, part-owned by Kiwi cricket great Mark Greatbatch, is an outsider, while Soul Of Spain ran second in the Sydney Cup before an eighth in the Caulfield Cup. Perhaps his best chances are still to make the cut-off. Gai Waterhouse (right) with Francesca Cumani at the launch of the Melbourne Cup carnival on Monday. Wayne Taylor



Up-and-coming stayer Pinhole needs at least four horses to withdraw before next Tuesday to gain a start, while 2023 runner-up Soulcombe – owned by a group of premiership Tigers including Tom Lynch – needs to finish in the top three in Wednesday’s Bendigo Cup to pass the ballot clause. Hall-of-fame trainer Gai Waterhouse will also be sweating on the Bendigo Cup result – she needs The Euphrates to win to be assured a Melbourne Cup start. “He was off the scene for two years, so this is a big step for him,” she said. “Tomorrow is a vital race for him, and if he can run really well or win it, then we are in.” Waterhouse and her co-trainer Adrian Bott are guaranteed at least one Cup runner.



Vauban is lining up for his fourth start in the race that stops the nation, having previously finished 14th, 11th and sixth. They took over training the Irish import from Willie Mullins at the end of 2024. “I love this gelding, I really do,” Waterhouse said. “He’ll be going in with only one run under his belt, which is a bit unorthodox. But, you know, why not roll the dice a different way?” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Albanese confirms bolstered security for MPs after Haines attack
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack Albanese confirms bolstered security for MPs after Haines attack Natassia Chrysanthos and Paul Sakkal Updated October 27, 2026 — 5:24pm ,first published 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Politicians will receive a security boost that could include a wider use of emergency alarms in their offices, as the government treats last week’s attack on independent Helen Haines as a turning point for MPs’ safety. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese told the Labor caucus on Tuesday morning that the government would speed up an existing security review that had been due to report next year. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen “Last week was a turning point, and people have been putting up with this growing threat environment for too long,” he told his MPs. “More can and should be done. I understand you want to feel safe when you’re in the community and have better security at your office and your home. There are a series of options you have raised including duress alarms, and we are looking at all of it.”



MPs of all stripes attended briefings with intelligence agencies following the attack on Haines. Many aired their ongoing frustrations about how long it took for their security requests to be actioned, and several MPs also made requests about duress alarms. Related Article Workplace culture ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud This masthead revealed last week that the government was examining a major round of security upgrades for MPs’ homes, as well as swifter upgrades for offices and more proactive threat assessments from the AFP. Albanese said the government had already taken steps recently to step up resourcing for politicians’ safety and the Australian Federal Police, but recognised more could be done. He has asked for the security review recommendations to be fast-tracked, and requested Special Minister of State Don Farrell, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke work together on delivering a “swift government response”.



“I know so many of you have experienced an increase in aggressive and threatening behaviour online and in person. There have been vile threats towards you and your family and damage to your electorate offices,” Albanese said. Related Article Haines attack The cardboard cockatoo, the empty seat and a parliament’s reckoning with rage “This is particularly acute for women members of the caucus, who often receive vile and misogynistic threats to their safety and increased hatred online, often of a violent and sexual nature. “I know how hard every single one of you works each day to ensure that we are accessible to our community and that people can speak to us... We need to do more to combat these threats.” Last week’s four-wheel-drive attack on the independent MP has exposed long-running tensions between federal parliamentarians and the authorities responsible for protecting them.



Elected officials claim security agencies are too reactive and need to modernise their communication with MPs to ensure politicians and their staff feel safe. But authorities have also expressed frustration with MPs who fail to follow protocol when flagging high-risk events or reporting incidents. Opposition leader Angus Taylor also addressed the security concerns of MPs in a joint party room meeting of Coalition MPs on Tuesday morning, saying it was important to “get that right”. On Monday evening independent senator Fatima Payman stunned a parliamentary hearing by asking whether Albanese was waiting for a Haines-style attack against her to provide her with comparable staffing levels to other senators. Payman refused to withdraw her comments unless provided additional staff. Payman has long petitioned the prime minister for additional staffing, and was one of four independent and crossbench MPs to tell this masthead their staff were suffering under a deluge of vitriol coming into their offices. More from our Helen Haines coverage

World.title: Stalled opening of Waitākere Hospital intensive care unit a 'smack in the face' for community, leader says
World.content:
The stalled opening of Waitākere Hospital's long awaited intensive care unit is a "smack in the face" for the community, a West Auckland leader says.

Waitākere Hospital's brand new six bed unit is fully equipped and had originally been due to open by the end of the year.

It was part of the new Manaaki Hōhonu building that opened last month, but the ICU was sitting empty with no operating budget, no staff and no opening date.

Audio player for " Waitakare Hospital's new ICU unit sitting empty with no staff " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2194530%2Fstalled-opening-of-waitakere-hospital-intensive-care-unit-a-smack-in-the-face-for-community-leader-says

Waitakare Hospital's new ICU unit sitting empty with no staff Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Waitākere Ranges local board chairperson Mark Allen said the current default ICU for the areas is North Shore Hospital which can take 90 minutes to get to for some people in the areas he represents.

It had long been acknowledged more health services - including the ICU - were needed in the west, he said.

"Then to find it's not being resourced is like a smack in the face," he said.

"It takes years, I know, to plan these things but I just don't understand how we couldn't have had the staffing and the operating system decided before [the building] was opened."

Auckland Council's Waitākere ward councillor Shane Henderson said the situation was a disgrace and a lot of people in the community were angry.

Councillor Shane Henderson. (File photo) Facebook / Shane Henderson

"We've been slammed for so long but now we're feeling let down and we feel like we're getting the raw end of the stick again and we're being sent half way across the city for treatment when we shouldn't be," he said.

West Auckland resident and former pro wakeboarder Brad Smeele was a regular user of the health system as someone with C4 quadraplegia.

Being close to a hospital could make a big difference to whether patients could easily get support from those who cared about them, he said.

"I spent five weeks in an ICU after my accident and I know the importance of not only quality care but also the added comforts that allow family members to be able to stay and to really be able to support someone in a tough situation," he said.

That support can help seriously ill people survive, he said.

Last year, Smeele advocated online for West Foundation's fundraising drive for the ICU, particularly for family services, and said he was disappointed its opening was delayed.

Brad Smeele on a hike with friends. (File photo) Brad Smeele

Health NZ's operations director for Waitematā Brad Healey said the plan had always been to open the new Waitākere development in stages.

"This includes the intensive care service, which requires a specialist workforce and clinical arrangements to be in place before it can safely open," he said.

Health NZ's infrastructure plan does note that the services will open in stages, with the intensive care unit last, however it has previously said the ICU would be open by the end of this year.

An earlier 2024 official document had estimated April 2026.

Healey said the details of how the unit would be run were still being worked out - until that happened an operating budget could not be set and all the staff needed could not be hired.

It was important to get it right for a service where safety was so important, he said.

Health NZ was recruiting only for a clinical lead for the ICU - a one year, part time contract.

World.title: Rightful homes for more than 200 stolen garden gnomes sought by police
World.content:
The owners of more than 200 stolen garden gnomes and other ornaments are being sought by police after being found during a search warrant.

Wairarapa police said the gnomes had been stolen from the Wairarapa region in the past six to 12 months.

The ornaments were discovered during a search warrant at a home in Masterton on 17 October.

The extensive collection was found at a Masterton home. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

The haul also included bird baths, outdoor furniture, a gazebo, trollies, windmills, solar lights, children's wheelbarrows, metal birds, pot plants, statues, sculptures, a concrete giraffe and even a few buddha, police said.

The ornaments were at the Masterton Police Station, Sergeant Nick Bunny said.

"We'd really like people to check their gardens and outdoor areas, and if they are missing anything, they should pop into the station with their identification, and we'll work with them to identify items.

"We're hoping the public can help us get them gnome sweet gnome."

World.title: Injured Kiwis left to 'fall off the cliff' as approval of ACC claims becomes harder
World.content:
Audio player for " Lawyer questions ACC's approach to investigating claims " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2193578%2Finjured-kiwis-left-to-fall-off-the-cliff-as-approval-of-acc-claims-becomes-harder

Lawyer questions ACC's approach to investigating claims Morning Report Download MP3 7m

A Wellington lawyer is worried it's becoming harder to get ACC claims approved.

Hazel Armstrong, who has represented ACC claimants for nearly 30 years, told Morning Report the requirements to get compensation and treatment costs paid were already tough.

She said GPs were facing increasing pressure and had less time to help their patients meet the increasingly rigourous requirements.

It follows comments by general practitioner Dr Rachelle Pound last week who said a recent request by ACC for decades worth of patient notes was taking up valuable appointment time.

"We've had a request come in for 40 years of mental health notes for a patient in their 40s. That means 40 years of notes will need to be read through, redacted, all the relevant information removed and then sent back through to ACC."

Audio player for " ACC requests for historic patient notes add to GP workload " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2193578%2Finjured-kiwis-left-to-fall-off-the-cliff-as-approval-of-acc-claims-becomes-harder

ACC requests for historic patient notes add to GP workload Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Pound said it left more questions as to what was happening to their information at the other end.

Armstrong told Morning Report complex claims like those for mental injury and work-related gradual injury were particularly difficult to prove, especially without fulsome GP notes.

While she agreed with Pound's perspective on the problem, she said claimants were squeezed, too.

"ACC is a big machine and in my view, it's getting tougher and tougher for claimants to get claims accepted - particularly if they're complex claims, which is what the GP that you interviewed is suggesting - it would've been a sensitive claim, probably, or a mental injury claim that's complex and those claims and work-related graduate process claims are very difficult to prove and the GP doesn't have the time to back their patient now.

"In the past, you could form quite good relationships with your GP and they would back you, but now they're under pressure and they don't."

The exterior of the ACC Building in Auckland. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Armstrong claimed ACC was very political and used rejecting people's claims as a way to cost costs.

She claimed they "don't care" what happens to the injured person once they are out of the scheme and lets them "fall off the cliff".

The injured person is "up against it" and most don't have representation and don't know what to do, she said.

ACC declined to speak on Morning Report on Tuesday. However, in a statement, ACC head of service operations Phil Riley said ACC's focus is on helping injured New Zealanders get the right support at the right time so they can return to work and independence.

"We are strengthening how we commission services and work with the health sector so people can access effective rehabilitation sooner," he said.

Riley said ACC is an entitlement-based scheme established in law and that they "do not delay individual entitlement decisions to manage budgets, and entitlements are not subject to funding caps, targets or annual quotas".

Decisions are based on a client's covered injury, individual circumstances and the Accident Compensation Act 2001, he said.

"Ninety-nine percent of new claims were accepted, with 65 percent accepted within one minute and 88 percent accepted within 24 hours."

In a statement on Friday, the Royal NZ College of GPs said it had raised concerns on multiple occasions about the time demands being placed on GPs.

"ACC has given assurance that they are working to improve the process with regards to requests such as these. GPs are encouraged to advise ACC and get sign-off for payment to be authorised beforehand for work that will take the GP more than an hour to complete."

On Friday, ACC also said in a statement: "Access to relevant medical information is an important part of making timely and appropriate decisions about a client's cover and entitlements.

"We know the GP workforce is under pressure, and we acknowledge it can take time to collate these notes, especially when a client has a complex injury or is seeking backdated support. We are conscious of only asking for information that is required to make these decisions and the level of information required will depend on an individual client's circumstances, including the nature and complexity of their claim. ACC does fund GPs for the time it takes them to provide us with medical notes."

ACC said it has been working to improve its processes to ensure it only requests the information it needs.

World.title: NZ First announces $4b 'Commonsense Express' plan for rail
World.content:
New Zealand First has announced a 10-point rail policy, building on its commitment to trial commuter rail in Canterbury and bring back the Southerner Train as well as commitments from the coalition already underway.

Making the announcement at a public meeting in Levin, Winston Peters says his party is the "Commonsense Express" and had always backed rail.

"Unlike the other parties that sold it off, ran it down, or talked about it without delivering, we have the track record to prove it."

He said New Zealand First would continue to deliver the goods for rail by maintaining and improving the national network, removing bottlenecks, strengthening regional connections, and putting existing rail assets to better use.

The party outlined 10 points, including some commitments that have already been announced or are underway, with a cost for each. The total cost would be nearly $4 billion, but some of that has already been allocated.

The policy commits New Zealand First to delivering the $1.35 billion Rail Network Investment Programme announced earlier this year, building the Marsden Point Rail Link, and introducing the two new Cook Strait ferries, Kupe and Cook, in 2029.

The 10 points are to:

Deliver the $1.135 billion Rail Network Investment Programme. Cost: already fully funded and reflected in the PREFU.

Build the Marsden Point Rail Link.Cost: The $410 million already allocated will support delivery and is already reflected in the PREFU, with the remaining funding determined following the current KiwiRail competitive design and tender process involving Acciona, Downer/HEB, and Martinus Rail which will result in a firm construction price substantially below KiwiRail's previous $1.1 billion estimate.

Unlock capacity through the Kaimai Tunnel. Cost: Less than $100 million, primarily for additional passing loops.

Establish Auckland Rail and Wellington Rail as companies co-owned by taxpayers and ratepayers, bringing metropolitan rail infrastructure and passenger trains under clear, accountable ownership that responds to taxpayers and ratepayers. Cost: $5 million establishment and transition costs.

Make Te Huia permanent. Cost: $130 million from capital allowance to purchase new trains, Government's operating co-funding from the National Land Transport Fund.

Back permanent passenger rail in Christchurch. Cost: $4 million per annum for Government's operating co-funding for commuter rail, low millions in commercial finance deal to procure new locomotives for Mainlander.

Continue removing dangerous level crossings. Cost: national level crossing upgrades included in the Rail Network Investment Programme, $300 million fund from the capital allowance to progress the next three-year stage of level crossing removals in Auckland and Kapiti.

Deliver the new Cook Strait ferries. Cost: $1.7 billion upper limit already fully funded and reflected in the PREFU.

Plan Auckland's third and fourth main lines and protect the Avondale-Southdown rail corridor. Cost: $50 million to progress engineering planning, with bulk of funding allocated to land acquisitions.

Protect heritage rail. Cost: $500,000 per annum already allocated and reflected in the PREFU.

World.title: New central Hamilton station and hourly trains to Auckland in Te Huia revamp proposal
World.content:
A new central Hamilton railway station and hourly trains to Auckland are focal in a plan proposed to revamp inter-regional passenger train service Te Huia.

A new Waikato Regional Council report proposes a major overhaul of the passenger rail service over time, including new stations, new trains and a new central Hamilton terminus.

But the preferred option comes with a price tag of more than half a billion.

The preferred plan boasts a new above-ground terminus in central Hamilton, new stations at Ngāruawāhia, Te Kauwhata, Pōkeno, and Tūākau, new battery-electric trains, and eventually hourly trains to Auckland.

Over 60 years, the local share of capital and operating costs was estimated to $31.5 million per annum.

The report said the central Hamilton station would sit between Seddon Rd and Tristram St and was a critical part of the plan.

It would replace Frankton as the Hamilton terminus, and would improve access to employment, education, civic, retail and leisure destinations and provide a stronger interchange with Hamilton's bus, walking, and cycling networks.

Passengers would have to wait until 2033 or 2035 for the hourly service to Auckland, depending on how quickly the new trains could be acquired.

Hamilton's mayor Tim Macindoe said while the city council did not have a position at this stage, it would like to see Auckland Council contributing, and the government assistance rate maintained and not reduced as proposed.

"I support a range of transport options as Hamilton continues to grow, but any expansion needs to be matched by appropriate government funding. Local ratepayers should not be expected to shoulder the full cost."

With that being said, Macindoe said it would be fantastic to see a central transport hub or railway station in Hamilton.

"A well-located central station could help improve connectivity, support public transport use, reduce congestion, and make it easier for people to access the city centre.

"It would also support economic growth, encourage investment and development around the station precinct, and provide a gateway to our city for visitors and commuters alike."

Waikato District mayor Aksel Bech said it was a wishlist, but its things they actually wished for.

"To take the trial service to something that's actually more meaningful as a commuter rail, is quite exciting. It's a long time frame for it to fully stand up and it requires political support in terms of whoever forms a new government and so on, but it would materially influence or improve access in the north of the Waikato."

He said they had land sitting there already in Ngāruawāhia, Te Kauwhata, Pōkeno, and Tūākau in anticipation of future railway stations and this made that dream potentially real.

Waikato District mayor Aksel Bech. Supplied

He admitted the price tag was steep and said there would always be people who said it's too much and they should do something else.

"But my challenge is what else can you do. With more frequency on the rail you've got the real opportunity to provide an alternate means of public transport that just isn't there."

Another lane on the motorway wasn't a real solution, he said, but getting hundreds of cars off the road in favour of rail was.

Bech said Waikato's northern communities look north for healthcare, education, entertainment, etc. and right now they saw a train going past without stopping "and it's frustrating".

Waikato Regional Councillor Noel Smith said he was worried about how unrealistic the wishlist was.

"In a few weeks I'm going to be getting on a plane and landing in the middle of Sydney and then getting on a train and then getting on a bus and arriving within 100 metres of my destination. Wouldn't it be wonderful to have that situation in the Waikato?"

But he said it was a matter of who would pay for it.

Regional councillor Chris Hughes said the price tag was huge and would increase the burden on Hamilton City ratepayers by 700 percent.

"Honestly, this will not fly. It is stupid. We shouldn't be wasting money on it."

He said the train was already running at under 50 per cent occupation.

"I just cannot see any way you're going to increase the demand and it's currently running an hourly service in dreamland."

Te Huia has operated between Hamilton and Auckland since April 2021, for a five-year trial which was due to end in June 2026. It was then extended until the end of June 2027 with government funding at a 60 percent.

This proposal was an end of trial requirement ahead of consideration of permanent funding.

The report said no decisions had been made and regional councilors were not being asked to approve a permanent service yet.

World.title: Gap narrows between National and Labour in new poll
World.content:
The two major parties have narrowed the gap between them, with National dropping to 29 points and Labour remaining the same on 27 percent.

That's according to the latest 1News-Verian poll which has seen National topple from its result last week, 32 points.

The Green Party is down one point to 15 and Te Pāti Māori is down to 0.1 points - their lowest ever result on the poll. However, they are pursuing a candidate-only campaign.

The coalition partners are both up: ACT is up one point to 12 and New Zealand First is up two points to 10.

Opportunity has fallen slightly to six points, down one point.

On these numbers Labour would have 33 seats, the Greens 18, Te Pāti Māori would have four and Te Tai Tokerau Party would have one.

That's a total of 56.

Meanwhile National would have 34, ACT 15 and New Zealand First would pick up 12 seats - a total of 61.

Opportunity would have eight seats and remains the power broker between the right and left blocs.

Last week, the poll had National on 32, Labour on 27, the Greens on 16, ACT on 11, New Zealand First on eight percent and Te Pāti Māori on 0.7 percent - but they are running a candidate vote campaign.

An overhang on either side could add extra seats in Parliament and alter the results.

On the preferred prime minister rankings, Christopher Luxon is on 24 percent - up four points - while Chris Hipkins sits on 18, up one.

World.title: Sensible Sentencing Trust removes images of politicians from attack advertisement
World.content:
The Sensible Sentencing Trust says it has removed images of Chris Hipkins, Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson from an attack , but not the message.

The lobby group launched election attack ads featuring the party leaders alongside the text "BACKING THE GANGS", above the Greens' campaign slogan "for all of us".

Speaking to RNZ's Checkpoint programme, the trust's national director Louise Parsons said their images had been removed.

Audio player for " Greens lodge complaint over 'Backing the Gangs' billboard " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2192780%2Fsensible-sentencing-trust-removes-images-of-politicians-from-attack-

Greens lodge complaint over 'Backing the Gangs' billboard Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

"Apparently that seems to be an issue for Chlöe, which I think is a bit of a double standard because their images are all over the place and associated with gang members," she said.

"Are they saying that they don't back the gangs? Because the way we see it, and the reason we've responded, is from their actions, not our actions."

Asked if the ad could potentially confuse people into thinking it was a legitimate party campaign ad, Parsons said it was "satire".

The Greens accused the SST of being a Taxpayers' Union "astroturf group" - a fake grassroots organisation supporting the same cause.

Parsons denied that, but told Checkpoint the two organisations worked together for media campaigns.

"We're not Taxpayers Union. We don't campaign for their things that they do, and they don't campaign for things that we do."

The billboard ads were created by the Campaign Company, owned by Taxpayers' Union boss Jordan Williams. The SST and the Taxpayers' Union also run a shared website called 'We can't afford Labour'.

Swarbrick said those behind the ads knew they were mis-representing the Green Party - and things crossed a serious line when it turned into impersonation the SST knew can confuse voters.

The party complained to the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA).

Swarbrick said they were pleased the digital billboard company had suspended their advertising for the time being.

Parsons said she still wanted to see the Green Party meet with victims of gang violence.

The ads follow the saga involving Labour, Greens and Te Pāti Māori candidates campaigning with gang members.

World.title: 'He's dead': Teen's boast before filming bloody video following stabbing of Kaea Karauria
World.content:
"He's dead. We stabbed him because we're Bay dogs."

The Crown says those words rang out about 3am on May 11 last year when people involved in a fatal attack on 15-year-old Napier teen Kaea Karauria were asked what happened.

One of the attackers, also 15 at the time, is now facing trial for Kaea's murder.

After Kaea was attacked the teen recorded a 10-second video of his bloodied right hand and the 7 centimetre blade the teen stabbed him with.

The Crown alleges the teen, who has significant intellectual impairments, is guilty of murder.

It said Kaea was attacked because of a minor incident at a party a few weeks earlier, and because of the mistaken belief he was associated with Black Power, the High Court at Palmerston North heard on Tuesday.

Kaea Karauria in his school uniform. Supplied

Dog is a term for Mongrel Mob gang members and the teen on trial, whose name is suppressed, has Mob insignia tattooed across his face. That wasn't there in May 2025.

The defence acknowledges the teen stabbed Kaea, but say he's guilty of manslaughter.

Attack over 'trivial incident' - Crown

Crown prosecutor Steve Manning said Kaea's night began when he attended the 16th birthday party of a rugby mate in Maraenui.

Crown prosecutor Stephen Manning says the teen is guilty of murder. JIMMY ELLINGHAM / RNZ

Kaea, a sporty Napier Boys' High School student, was dropped off and picked up by friends' parents.

"That should have been the end of the night. Kaea, however, wanted to return to the party later in the night because his girl friend was there," Manning said.

When he and a mate made it back, the party had been shut down not long after the teen on trial and his associates had shown up.

A large group then decided to go to a party in Onekawa. Kaea and the teen may have made contact there, but otherwise were unknown to each other.

When they arrived at the Dinwiddie Ave property, Kaea and a friend never went inside, instead sitting on a low concrete wall outside.

One of the teen's mates, however, saw red and decided to attack Kaea over a minor incident at a party a few weeks before, when there might have been accidental contact between Kaea and a girl.

Manning said while the Crown didn't need to prove motive, the attack began over something trivial.

Running for his life

Kaea Karauria died in Onekawa. Supplied

The Crown alleges five people attacked Kaea on Dinwiddie Ave and there the teen on trial stabbed him in the neck, severing an artery. The defence doesn't dispute this.

"No doubt fearing for his life Kaea then took off, ran up the street, over a fence, into a another property," Manning said.

As blood spurted from his wound Kaea cleared a couple more fences before ending up in the yard of a house on Alexander Ave, about 100 metres away from where he was stabbed.

"Come here you f...... n..... Get him, dog. Get him, dog," the Crown says the attackers yelled as they egged each other on. The n-word is a Mob name for Black Power members or associates.

Manning said the group followed Kaea and found him lying on his back. He was set upon again, and the teen again stabbed him. The defence disputes this.

The attackers returned to Dinwiddie Ave, where they boasted about what they'd done and the teen recorded his bloody video.

"They've left Kaea ostensibly bleeding to death on the grass in front of this random house...," Manning said.

Kaea was found crying in pain by one of his friends. By the time emergency services turned up he was dead.

Manning said it was agreed that as a 15-year-old, the teen would have had less self-control and would more impulsive and likely to act recklessly.

On top of that, the teen's IQ of 70 put him in the bottom 2 percent of the population and showed he had an even lower chance of controlling his behaviour or impulses.

Death devastating, but not murder - defence

Defence lawyer Tim Braithwaite acknowledged the profound loss for Kaea's family.

Defence lawyer Tim Braithwaite acknowledges Kaea Karauria's death is devastating. JIMMY ELLINGHAM / RNZ

"You'll not hear me suggest that his death was anything other than devastating. You will not hear me suggest on behalf of [the teen] that he was not the one who caused this devastation."

However, Braithwaite said the Crown could not prove that the teen acted with murderous intent nor that he should have known his reckless actions could have caused death.

Most people would understand that brandishing a knife could result in serious harm, but the teen did not due to his significant impairment.

The teen didn't view the world like an average 15-year-old and instead had the functioning age of a 7-year-old. He had prenatal alcohol exposure, which is caused by a mother drinking when pregnant.

"His world is smaller, simpler and often confusing. [The teen] has a significantly reduced capacity in rapidly evolving situations," Braithwaite said.

"[The teen] did not intend death and he did not think that death was likely."

The defence disputed that Kaea was attacked twice and said evidence for the second attack, on Alexander Avenue, came from an unreliable witness.

The attackers chased Kaea, but never saw him again after the brief initial encounter.

Braithwaite said the teen was taking responsibility for stabbing Kaea. The defence lawyer said the jury should find the teen guilty of manslaughter.

Two others have pleaded guilty to Kaea's manslaughter, and two others faced charges of injuring with intent in the Youth Court.

World.title: AFL abandons Opening Round for season 2027
World.content:
The AFL has abandoned the Opening Round fixture from the past two seasons, with all 18 clubs now set to play in Round One in 2027.

The previous seasons saw the four teams based in New South Wales and Queensland play home games, while this year's draw also included one game at the MCG.

The split fixture meant each of the teams that played in the Opening Round — also referred to as round zero — subsequently had an early season bye.

Marcus Bontempelli of the Bulldogs during Opening Round in 2026 in Brisbane. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Critics say the fixturing caused distortions in the draw, giving an advantage to the teams that played in Opening Round.

"We have listened to feedback and are pleased to be able to deliver a Round One for all our 18 clubs and fans as we bring back a traditional nine-game opening weekend across the country," AFL chief Andrew Dillon said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon announced the codes in-principle agreement to a new Illicit Drugs Policy in March. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Former premiership coach with West Coast and Collingwood and now ABC analyst, Mick Malthouse, said Opening Round compromised the fixture.

"We don't need it and it's a blessing now that we don't have it," he told ABC Sport.

"Let me say that 'zero round' was appropriately named.

"It had zero impact on the public; in fact, I'll go in the reverse and say it had a completely negative impact."

Malthouse said the early season byes caused by the Opening Round meant the ladder was not meaningful until all teams had played the same number of games, which in the season just passed did not happen until the end of Round 4.

"All round zero did was compromise the ability of sides to be ready for the next game," Malthouse said.

Mick Malthouse said Opening Round compromised the AFL draw. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

"If you've got a game tucked under your belt, you're ready; you're miles in front of the next side.

"And don't worry about the results of those games; it's more important about the long-term effect on players.

The president of the AFL Fans' Association, Ron Issko, welcomed the move to reinstate a full Round One.

"Credit to the AFL for listening," he told ABC Sport.

"When you start a season after waiting six months for the season to start and not all teams are playing, it's sort of like a soft launch.

"It just didn't have that energy.

"We're a national competition and what's better than having all teams playing on Round One."

The AFL's move to highlight games in NSW and Queensland was seen as a response to the National Rugby League's move to stage that competition's opening games in Las Vegas.

Opening Round was seen as a response to the NRL starting its season in Las Vegas, in the United States. (AAP: Supplied/NRL Photos)

"We've looked over the border and so seeing that there's games played in Las Vegas, [said] 'Wow, if that's the way they operate, let us do something similar,'" Malthouse said.

"Forget about what's happening over the border and in fact embrace what's over the border and applaud them," he said.

Round One of the 2027 season will be played from March 17-21, with matches in NSW, Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria.

Hawthorn will play triple-premiers Brisbane in Round One of the 2027 AFL season. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

It has been delayed one week from the usual season start time by the test cricket 150th anniversary match between Australia and England at the MCG.

The season will kick off with a match between the Sydney Swans and Geelong at the SCG on Wednesday, March 17.

The following night, losing grand finalist Fremantle will play the Western Bulldogs at home.

Three-time reigning premiers Brisbane will play on the Friday night against Hawthorn at the MCG.
